Chart Capability What to do Stable Capable Monitor Stable Not capable Reduce variation, recenter, or redesign the process Unstable Looks capable Fix special causes first; the indices cannot be trusted Unstable Not capable Stabilize first
Capability indices computed on an unstable process are not valid; the correct first step is addressing special causes
Capability indices computed on an unstable process are not valid . The correct first step is to find and remove the special causes.
Reference-sheet formulas: Cp = (USL − LSL) / 6s; Z_upper = (USL − X̄)/s; Z_lower = (X̄ − LSL)/s; Cpk = min(Z_upper/3, Z_lower/3). The sheet uses the sample standard deviation s throughout.
The exam reference sheet gives: Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6s Z(upper) = (USL − X̄) ÷ s and Z(lower) = (X̄ − LSL) ÷ s Cpk = min(Z(upper) ÷ 3, Z(lower) ÷ 3) It uses the sample standard deviation s throughout.
Cpk from attribute data: Cpk = (1.5 + Z of the proportion good) / 3, with Z read from the Z table

The reference sheet gives Cpk = (1.5 + Z of the proportion good) ÷ 3 , with Z read from the Z table. Example: yield 99.379% gives Z = 2.5, so Cpk = 4.0 ÷ 3 = 1.33 . Yield 93.32% gives Z = 1.5, so Cpk = 1.00 .
Confidence interval for Cpk: Cpk ± Z(α/2) × √[1/(9n) + Cpk²/(2n − 2)]. The same square root is the standard error of Cpk.

Cpk ± Z(α/2) × √[ 1 ÷ (9n) + Cpk² ÷ (2n − 2) ]. The same square root is the standard error of Cpk. Example: Cpk = 1.33, n = 50, 95% confidence. Square root = √(0.00222 + 1.7689 ÷ 98) = √0.02027 = 0.142. Margin = 1.96 × 0.142 = 0.28. Interval = 1.05 to 1.61 . Because it includes values below 1.33, you cannot claim 4σ capability with confidence at this sample size.
A stable process has only common-cause variation: the natural, built-in noise. It is predictable , so you can say what it will do tomorrow.
Special-cause (assignable) variation comes from a specific, unusual event: a tool breaks, a new supplier lot arrives, an operator skips a step. It makes the process unpredictable.
Tampering/over-adjustment on common-cause noise increases variation (Deming funnel)

Reacting to every small deviation as if it were a special cause makes the process worse . Deming's funnel experiment shows this: adjusting after each result increases variation. Leave common-cause noise alone and change the system instead. Example: an operator re-tunes the machine after every part that misses target by a hair. The result is more variation, not less.

Short-term (within-subgroup) variation: the noise inside a small group sampled close together. Long-term (between-subgroup) variation: the noise plus drift and shifts over time. A stable process has long-term variation close to short-term variation.
Stability must be established before capability means anything
Stability must be established before capability means anything. Capability describes what a stable process can deliver.
Stable but incapable versus capable but unstable
"Stable but incapable" vs "capable but unstable." Know the correct fix for each.

Stable but incapable: predictable, but the natural spread is too wide or off target. Fixing it takes a change to the process itself (reduce variation, recenter, redesign). Chasing individual points will not help. Capable but unstable: it meets the spec for now, but special causes are present. Find and eliminate the special causes.
Defects per unit and DPMO for defect counts (Poisson)
For counts of defects per unit, use DPU and DPMO (Poisson thinking).
Percent defective and yield for pass/fail (binomial)
For pass/fail results, use percent defective and yield (binomial thinking).
From yield or DPMO to sigma level
Convert yield or DPMO to a Z value, then add 1.5 for the short-term sigma convention
Convert to a tail area (DPMO ÷ 1,000,000, or 1 − yield). Read the Z value from the Z table. Add 1.5 for the short-term sigma convention.
Check stability first (control chart and special-cause tests) before interpreting binomial or Poisson capability
Before interpreting attribute capability, confirm the process is stable with a control chart and special-cause tests.
Defects vs defectives picks the right distribution and chart.
Counting defects (several per unit possible) points to the Poisson distribution and a c or u chart . Counting defective units (pass/fail) points to the binomial distribution and a p or np chart .
Sigma level from DPMO with the Z table
Sigma level from DPMO using the Z table: DPMO ÷ 1,000,000 = right-tail area; read Z; add 1.5. Example: 66,807 DPMO gives area 0.06681, Z ≈ 1.5, so 3.0σ.
DPMO ÷ 1,000,000 = tail area. Read Z. Add 1.5. Examples: 66,807 DPMO gives area 0.06681, Z = 1.5, so 3.0σ . 12,000 DPMO gives area 0.012, Z ≈ 2.26, so about 3.76σ .
Ongoing monitoring of capability with control charts (Xbar-R, I-MR, p, u)
Ongoing monitoring uses control charts matched to the data: Xbar-R (subgroups of continuous data), I-MR (individual readings), p (proportion defective), u (defects per unit). Details are in SG-5.2.
Monitor with time-ordered SPC first; re-evaluate capability after a stable period or a process change. Rolling capability indices on an unstable process mislead.
Monitor the process over time with SPC. Re-evaluate capability after a stable period or after a process change . Calculating capability indices over and over on an unstable process misleads.
Sampling frequency and rational subgrouping decide what the chart can detect

How often you sample and how you group the samples decide what the chart can detect . Subgroups should be formed so that variation inside a subgroup is common cause and variation between subgroups shows change over time.
Run charts for early monitoring when data are scarce
When data are scarce or you are starting out, a run chart shows trends and shifts without requiring control limits.
Pre-control charts (green/yellow/red zones based on spec limits): glossary only, low exam yield
Extension, glossary only. Pre-control charts use green, yellow, and red zones set from the spec limits. Low exam yield.
The BOK names this topic without detail. Expect "which monitoring tool fits" scenarios.

Read the data: continuous individual readings point to I-MR , continuous in subgroups to Xbar-R , counts of defective units to p or np , counts of defects to c or u , and a time-ordered view with little data to a run chart .
Distinguish: monitoring stability (control chart), monitoring conformance of output, periodic capability reassessment, sampling frequency, and reaction/escalation

Do not mix these up: Monitoring stability: control chart. Monitoring conformance of output: are units meeting the spec? Periodic capability reassessment: recompute Cp/Cpk/Pp/Ppk after stability is confirmed. Sampling frequency: how often to look. Reaction and escalation: what to do when a signal appears.
Interpreting capability output: histogram with specs, Cp/Cpk/Pp/Ppk, PPM within vs overall

A typical capability report shows a histogram with the spec limits , the indices Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk , and PPM within and overall . Cpk close to Ppk: the process is stable; within and overall variation agree. Ppk well below Cpk: shifts or drift between subgroups . Look for special causes.
Purpose: find which family of variation is largest, before running tests

A multi-vari study finds which family of variation is largest , so the team knows where to look. It is graphical and uses a structured sampling plan, not a hypothesis test. Use it early in Analyze, before you spend effort testing individual causes.

Within-piece (positional): variation across a single unit. Example: the diameter at different positions along one shaft. Piece-to-piece: variation between units made close together in time. Example: five consecutive shafts. Time-to-time (temporal): variation between time periods. Example: morning versus afternoon, one day versus the next, one shift versus another.
Sample several pieces per time period, plot the readings, and compare the sizes of the three kinds of variation

Pick a sampling interval (for example every hour). At each interval, take several consecutive pieces. Measure each piece at several positions. Plot every reading on a chart with time on the horizontal axis, joining the piece averages and the time-period averages. Compare the size of the three kinds of variation visually.
The largest family points to the Red X
The largest family points to where the Red X lives

The family with the biggest swing tells you where the key cause lives. Mostly within-piece: look at things that act on one piece (fixture, clamping, tool geometry). Mostly piece-to-piece: look at things that change from unit to unit (material, setup repeatability). Mostly time-to-time: look at things that change over time (tool wear, shift, ambient temperature, material lot).
Nested ANOVA / variance components quantify the same idea

Extension. A nested ANOVA puts numbers on the same idea by splitting total variance into components. Example: positional σ = 0.002, piece-to-piece σ = 0.003, time-to-time σ = 0.010. Variances: 0.000004, 0.000009, 0.0001. Total = 0.000113. Time-to-time share = 0.0001 ÷ 0.000113 = 88% .
Given a multi-vari chart, name the dominant source of variation.

On a chart, find which swing is widest: the spread inside each cluster of readings (within-piece), the spread between pieces in a cluster (piece-to-piece), or the movement of the cluster averages over time (time-to-time).
Continuous: normal, lognormal, Weibull, exponential, uniform

Normal: symmetric bell curve; most measurements of a stable process. Lognormal: positively skewed, cannot go below zero (repair times, some cycle times). Weibull: flexible shape; time to failure. Exponential: time between random events. Uniform: every value in a range equally likely.
Discrete: binomial (pass/fail counts), Poisson (defect counts), hypergeometric (sampling without replacement)

Binomial: counts of pass/fail results (defectives) in a fixed number of trials. Poisson: counts of defects over a fixed amount of opportunity. Hypergeometric: like the binomial, but sampling without replacement from a small population.
Binomial: P(x) = nCx · p^x · (1−p)^(n−x); mean = np
P(x) = nCx · pˣ · (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ˣ. Mean = np. Standard deviation = √[np(1 − p)]. Example: n = 10, p = 0.1. P(2 defectives) = 45 × 0.01 × 0.9⁸ = 45 × 0.01 × 0.4305 = 0.194 . Mean = 1.
Poisson: P(x) = e^(−λ) λ^x / x!; mean = variance = λ
P(x) = e^(−λ) · λˣ ÷ x!. Mean = variance = λ . Example: λ = 3 defects per unit. P(0) = e⁻³ = 0.0498 . P(1) = 3e⁻³ = 0.1494, so P(1 or fewer) = 0.199 .

Models the time between events when events occur at a constant average rate. It is memoryless : the chance of an event in the next hour does not depend on how long you have already waited. P(T beyond t) = e^(−t ÷ mean). Example: mean time between failures is 50 hours. P(no failure for 100 hours) = e⁻² = 0.135 .
Sampling distributions: t (heavier tails, df), chi-square (variances), F (ratio of variances)

These describe test statistics. t: like the normal but with heavier tails; depends on degrees of freedom and approaches the normal as df grows. Used for means when σ is estimated. Chi-square (χ²): positive and skewed; used for variances and contingency tables. F: a ratio of two variances; used for comparing variances and in ANOVA.
Time-to-failure data often follow Weibull or exponential; positively skewed bounded data often lognormal
Time-to-failure data often follow Weibull or exponential . Positively skewed data bounded at zero often follow lognormal .
Poisson approximates binomial for small p; normal approximates binomial when both np and n(1−p) are at least 5 (some use 10). Exam rule of thumb.

Extension. The Poisson approximates the binomial when p is small and n is large. The normal approximates the binomial when both np and n(1 − p) are at least 5 (some use 10). Treat these as exam rules of thumb.
Match a scenario to the distribution (defects on a unit = Poisson).
Defects on a unit = Poisson . Defective units in a sample = binomial . Time between breakdowns = exponential . Right-skewed, strictly positive times = lognormal or Weibull .
Assumptions: binomial = fixed n, independent trials, constant p; Poisson = counts over a fixed exposure at a constant rate; exponential = time between events; Weibull = flexible failure shape

Binomial: a fixed number of trials, each independent, with the same probability of a defective. Poisson: counts over a fixed exposure (area, time, unit) at a constant average rate. Exponential: time between events that occur at a constant rate. Weibull: flexible failure behavior, controlled by a shape parameter.
Which distribution goes with which data
Link to data: binomial for defectives; Poisson for defects; normal, lognormal, and Weibull for continuous measures; t, F, and χ² are the sampling distributions behind the tests

Defectives, binomial . Defects, Poisson . Continuous measurements, normal , lognormal , or Weibull . The t, F, and χ² are not data distributions. They are the sampling distributions behind the tests in 3.3 to 3.5.
Weibull shape β: below 1 early failures, 1 random (exponential), above 1 wear-out. Hypergeometric applies when sampling without replacement from a small population (n about 5% of N or more).

Extension. Weibull shape β: below 1 means early failures, equal to 1 is random failures (exponential), above 1 means wear-out. The hypergeometric applies when you sample without replacement from a small population, roughly when the sample is about 5% of the population or more.
Inference: drawing conclusions about a population from a sample
Inference means drawing conclusions about a population from a sample . You cannot measure everything, so you measure part and use statistics to say what the whole is likely to be.

A point estimate is a single number (the sample mean x̄). An interval estimate is a range likely to contain the true value (a confidence interval). It shows how much uncertainty surrounds the estimate.
CI for a mean: x̄ ± t(α/2, n−1) × s/√n
x̄ ± t(α/2, n − 1) × s ÷ √n. Example: n = 16, x̄ = 50, s = 8. Standard error = 8 ÷ 4 = 2. For 95% confidence with df = 15, t = 2.131. Margin = 2.131 × 2 = 4.26. Interval = 45.7 to 54.3 .
SE = s ÷ √n. It measures how much the sample mean varies from sample to sample.
What makes the interval wider or narrower
Interval width: shrinks with larger n, grows with higher confidence and higher variation
Larger n: narrower. Higher confidence level (99% versus 95%): wider. More variation (larger s): wider.
A 95% CI means the method captures the true value in 95% of repeated samples. It is not "95% chance this interval contains it."

If you repeated the sampling many times and built an interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true value . It is not correct to say "there is a 95% chance this particular interval contains the true mean."
Use z when σ is known, t when σ is estimated
Use z when the population σ is known . Use t when σ is estimated from the sample (the usual case).
For a single sample, df = n − 1 . One degree of freedom is "used up" estimating the mean. Smaller samples have smaller df and wider t-values.
Which change narrows the interval? Increase sample size.
Increase the sample size. Because SE contains √n, you need four times the data to cut the width in half.
CI for a proportion: p̂ ± z × √(p̂(1 − p̂) / n)

t tables (reference document): Table 1 columns are cumulative probabilities 0.600 to 0.995 (headed "Alpha Risk" but equal to 1 − α). Table 2 columns are one-tail α (0.25 to 0.005) with more decimals. Rows are df = n − 1 for 1 to 30, then 40, 60, 120, ∞. Two-tailed α = 0.05 uses the 0.975 column (Table 1) or 0.025 (Table 2); one-tailed uses 0.950 or 0.05. For an unlisted df use the next lower listed df.

The t table in the exam reference document works like this: Table 1 columns are cumulative probabilities, 0.600 to 0.995. The header says "Alpha Risk," but the values are really 1 − α . Table 2 shows the same critical values to more decimals, with columns labeled by one-tail α (0.25, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025, 0.01, 0.005). Rows are df = n − 1 : 1 to 30, then 40, 60, 120, and ∞. Two-tailed α = 0.05 uses the 0.975 column of Table 1 (or the 0.025 column of Table 2). One-tailed α = 0.05 uses the 0.950 column (or the 0.05 column of Table 2). If your df is not listed, use the next lower listed df (it is conservative). Examples: df = 9, 0.975 column: 2.262 . df = 9, 0.950 column: 1.833 . df = 35 is not listed, so use df = 30: 2.042 .
Random, stratified, systematic, cluster, convenience, judgment

Simple random: every unit has an equal chance of being chosen. Stratified: divide the population into groups (strata), then sample from each. Systematic: take every k-th unit. Cluster: randomly choose whole groups (clusters), then measure everything in them. Convenience: whatever is easy to reach. Prone to bias. Judgment: the sampler chooses what they think is representative.
Stratified when the population has distinct subgroups; systematic = every kth unit
Use stratified sampling when the population has distinct subgroups (shifts, machines, suppliers) you want represented. Use systematic sampling for steady line-based sampling (every 10th unit).
Sample size for a mean: n = (Zα/2 · σ / E)²
n = (Z(α/2) × σ ÷ E)² , where E is the margin of error you can tolerate. Example: σ = 12, E = 3, 95% confidence. n = (1.96 × 12 ÷ 3)² = 7.84² = 61.5, so round up to 62 .
Sample size for a proportion: n = Z² p(1−p) / E²

n = Z² × p(1 − p) ÷ E². If you have no estimate for p, use p = 0.5 , which gives the largest (safest) n. Example: E = 0.05, 95% confidence, p = 0.5. n = 3.8416 × 0.25 ÷ 0.0025 = 384.2, so round up to 385 .
Sample size depends on α, power, variation, and the smallest difference worth detecting
Sample size depends on the confidence level (α) , the power you want, the variation (σ) , and the smallest difference worth detecting .

Selection bias: the way units are picked favors some over others. Non-response bias: the people who respond differ from those who do not. Undercoverage: part of the population is left out of the list you sample from.
Name the method from the description
Identify the sampling method from a description (every 10th unit = systematic).
"Every 10th unit off the line" is systematic . "Pick five units from each of the three shifts" is stratified . "Randomly choose two plants and inspect every unit there" is cluster .
Two kinds of sample size: precision for an estimate (formulas above) vs power for a hypothesis test (needs α, power, σ, and the smallest difference worth detecting)

Precision (for an estimate): how tight do you want the interval? (Formulas above.) Power (for a hypothesis test): how likely do you want to detect a real difference? This needs α, power, σ, and the smallest difference worth detecting.
Sample size for a hypothesis test
1-sample t: n ≈ (Zα/2 + Zβ)² σ² / δ². 2-sample t, equal n per group: n ≈ 2(Zα/2 + Zβ)² σ² / δ². n rises with σ and power, falls with δ and α.

1-sample t: n ≈ (Z(α/2) + Z(β))² × σ² ÷ δ². 2-sample t, equal n per group: n ≈ 2 × (Z(α/2) + Z(β))² × σ² ÷ δ². Here δ is the smallest difference worth detecting and Z(β) goes with the power you want. n rises with σ and power, and falls with δ and α. Example: σ = 4, δ = 2, α = 0.05 two-sided (Z = 1.96), power 0.90 (Z(β) = 1.28 from the Z table). (1.96 + 1.28)² = 10.50. 1-sample: 10.50 × 16 ÷ 4 = 42. 2-sample: 2 × 10.50 × 16 ÷ 4 = 84 per group .
Sample means tend toward a normal distribution as n increases, regardless of the population shape
As the sample size increases, the distribution of sample means becomes approximately normal , regardless of the shape of the population the data come from.
Mean of sample means = μ. Standard error = σ/√n.
The mean of the sample means equals the population mean μ. The standard deviation of the sample means (the standard error ) is σ ÷ √n .
n ≥ 30 is a classroom heuristic only; the n needed depends on skewness, tails, and outliers
n of 30 or more is a classroom rule of thumb. The sample size you actually need depends on how skewed the population is, how heavy its tails are, and whether there are outliers.
Why Xbar charts and t-tests work reasonably with non-normal data
This is why Xbar charts and t-tests for means work reasonably well even when individual values are not normal: they are built on averages.
CLT does not make individual values normal
The CLT does not make individual values normal. It is a statement about averages .
Compute the standard error and probabilities for a sample mean

Use the standard error in the z-score: z = (x̄ − μ) ÷ (σ ÷ √n). Example: μ = 100, σ = 10, n = 25. SE = 10 ÷ 5 = 2. P(x̄ above 103): z = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5, right tail = 0.0668 . Compare an individual value above 103 (assuming normal data): z = 0.3, tail = 0.382.
σ = 10, n = 25 gives SE = 2. A common trap is using σ instead of SE for a mean.
With σ = 10 and n = 25, the standard error is 2 , not 10. Using σ when the question is about a sample mean is the most common mistake.
H0: no difference, status quo, equality. Ha: the claim you are looking for evidence of (≠, <, >).

H0 (null): no difference, no effect, the status quo, equality. Ha (alternative): what you are looking for evidence of. It can be "not equal" (two-sided), "less than," or "greater than." You never prove the alternative. You collect evidence against the null.
Steps: practical problem, hypotheses, choose α, choose test, sample size, collect data, test statistic and p-value, decision, practical conclusion

State the practical problem. State H0 and Ha. Choose the risk level (α, often 0.05). Choose the test. Decide the sample size. Collect the data. Compute the test statistic and the p-value. Make the decision (reject or fail to reject H0). State the practical conclusion.
p-value: probability of data this extreme if H0 were true. If p < α, reject H0.
The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if H0 were true . If p is below α, reject H0 . Memory aid: low p, null must go.
Never "accept H0." Say "fail to reject H0."
Never say "accept H0." Say "fail to reject H0." A failure to reject means you did not find enough evidence, not that the null is proven.
One-tailed or two-tailed; independent or paired
One-tailed vs two-tailed; independent vs paired samples

Two-tailed: you care about a difference in either direction. One-tailed: you care about only one direction, stated in advance. Independent samples: two separate groups. Paired samples: the same units measured twice (before and after) or matched pairs.
CI and test agree: a CI that excludes the hypothesized value means reject H0
If a 95% confidence interval for the difference excludes the hypothesized value (often zero), a two-sided test at α = 0.05 rejects H0 . If the interval includes it, the test fails to reject.
p = 0.08 with α = 0.05: fail to reject. Watch the conclusion wording.
With p = 0.08 and α = 0.05 , you fail to reject H0. The correct statement is "there is not enough evidence of a difference at the 5% level," not "there is no difference."
Huge samples can make trivial differences statistically significant
With a very large sample, even a trivial difference can produce a tiny p-value. It is statistically significant without being important.
Small samples can miss large, real differences
With a small sample, a large and real difference can fail to reach significance because there is too little data.
The effect size is the size of the difference, often relative to the variation. The minimum detectable difference is the smallest difference you care about finding.
Practical significance asks whether the difference matters to the business or the customer
Ask: does the difference matter to the customer, the process, or the business? That question is separate from the p-value.
p = 0.001, but the difference is 0.01 mm inside tolerance: statistically significant, not practically significant.
p = 0.001, but the difference is 0.01 mm and the tolerance is ±0.5 mm. It is statistically significant but not practically significant . Do not re-tool the process because of it.
Not significant, but not proven the same
p = 0.07 with low power and a large observed effect: 'insufficient evidence; check power and sample size,' not 'no difference'
p = 0.07 with a small sample and a large observed effect. The correct reading is "insufficient evidence; check power and sample size," not "no difference."
Type I (α): reject a true H0; false alarm; producer's risk
Rejecting a true H0. A false alarm: you conclude there is a difference when there is none. Its probability is α .
Type II (β): fail to reject a false H0; missed detection; consumer's risk

Failing to reject a false H0. A missed detection: a real difference goes unnoticed. Its probability is β . H0 is true H0 is false Reject H0 Type I error (α) Correct decision (power = 1 − β) Fail to reject H0 Correct decision (1 − α) Type II error (β)
Power = 1 − β. Typical α = 0.05, power = 0.80 to 0.90.
Power = 1 − β , the chance of detecting a real difference. Typical values: α = 0.05 and power of 0.80 to 0.90.
Power rises with larger n, larger effect, larger α, or lower variation
A larger sample size A larger real effect A larger α (at the cost of more false alarms) Less variation
Confidence level = 1 − α. A 5% α gives 95% confidence.
"Concluding the new process is better when it is not" is a Type I error.
"Concluding the new process is better when it is not" is a Type I error . "Concluding there is no improvement when there actually is" is a Type II error .
Producer's and consumer's risk wording comes from acceptance-sampling framing; the Type I and Type II definitions are the primary ones
The names producer's risk (α) and consumer's risk (β) come from acceptance-sampling language. The Type I and Type II definitions are the primary ones.
Selection depends on: data type, number of groups, normality, and the parameter (mean/median, variance, proportion)
The right test depends on data type , number of groups , whether groups are independent, paired, or blocked , the parameter being compared (mean or median, variance, proportion), and normality .
Normal, mean: 1-sample t (or Z), 2-sample t, paired t, one-way ANOVA
One sample versus a target: 1-sample t (or Z if σ is known). Two independent groups: 2-sample t . Two paired measurements: paired t . Three or more groups: one-way ANOVA .
Normal, variance: 1-sample variance (chi-square), 2 variances (F-test), several (Bartlett, Levene)
One sample versus a target variance: chi-square test for a variance . Two variances: F test . Several variances: Bartlett (needs normality) or Levene (robust to non-normality).
Non-normal, median: 1-sample sign / Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, Mood's median, Friedman

One sample versus a target: 1-sample sign or 1-sample Wilcoxon . Two independent groups: Mann-Whitney . Three or more independent groups: Kruskal-Wallis (or Mood's median ). Blocked or repeated measures: Friedman .
One proportion versus a target: 1-proportion test . Two proportions: 2-proportion test . Association between categorical variables: chi-square contingency table .

Parametric vs non-parametric. Non-parametric tests often have lower power when the parametric model holds. The BOK splits normal-data and non-normal-data testing, so the exam default is the normal vs non-normal fork; robustness nuances (large-n t-tests, shape assumptions) sit on top of it.

Parametric tests (t, ANOVA) assume a distribution. Non-parametric tests use ranks or signs and assume less. They often have lower power when the parametric model really does hold. The BOK separates normal-data testing (3.4) from non-normal-data testing (3.5), so the exam's default fork is normal versus non-normal. Robustness points (a t-test with a large sample, shape assumptions for rank tests) are refinements on top of that.
The "which test?" question is core exam content. Build the decision tree (SG-0) and drill it.
Read the scenario for the clues. The tree below turns the clues into a test.
For exam purposes decide in this order: data type, number of groups, paired/independent/blocked, parameter (mean/median, variance, proportion), then normality; check sample size and robustness last

Data type: continuous or discrete? How many groups: one, two, or three or more? Structure: independent, paired, or blocked? Parameter: mean or median, variance, or proportion? Normality: decides parametric versus non-parametric. Then check sample size and robustness. The selection tree Data Question Normal data Non-normal data Continuous One sample versus a target (mean or median) 1-sample t 1-sample sign or Wilcoxon Continuous Two independent groups 2-sample t Mann-Whitney Continuous Two paired measurements Paired t Wilcoxon on the differences Continuous Three or more groups One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis or Mood's median Continuous Blocked or repeated measures Two-way ANOVA (recognition) Friedman Continuous Variance versus a target Chi-square for a variance not applicable Continuous Two variances F test Levene Continuous Three or more variances Bartlett Levene Discrete One proportion 1-proportion exact binomial if n is small Discrete Two proportions 2-proportion Fisher's exact if counts are small Discrete Categories by categories Chi-square contingency Chi-square contingency

t = (x̄ − μ0) ÷ (s ÷ √n) , with df = n − 1. It compares one sample mean to a target value μ0. Example: n = 9, x̄ = 12.5, μ0 = 12, s = 0.9. SE = 0.9 ÷ 3 = 0.3. t = 0.5 ÷ 0.3 = 1.67. For df = 8 the two-tailed critical value (0.975 column) is 2.306. Since 1.67 is below 2.306, fail to reject H0.
2-sample: t = (x̄1 − x̄2) / √(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2) (Welch), or pooled if variances are equal

t = (x̄1 − x̄2) ÷ √( s1²/n1 + s2²/n2 ) (the Welch version, which does not assume equal variances). The pooled version assumes equal variances. Example: group 1: x̄ = 20.0, s = 2, n = 10. Group 2: x̄ = 22.0, s = 3, n = 12. s1²/n1 = 0.40, s2²/n2 = 0.75. SE = √1.15 = 1.072. t = −2.0 ÷ 1.072 = −1.87 . Welch df ≈ 19, critical value 2.093. Since 1.87 is below 2.093, fail to reject H0.
Paired: t = d̄ / (s_d/√n) on within-pair differences
t = d̄ ÷ (s_d ÷ √n) , where d is the difference within each pair , n is the number of pairs, and df = n − 1. Pairing removes unit-to-unit variation, which makes the test more sensitive.
Assumptions: independence, approximate normality, equal variance for the pooled version

The observations are independent . The data (or the differences, for a paired test) are approximately normal , which matters most with small samples. The pooled t-test also needs equal variances . The Welch version does not.
Interpret p-value and CI of the difference
Report the p-value and the confidence interval for the difference . If the interval excludes zero, the means differ. Always translate the result back to the practical question.
Extension. When the population σ is known , use a z-test: z = (x̄ − μ0) ÷ (σ ÷ √n). In practice σ is rarely known.
Before/after on the same units means paired. Two separate groups means 2-sample.
Before and after on the same units, or matched pairs, means paired. Two separate groups means 2-sample. Using the wrong one is the most common error on this topic.

Reference-sheet versions: Welch df = (A + B)² / [A²/(n1 − 1) + B²/(n2 − 1)] with A = s1²/n1, B = s2²/n2; pooled s_p = √[((n1 − 1)s1² + (n2 − 1)s2²) / (n1 + n2 − 2)]; 2-sample Z when the σ's are known. The sheet's df subscripts are generic; pooled df = n1 + n2 − 2.

Welch df = (A + B)² ÷ [ A² ÷ (n1 − 1) + B² ÷ (n2 − 1) ] , where A = s1²/n1 and B = s2²/n2. Pooled s_p = √{ [ (n1 − 1)s1² + (n2 − 1)s2² ] ÷ (n1 + n2 − 2) }. For the pooled t-test, df = n1 + n2 − 2. 2-sample Z is used when the population σ's are known. The sheet's subscripts show "n − 1" generically, so always use the df that matches the test.
The chi-square test for a variance

χ² = (n − 1) × s² ÷ σ0² , with df = n − 1. It compares a sample variance to a target variance σ0². Example: the target σ0 = 4. A sample of n = 16 has s = 5.2. χ² = 15 × 27.04 ÷ 16 = 25.35. For df = 15, the upper 0.05 critical value is 24.996. Since 25.35 exceeds it, reject H0 and conclude the variation exceeds the target (one-sided test).
Tests whether process variation differs from a target
Whether the process variation is different from, greater than, or less than a target . Variance questions are about consistency, not the average.
The χ² test for a variance is very sensitive to departures from normality. Check normality first.
2-sample variance: F = s1²/s2²; Levene's test is robust to non-normality
F = s1² ÷ s2². Levene's test is the version that is robust to non-normality.
"Did variation decrease?" means a variance test, not a mean test.
That is a variance test , not a mean test. A change in the average tells you nothing about consistency.
The F test for two variances
F test for variances: F = s1² / s2² with df (n1 − 1, n2 − 1). The sheet also shows a confidence interval for the ratio of variances using F values in both directions.

F = s1² ÷ s2² , with df (n1 − 1, n2 − 1). Put the larger variance in the numerator. The reference sheet also shows a confidence interval for the ratio of variances using F values in both directions. Example: s1 = 4.0 (n1 = 11), s2 = 2.5 (n2 = 13). F = 16 ÷ 6.25 = 2.56 , df = (10, 12). The F table (α = 0.05, one-sided) gives 2.75. Since 2.56 is below 2.75, fail to reject H0.

χ² table: right-tail probabilities. Table 1 columns 0.250 to 0.001; Table 2 columns 0.995 to 0.500; df 1 to 30, then 40 to 100 by 10. For a two-sided variance test use the α/2 (upper) and 1 − α/2 (lower) columns.

The χ² table gives right-tail probabilities. Table 1 has columns 0.250 down to 0.001. Table 2 has columns 0.995 down to 0.500. Rows are df 1 to 30, then 40 to 100 by 10. For a two-sided variance test use both ends: the α/2 column for the upper critical value and the 1 − α/2 column for the lower. Example: df = 15, α = 0.05 two-sided. Upper critical (0.025 column) = 27.488. Lower critical (0.975 column) = 6.262. Reject H0 if χ² falls below 6.262 or above 27.488.
H0: all means equal. Ha: at least one mean differs.
H0: all the means are equal. Ha: at least one mean differs. ANOVA compares three or more group means.
Multiple t-tests inflate the overall α risk; ANOVA keeps it controlled

Each test carries its own α risk, and the risks add up. With three groups (three pairwise tests) at α = 0.05, the chance of at least one false alarm is about 1 − 0.95³ = 14%. ANOVA keeps the overall risk at α.
SST = SS between + SS within; MS = SS/df; F = MS between / MS within
SS total = SS between (treatment) + SS within (error). MS = SS ÷ df. F = MS between ÷ MS within. A large F means the group means differ by more than the noise within the groups would explain.
df between = k−1; df within = N−k; df total = N−1
With k groups and N observations in total: df between = k − 1 df within = N − k df total = N − 1
Assumptions: independence, normal residuals, equal variances (check Levene or Bartlett)
Independent observations, normal residuals , and equal variances across groups (check with Levene's or Bartlett's test).
ANOVA says "at least one differs," not which. Use post-hoc (Tukey, Fisher, Dunnett) or interval plots.
ANOVA says "at least one differs," not which. Use a post-hoc comparison (Tukey, Fisher, or Dunnett against a control) or an interval plot to find the differences.
Includes equal-variance tests, normality tests, sample-size calculation, and reading output
Equal-variance tests, normality tests, sample-size calculation, and reading ANOVA output.
Fill in a missing ANOVA table cell. Interpret a p-value and name which test to run next.

Use the relationships above. Given SS between = 40 (df 3) and SS within = 80 (df 16): MS between = 13.33, MS within = 5.00, F = 2.67. The F table (α = 0.05, df 3 and 16) gives 3.24, so fail to reject. Then name the next step (if significant, a post-hoc test).
Bartlett's test assumes normality; Levene's test is robust to non-normality
Bartlett's test assumes the data are normal . Levene's test is robust to non-normality. If normality is doubtful, use Levene's.

A significant ANOVA means at least one mean differs. Do not name the largest sample mean the winner without post-hoc evidence. In Tukey/Fisher pairwise intervals, an interval containing 0 means no evidence of a difference.

A significant ANOVA means at least one mean differs. Do not declare the largest sample mean "the best" without post-hoc evidence. In Tukey or Fisher pairwise intervals, an interval that contains 0 means no evidence of a difference for that pair.
Sample size and power for ANOVA
Sample size and power for ANOVA: inputs are number of levels, the smallest difference between means worth detecting, σ, α, and power
The inputs are the number of levels , the smallest difference between means worth detecting , σ , α , and the power you want. Smaller differences and larger σ need more data.

F tables (reference document): upper-tail critical values for α = 0.05, 0.01, and 0.10, each in two parts. Columns are numerator df (1 to 10, then 12, 15, 20, 24, 30, 40, 60, 120, ∞); rows are denominator df. The ANOVA F test is upper-tailed. For a two-sided variance test, put the larger variance in the numerator; the α = 0.05 table gives a two-sided test at α = 0.10, and there is no α = 0.025 table.

The F tables in the reference document give upper-tail critical values for α = 0.05, α = 0.01, and α = 0.10 , each in two parts (columns 1 to 10, then 12 to infinity). Columns are the numerator df : 1 to 10, then 12, 15, 20, 24, 30, 40, 60, 120, ∞. Rows are the denominator df. The ANOVA F test is upper-tailed, so α = 0.05 works directly. For a two-sided variance test, put the larger variance in the numerator. The α = 0.05 table then corresponds to a two-sided test at α = 0.10 , and the α = 0.01 table to α = 0.02. There is no α = 0.025 table, so a two-sided test at exactly 0.05 cannot be read from the sheet. Examples: df (2, 9) gives 4.26. df (3, 16) gives 3.24. df (10, 12) gives 2.75.
ANOVA by hand with the reference-sheet formulas

ANOVA by hand (reference sheet): C = T²/N; SS_total = ΣX² − (ΣX)²/N (= ΣX² − C), or (N − 1)s²; SS_treatment = Σ(Tᵢ²/nᵢ) − C, or Σnᵢ·X̄ᵢ² − N·X̿², or for equal n n(k − 1)·s² of the group means; SS_error = SS_total − SS_treatment

C = T² ÷ N , the correction factor (T is the grand total of all data). SS total = ΣX² − (ΣX)² ÷ N , which equals ΣX² − C. It also equals (N − 1) × s² of all data. SS treatment = Σ(Tᵢ² ÷ nᵢ) − C , where Tᵢ is the total of group i. Equivalent forms: Σnᵢ·X̄ᵢ² − N·X̿², or for equal group sizes n(k − 1) × s² of the group means. SS error = SS total − SS treatment.
What is not on the sheet
Not on the sheet: df (k − 1, N − k, N − 1), MS = SS/df, and F = MS_treatment / MS_error. Know them.
The sheet does not give df (k − 1, N − k, N − 1), MS = SS ÷ df , or F = MS treatment ÷ MS error. Know them.

2 independent samples, non-normal; rank-based. It compares medians strictly only if the two distributions have similar shape and spread; otherwise it is a rank/distribution comparison. Exam default: Mann-Whitney is the non-normal 2-sample test.

A rank-based test for two independent samples of non-normal data. All values from both groups are ranked together (smallest = 1), the ranks are added up for each group, and the test asks whether one group's ranks are systematically higher. It is described as comparing medians , strictly true only when the two distributions have a similar shape and spread . Otherwise it is a general comparison of the distributions. Exam default: Mann-Whitney is the non-normal 2-sample test.
Use it where you would use a 2-sample t-test if the data were normal.
Skewed cycle-time data from two small shifts means Mann-Whitney. With large n a 2-sample t can also be reasonable.

Strongly skewed cycle times from two small shifts means Mann-Whitney. With large samples a 2-sample t-test can also be reasonable because of the central limit theorem, but on the exam, small non-normal samples point to Mann-Whitney.
3 or more independent groups, non-normal; rank-based. The same shape caveat applies to a clean median interpretation.

A rank-based test for three or more independent groups of non-normal data. All values are ranked together and the average rank per group is compared. The statistic follows approximately a chi-square distribution with k − 1 degrees of freedom. The same shape caveat as Mann-Whitney applies to a clean median interpretation.
Use it where you would use one-way ANOVA if the data were normal.
Three suppliers with skewed lead times means Kruskal-Wallis.

Three suppliers with skewed lead times means Kruskal-Wallis. If the output shows a significant p-value, the conclusion is "at least one group differs," and you still need a follow-up comparison to say which.
3 or more groups; tests whether medians are equal using counts above and below the overall median

Tests whether the medians of three or more groups are equal. It finds the overall median , then counts how many values in each group fall above and below it. A chi-square test is applied to that table of counts.
More robust to outliers, less powerful than Kruskal-Wallis
It is robust to outliers because only above-or-below matters, not how far. The price is lower power than Kruskal-Wallis.
Often preferred when outliers matter; less powerful than Kruskal-Wallis.
Often preferred when outliers matter . It is less powerful than Kruskal-Wallis.
Blocked or repeated-measures design, non-normal data
A rank-based test for blocked or repeated-measures designs with non-normal data. Within each block (for example one operator), the treatments are ranked, and the rank sums per treatment are compared.
The alternative to two-way ANOVA with blocks
Non-parametric analog of two-way ANOVA with blocks
It is the non-parametric counterpart of a two-way ANOVA with blocks. Each block must see every treatment.
Same operators rate multiple methods, so operator is the block.
The same operators rate multiple methods, so operator is the block , and Friedman applies. If the groups were independent, it would be Kruskal-Wallis instead.
Tests a median against a target using only the sign of each difference

Tests a median against a target using only the sign of each difference (above or below the target). If the median equals the target, each value is equally likely to fall on either side, so the count of "above" values follows a binomial with p = 0.5. Values exactly on the target are dropped.
It makes the fewest assumptions (no symmetry needed) but has the lowest power , since it ignores how far each value is from the target.
Tests a median against a target using signed ranks; assumes a roughly symmetric distribution

Tests a median against a target using signed ranks . It takes each difference from the target, ranks the absolute differences, and sums the ranks of the positive and negative differences. It assumes a roughly symmetric distribution , so the location is well defined.
More power than the sign test
More powerful than the sign test when symmetry holds
When symmetry holds, Wilcoxon is more powerful than the sign test because it uses the sizes of the differences, not just the direction.
Sign vs Wilcoxon: no symmetry assumption means sign.
If the distribution cannot be assumed symmetric, use the sign test. If it is roughly symmetric, use Wilcoxon. For paired non-normal data, apply the Wilcoxon test to the pair differences.

z = (p̂ − p0) ÷ √[ p0(1 − p0) ÷ n ] , where p̂ is the sample proportion and p0 is the target (π on the sheet). Example: a claimed defect rate is 5%. A sample of n = 200 has 16 defective. p̂ = 0.08. SE = √(0.05 × 0.95 ÷ 200) = 0.0154. z = 0.03 ÷ 0.0154 = 1.95. The two-sided critical value is 1.96, so fail to reject (p is about 0.051). A one-sided test (critical value 1.645) would reject. State the direction before looking at the data.
For two proportions, the pooled value is p̂ = (x1 + x2) ÷ (n1 + n2) , total successes over total sample.
Conditions: np and n(1−p) both at least 5 (some use 10); exact binomial otherwise
The normal approximation needs np and n(1 − p) both at least 5 (some sources use 10). With small counts, use an exact binomial test.
Defective rate before vs after: 2-proportion test.
Defective rate before versus after a change is a 2-proportion test.
The reference-sheet form of the 2-proportion test

Two-proportion z, reference-sheet form (unpooled): z = (p1 − p2) / √[p1(1 − p1)/n1 + p2(1 − p2)/n2]. Software tests of H0: p1 = p2 usually pool: z = (p̂1 − p̂2) / √[p̂pool(1 − p̂pool)(1/n1 + 1/n2)]. Expect small numeric differences; use the sheet's form for hand calculation unless the question says otherwise.

The reference sheet uses the unpooled form: z = (p1 − p2) ÷ √[ p1(1 − p1)/n1 + p2(1 − p2)/n2 ]. Software tests of H0: p1 = p2 usually use the pooled form: z = (p̂1 − p̂2) ÷ √[ p̂pool(1 − p̂pool)(1/n1 + 1/n2) ]. The numbers differ only slightly. Use the sheet's form for hand calculations unless the question says otherwise.
Exact binomial test, or Fisher's exact test, when counts are small
Extension. With small counts, use the exact binomial test (one proportion) or Fisher's exact test (two proportions).
Confidence interval for the difference of two proportions (on the sheet): (p1 − p2) ± z(1 − α/2) × √[p1(1 − p1)/n1 + p2(1 − p2)/n2]
H0: the two categorical variables are independent
H0: the two categorical variables are independent. Ha: they are related (the distribution of one depends on the other).
Expected = (row total × column total) / grand total
Expected = (row total × column total) ÷ grand total , for each cell.
χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E , summed over all cells, with df = (rows − 1) × (columns − 1).
The rule of thumb on expected counts
Rule of thumb: expected counts at least 5. It is an exam heuristic, not a law; expected counts under 1 are especially problematic.
Expected counts should be at least 5 . This is an exam heuristic, not a law. Expected counts below 1 are especially problematic.
Includes sample-size reasoning and interpreting output
Sample-size reasoning and interpreting software output.
Goodness-of-fit chi-square (glossary only, low exam yield)
Extension, glossary only. A goodness-of-fit chi-square compares observed counts to a hypothesized distribution. Low exam yield.
Defect type by shift counts in a table: contingency chi-square.
Defect type counted by shift (counts in a table of categories) is a contingency chi-square.
Fisher's exact test for sparse 2×2 tables (recognition only)
Extension, recognition only. For sparse 2×2 tables where expected counts are small, use Fisher's exact test.
Sample-size reasoning for proportion and contingency tests: depends on the proportions, α, and power; small differences need large samples
The sample needed depends on the proportions, α, and power. Small differences need large samples.
Use the χ² table for the critical value: df = (r − 1)(c − 1), pick the α column, compare to the computed χ². Expected-count formula is not on the sheet.
Find the critical value from the df and the α column (right-tail), and compare it with the computed χ². The expected-count formula is not on the sheet, so memorize it.
Always plot Y against X before computing anything. The picture shows whether the relationship is linear, curved, clustered, or driven by a few unusual points. A single number can hide all of that.
Pearson r ranges from −1 to +1; r² = coefficient of determination

Pearson r measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship and ranges from −1 to +1. The reference sheet gives r = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) ÷ √[ Σ(X − X̄)² × Σ(Y − Ȳ)² ]. r² is the coefficient of determination , the share of the variation in Y explained by the straight-line relationship with X. Example (the data above): r = 6 ÷ √(10 × 6) = 6 ÷ 7.746 = 0.775 , and r² = 0.60.
r near 0 means no linear relationship, not necessarily no relationship
r near 0 means no linear relationship. It does not mean no relationship at all. A perfect U-shaped relationship (Y = X²) can give r near 0.
Correlation is not causation; watch for lurking variables and outliers

Two variables can move together because of a third (lurking) variable. Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer because of temperature, not because one causes the other. Outliers can also create or hide a correlation.
Spearman rank correlation for monotonic or non-normal data
Extension. Spearman correlation uses the ranks of the data. It handles monotonic (always rising or always falling, not necessarily straight) and non-normal relationships.
r = −0.9 is a strong negative relationship, stronger than r = +0.6.
r = −0.9 is a strong negative relationship, stronger than r = +0.6. The sign gives the direction. The distance from zero gives the strength.
One influential point can create or destroy a correlation; r near 0 can hide a curved relationship
One influential point far from the rest can create a high r, or destroy one. And r near 0 can hide a strong curved relationship. Look at the plot.
Ŷ = b0 + b1·X (the reference sheet writes Ŷ = a + bX ). Ŷ is the predicted value of Y. b0 is the intercept and b1 is the slope.
Slope b1 = Sxy / Sxx; intercept b0 = ȳ − b1·x̄

Slope b1 = Sxy ÷ Sxx , where Sxy = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) and Sxx = Σ(X − X̄)². Intercept b0 = Ȳ − b1·X̄. Example (the data above): b1 = 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6. b0 = 4 − 0.6 × 3 = 2.2. The equation is Ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6X.
Slope: change in Y for a one-unit change in X. Intercept: Y when X = 0 (may be meaningless).

Slope: the change in Y for a one-unit increase in X. Here, each extra unit of X adds about 0.6 to Y. Intercept: the predicted Y when X = 0. It is often not meaningful, especially if X = 0 is outside the data.
R² = share of variation in Y explained by X; adjusted R²
R² is the share of the variation in Y explained by the model. Adjusted R² corrects for the number of terms, so adding a useless predictor does not inflate it. For one predictor, R² equals r².
S = standard error of the regression; p-value for the slope tests H0: slope = 0

S is the standard error of the regression : the typical distance of the data from the line, in the units of Y. S = √(SSE ÷ (n − 2)). The p-value for the slope tests H0: slope = 0 (no linear relationship).
Regression ANOVA table: SSR, SSE, SST, F
It splits the total variation: SST = SSR + SSE. SSR is explained by the line, SSE is the leftover (residual) variation, and F tests whether the model explains more than chance.
Do not extrapolate outside the data range
The line is only known to hold within the range of the data. Predicting outside that range (extrapolation) assumes the relationship continues, which may not be true.
Predict Ŷ at a given X
Plug X into the equation. Example: X = 3.5 gives Ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6 × 3.5 = 4.3. X = 6 is outside the data (1 to 5), so a prediction there is extrapolation and should not be trusted.
"R² = 0.72": 72% of variation in Y is explained by the model. Sign of r comes from the slope.
72% of the variation in Y is explained by the model. The sign of r comes from the slope (a negative slope gives a negative r). R² itself is always positive.
Regression ANOVA degrees of freedom: simple = 1, n−2, n−1; multiple = k, n−k−1, n−1. F = MS_reg / MS_error; R² = SS_reg / SS_total. Expect partially blank ANOVA tables.

Simple regression: df = 1 (regression), n − 2 (error), n − 1 (total). Multiple regression with k predictors: df = k, n − k − 1, n − 1. F = MS regression ÷ MS error , with MS = SS ÷ df. R² = SS regression ÷ SS total. Exams often give a partially blank table and ask you to fill it in. Example: n = 12, SST = 50, SSE = 20 (simple regression). SSR = 30. df = 1, 10, 11. MSR = 30, MSE = 2. F = 15. The F table for df (1, 10) gives 4.96, so the regression is significant. R² = 30 ÷ 50 = 0.60.
A slope confidence interval containing 0 corresponds to failing to reject slope = 0 at the matching α
If the confidence interval for the slope contains 0 , you fail to reject H0: slope = 0 at the matching α. If it excludes 0, the relationship is significant.
Reading a coefficient table: Coef, SE Coef, T, P; S, R-sq, R-sq(adj), R-sq(pred)
Columns: Coef (the estimate), SE Coef (its standard error), T (Coef ÷ SE Coef), P (the p-value). Below the table, S , R-sq , R-sq(adj) , and R-sq(pred) (how well the model predicts new data).
What the reference sheet does and does not give

Reference sheet: r = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) / √[Σ(X − X̄)² Σ(Y − Ȳ)²]; Ŷ = a + bX; multiple regression; multiple standard error SE = √[Σ(Y − Ŷ)² / (n − (k + 1))]. Not on the sheet: slope b = Sxy/Sxx, intercept, R², adjusted R², F, VIF, interval formulas. Know them or expect output tables.

The sheet gives r , Ŷ = a + bX , the multiple regression equation , and the multiple standard error SE = √[ Σ(Y − Ŷ)² ÷ (n − (k + 1)) ]. Not on the sheet: the slope and intercept formulas, R², adjusted R², F, VIF, and the interval formulas. Know them, or expect software output.

e = y − ŷ , the observed value minus the fitted value. The residuals from a least-squares line add up to zero. Example (the data above): Ŷ = 2.8, 3.4, 4.0, 4.6, 5.2 for X = 1 to 5. Residuals = 2 − 2.8, 4 − 3.4, 5 − 4.0, 4 − 4.6, 5 − 5.2 = −0.8, 0.6, 1.0, −0.6, −0.2. Sum = 0. Sum of squares = 2.4 = SSE.
Model assumptions: linear mean function, independent errors, constant variance, approximately normal errors; residuals centered near zero
The relationship is linear (a straight line is the right shape). Errors are independent. Errors have constant variance. Errors are approximately normal. The residuals should be centered near zero.
Normal probability plot of the residuals
Normal probability plot of residuals for normality
Checks the normality of the errors. Points near a straight line mean approximately normal.
Residuals vs fits: random scatter is good. Funnel = non-constant variance. Curve = non-linear model needed.
Random scatter with no pattern: good. A funnel (spread grows or shrinks): non-constant variance. A curve : the relationship is not linear and the model needs another term.
Residuals vs order: patterns indicate autocorrelation or time effects
Plot the residuals in the order the data were collected. A pattern (trend, cycles, runs) signals dependence between observations or a time effect.
An outlier has a large residual (far from the line in Y). High leverage means an X value far from the other X values. An influential point changes the fitted line substantially if removed.
Given a residual plot, diagnose the violation and name the fix (transform or add a term).
Given a residual plot, name the violation and the fix (transform the data, or add a term).

Diagnostic to action: curve = wrong functional form (add a term or transform); funnel = non-constant variance (transform); pattern vs order = dependence or time effect; one extreme point = check influence and data integrity

Curve in residuals versus fits: wrong functional form. Add a term (for example X²) or transform. Funnel: non-constant variance. Transform Y. Pattern versus order: dependence or time effect. Investigate how the data were collected. One extreme point: check influence and data integrity (is it a recording error?).
Curvilinear data: fit quadratic or cubic terms, or transform X or Y
When the relationship bends, fit a quadratic (Y = b0 + b1X + b2X²) or cubic term, or transform X or Y (for example take the log) so the relationship becomes straight.
Curved residual pattern signals a non-linear fit is needed
A curved pattern in the residuals (residuals versus fits) tells you a straight line is not enough and a non-linear fit is needed.
Higher R² is not always better
Higher R² is not always better; beware overfitting

Adding terms always raises R², even when they only fit noise. A complicated curve can match the data very closely and then predict new data badly ( overfitting ). Prefer the simplest model that fits well , and check adjusted R² and residuals.
Choose between a linear and quadratic model from a fitted-line plot.

From a fitted-line plot, choose the quadratic when the data clearly curve, the residuals of the linear fit show a pattern, and the quadratic term is significant. Choose the linear model when the quadratic adds almost nothing.
Ŷ = b0 + b1X1 + b2X2 + ... + bkXk. Each coefficient is the change in Y for a one-unit change in that X with the other X's held constant.
Overall F-test, individual t-tests, adjusted R² (it penalizes useless terms)

Overall F-test: is at least one predictor useful? (H0: all slopes are zero.) Individual t-tests: is this predictor useful given the others in the model? Adjusted R²: like R² but penalizes useless terms , so it can fall when a term does not help.

Multicollinearity: correlated predictors. VIF = 1 / (1 − R²j); above 5 (some use 10) is a rule-of-thumb warning, not an IASSC-defined cutoff. Symptom: high overall F and R² with insignificant individual t-tests.

Predictors that are strongly correlated with each other. The VIF (variance inflation factor) measures it: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − R²j) , where R²j comes from regressing predictor j on the other predictors. A VIF above 5 (some use 10) is a rule-of-thumb warning , not a fixed cutoff. Symptom: a high overall F and R², but individually insignificant t-tests. The model fits well, but the data cannot tell which of the overlapping predictors matters.
Model building: stepwise, best subsets; keep the model parsimonious
Common approaches: stepwise and best subsets. Keep the model parsimonious : as simple as possible while still explaining the data well.
An interaction (X1 × X2) means the effect of one predictor depends on the level of another. Example: a temperature change matters more at high pressure than at low pressure.
Categorical predictors (shift, supplier, machine) enter through indicator/dummy variables; recognition only, no hand coding
Shift, supplier, and machine enter the model as indicator (dummy) variables. Recognition only: you will not need to code them by hand.

Backward elimination (drop the highest-p term, refit, repeat) is standard. Keep lower-order terms of any retained interaction, and do not drop a term on p-value alone when it matters for the purpose. Adjusted R² can fall when a term does not help.

Backward elimination is standard: drop the term with the highest p-value , refit, and repeat. Two cautions: keep the lower-order terms of any interaction you retain , and do not drop a term on p-value alone when it matters for the purpose of the model. Adjusted R² can fall when a term is useless.
Interaction hierarchy: keep the main effects if the interaction stays, even when a main effect's p-value is weak
If an interaction stays in the model, keep its main effects even if a main effect's p-value is weak.
Mallows' Cp (glossary only, low exam yield)
Extension, glossary only. A model-selection statistic. Low exam yield.
Confidence interval for the mean response
Confidence interval: range for the mean response at a given X
A range for the average Y at a given X. It reflects uncertainty in the line itself.
Prediction interval for a single observation
Prediction interval: range for a single future observation at a given X, always wider

A range for one future individual value at a given X. It includes the uncertainty in the line plus the natural scatter of individual values, so it is always wider than the confidence interval at the same X.
Both are narrowest at x̄ and widen as X moves away from the mean
Both intervals are narrowest at the mean of X and widen as X moves away from it. That is another reason not to extrapolate.
Which interval for one new unit?
"Which interval for one new unit?" Prediction interval.
Wording cue: 'average output at X = 10' means a confidence interval; 'one next unit' means a prediction interval
"What is the average output at X = 10?" means a confidence interval. "What will the next unit be at X = 10?" means a prediction interval.
Same four residual checks as simple regression

The residual checks from SG-4.1.3 apply: normal probability plot, residuals versus fits, residuals versus order, and a histogram of residuals. Together they are often shown as the four-in-one residual plot.
Add VIF, leverage, and influence checks
Also look at VIF (multicollinearity), leverage (unusual combinations of X values), and influence (points that change the fit a lot).
Extension. Cook's distance is one statistic that measures how much a single point influences the fit. Recognize "influential observation"; the formula is not needed.
Combined diagnostics: interpret a full residual four-pack.

Combine the plots into one diagnosis. Points off the line on the probability plot suggest non-normal errors. A funnel on residuals versus fits suggests unequal variance. A pattern versus order suggests dependence or a time effect. One extreme point on every plot suggests a possible influential outlier.
Transform non-normal or non-constant-variance data to improve analysis
A transformation reshapes the data so that normality or constant variance holds better, which makes analysis and regression more reliable.
Box-Cox λ: 1 = no transform, 0.5 = square root, 0 = natural log (by definition/limit), −1 = reciprocal
Box-Cox raises the data to a power λ (lambda). λ = 1: no transformation. λ = 0.5: square root. λ = 0: natural log (by definition, as a limit). λ = −1: reciprocal. The software finds the best λ.
Requires positive data; for zero or negative values add a constant first
Box-Cox needs positive data. For zeros or negatives, add a constant to every value first.
Johnson transformation (glossary only, low exam yield)
Extension, glossary only. A more flexible transformation that can handle a wider range of data. Low exam yield.
After transforming, spec limits must be transformed too for capability work
If you transform the data and then do a capability analysis, transform the specification limits the same way.
Read the λ and its confidence interval from Box-Cox output and choose a transformation.
The plot shows the best (optimal) λ and a confidence interval for λ. Choose a transformation from that.
If the CI for λ contains 1, no transformation may be needed even when the optimal λ is not 1; otherwise pick a rounded, interpretable λ inside the CI

If the confidence interval for λ contains 1 , no transformation may be needed , even if the optimal λ is not exactly 1. Otherwise, pick a rounded, interpretable λ inside the interval (for example 0.5 for square root, or 0 for log).
Audits and checklists with scored 5S scorecards
Use a checklist scored on each S for every work area, and post the scorecard where everyone sees it. Scoring turns "it looks clean" into a number that can be tracked and compared.
Visual controls: floor markings, shadow boards, labels
Make the standard visible so deviations are obvious at a glance: floor markings (tape outlines for carts and bins), shadow boards (a painted outline for each tool), labels , and color coding.
Standard work and ownership by area
Document the standard for how each area should look and operate, and give each area a named owner who is accountable for it. Without an owner, nobody fixes drift.
Regular schedule: daily, weekly, and management audits
A common pattern: daily self-checks by the operators, weekly supervisor audits, and periodic management audits. Results are reviewed and acted on.
The gains decayed. Which S failed?
The 5S gains decayed. Which S failed? Self-Discipline/Sustain.
Self-Discipline (Sustain). The first four S's can be done in a one-time event. The fifth is the habit and the system that keeps them going.
A pull signal that authorizes production or movement only when downstream consumes

A kanban is a signal (often a card or an empty container) that authorizes production or movement only when the downstream step has used material. Nothing is made or moved until the signal arrives. This is how pull systems limit inventory.
Card types: production kanban and withdrawal (move) kanban
Production kanban: authorizes the upstream step to make more. Withdrawal (move) kanban: authorizes the downstream step to take material from the upstream supply.
Rules: downstream pulls, no defects passed on, produce only what was withdrawn, level the load

Downstream pulls from upstream, not the other way around. Upstream produces only what was withdrawn. No defects are passed downstream. Level the load (smooth the volume and mix) so the signals stay steady.
Number of kanbans N = (demand × lead time × (1 + safety factor)) / container size; round up to the next whole kanban

N = (demand × lead time × (1 + safety factor)) ÷ container size. Demand and lead time must use the same time unit. The result must be rounded up to the next whole number, because you cannot have a fraction of a kanban. Example: demand 120 units per day, replenishment lead time 0.5 day, safety factor 20%, container size 10. N = 120 × 0.5 × 1.2 ÷ 10 = 72 ÷ 10 = 7.2, so 8 kanbans.

A supermarket is a controlled stock location where the downstream step picks what it needs, and each pick sends a signal to replenish. A two-bin system uses two containers of the same item. When one empties, it is the signal to refill while the second bin keeps work going.
CONWIP (constant WIP): glossary only, low exam yield
Extension, glossary only. CONWIP (constant work in process) caps the total amount of work in a line instead of controlling each step. Low exam yield.
Compute N from demand, lead time, and container size.
Given demand, lead time, safety factor, and container size, use the formula, keep the time units the same, and round up.
Shingo's mistake-proofing: prevent the error or make it immediately obvious
Poka-yoke (mistake-proofing), from Shigeo Shingo, designs the process so an error cannot happen , or is caught immediately when it does. It does not rely on people being careful.

Control (prevention) type: physically prevents the error or stops the process. The mistake cannot be made. Warning (detection) type: signals the error (a light, buzzer, or message) but does not stop the process. A person still has to act. Control type is stronger.

Contact: uses shape, size, or color to allow only the correct part or position (a part that only fits one way). Fixed-value (counting): checks that the right number of items or motions occurred (a tray with a slot for each of 12 screws). Motion-step (sequence): checks that steps happen in the correct order (step 3 cannot start until step 2 is confirmed).
Source inspection and 100% automatic checking at the point of error

Source inspection checks the conditions that could cause an error before the defect happens, at the source, rather than finding the defect later. Combined with 100% automatic checking at the point of the error, it prevents defects from moving forward.
A fixture that only accepts a part in one orientation is a prevention poka-yoke.
A fixture that only accepts a part in one orientation is a prevention (control) poka-yoke using the contact method. A buzzer that sounds but does not stop the line is a warning (detection) poka-yoke.
Rational subgrouping: variation within a subgroup is common cause; variation between subgroups reveals special cause

Form each subgroup from items made under the same conditions, close together in time , so that variation within a subgroup is only common-cause variation. Then variation between subgroups reveals special causes such as shifts or drift. Example: take 5 consecutive parts from one machine each hour. Do not mix parts from two machines in one subgroup, because machine differences would hide inside the subgroup.

Subgroup size: commonly 3 to 5 for Xbar-R. Large enough to give a good average, small enough to stay "rational." Frequency: often enough to catch a change before much bad product is made. It depends on how fast the process can change and how costly sampling is. These choices decide what the chart can detect.
Variable vs attribute data drives chart choice
Continuous (variable) data and counted (attribute) data use different charts. The data type is the first step in the selection tree.
Phase I (establish limits; often about 20 to 25 subgroups, a guideline not a rule) vs Phase II (monitor)

Phase I: collect data (often about 20 to 25 subgroups, a guideline and not a rule), compute trial limits , find and remove special causes, and settle on the limits. Phase II: use those limits to monitor the process going forward.
Define exactly what counts as a defect and how it is measured, so every collector records the same thing. A check sheet is a simple form for recording data consistently as it is collected.
Pick the chart from the data type and subgroup size (see SG-0 selection tree).
Use the data type and subgroup size and read the chart off the selection tree above.
Rational subgrouping purpose: maximize the chance for common-cause variation within a subgroup and expose special-cause shifts between subgroups
Maximize the chance that common-cause variation shows up within subgroups, and that special-cause shifts show up between them. A poorly chosen subgroup can hide a problem or invent one.
Individuals data, subgroup size 1; moving range of consecutive points
The individuals and moving range chart. Each plotted point is a single reading (subgroup size 1). The moving range (MR) is the absolute difference between each reading and the one before it.
UCL/LCL = X̄ ± 2.66 × MR̄; UCL for MR = 3.267 × MR̄; the MR chart LCL = 0 (D3 = 0 for n < 7); 2.66 = 3 / 1.128
Individuals chart: center = X̄; UCL and LCL = X̄ ± 2.66 × MR̄. Moving range chart: UCL = 3.267 × MR̄ ; LCL = 0 (D3 is 0 for subgroups below 7). The number 2.66 comes from 3 ÷ 1.128.
Used for slow, low-volume, or batch data; sensitive to non-normality
For slow, low-volume, or batch data, where a subgroup is not practical. It is sensitive to non-normality because it works on individual values.
The I-MR formulas are not on the reference sheet, but the n = 2 row of the constants table gives them: 2.66 = 3 ÷ d2 (1.128); MR chart UCL = D4 × MR̄ = 3.267 × MR̄; LCL = D3 × MR̄ = 0.

The I-MR formulas are not on the reference sheet, but the n = 2 row of the constants table gives them: 2.66 = 3 ÷ d2 (d2 = 1.128), and MR chart UCL = D4 × MR̄ = 3.267 × MR̄. Know how to build them from that row.
Two charts together: an Xbar chart (subgroup averages, watching the center) and an R chart (subgroup ranges, watching the spread). Used for subgroups of 2 to 10 , commonly 3 to 5.
Xbar limits = X̿ ± A2 × R̄. R chart: UCL = D4 × R̄, LCL = D3 × R̄
Grand mean X̿ = ΣX̄ ÷ k , and R̄ = ΣR ÷ k , where k is the number of subgroups. Xbar chart: UCL and LCL = X̿ ± A2 × R̄. R chart: UCL = D4 × R̄ , LCL = D3 × R̄.

The reference document has a Control Charts Table of Constants for n = 2 to 25. Key rows: n A2 A3 d2 D3 D4 B3 B4 2 1.880 2.659 1.128 0.000 3.267 0.000 3.267 3 1.023 1.954 1.693 0.000 2.575 0.000 2.568 4 0.729 1.628 2.059 0.000 2.282 0.000 2.266 5 0.577 1.427 2.326 0.000 2.114 0.000 2.089 10 0.308 0.975 3.078 0.223 1.777 0.284 1.716 Xbar-R uses A2, D3, D4, and d2. Xbar-S uses A3, B3, and B4. Always use the values in the table you are given, since other published tables round slightly differently.
Review the R chart first (variation), then the Xbar chart (center)
Check the R chart (variation) before the Xbar chart (center). If the spread is out of control, the Xbar limits are not reliable.
The sheet gives the formulas and the constants table. Practice finding the right column (A2 for Xbar-R, A3 for Xbar-S) and the right row (your subgroup size n).
The sheet gives both the formulas and the constants table. Practice finding the right column (A2 for Xbar-R, A3 for Xbar-S) and the right row (your subgroup size n) quickly.
Defects per unit, variable sample size (Poisson)
Plots defects per unit when the sample size or area of opportunity varies. The count follows a Poisson pattern.

ū = Σc / Σn. The reference sheet limits use the average subgroup size: ū ± 3√(ū / n̄), with n̄ = Σnᵢ / k. Software draws limits that vary with each subgroup's nᵢ. Use the sheet's n̄ form for hand calculation unless told otherwise.

ū = Σc ÷ Σn (total defects over total units inspected). n̄ = Σnᵢ ÷ k (average subgroup size). UCL and LCL = ū ± 3 × √(ū ÷ n̄). Software usually draws limits that vary with each subgroup's own n. For hand calculation, use the sheet's n̄ form unless told otherwise.
c chart (on the reference sheet): constant area of opportunity; c̄ = total defects / number of subgroups; limits = c̄ ± 3√c̄. The sheet's notation for c̄ is loose.

The c chart counts defects when the area of opportunity is constant. c̄ = total defects ÷ number of subgroups , and limits = c̄ ± 3 × √c̄. The sheet's notation for c̄ is loose, so use the definition above.
Defects per invoice, different batch sizes
Defects per invoice with different batch sizes: U chart.
If the computed LCL is negative, set it to 0
If the computed LCL is negative, set it to 0 , since a count cannot be below zero.
Plots the proportion defective in each sample when the sample size varies. The counts follow a binomial pattern.
p̄ = Σ(np) / Σn. The reference sheet limits use the average subgroup size: p̄ ± 3√(p̄(1 − p̄) / n̄), with n̄ = Σnᵢ / k. Software varies the limits with each nᵢ.
p̄ = Σ(np) ÷ Σn (total defectives over total inspected). n̄ = Σnᵢ ÷ k. UCL and LCL = p̄ ± 3 × √[ p̄(1 − p̄) ÷ n̄ ]. Software varies the limits with each subgroup's n.
Percent of orders shipped late with varying daily volume: P chart.
The percent of orders shipped late, with changing daily volume, is a p chart.
If the computed LCL is negative, set it to 0; the UCL cannot meaningfully exceed 1
If the computed LCL is negative, set it to 0 , and the UCL cannot meaningfully exceed 1 (100%).
Number of defective units, constant sample size
Plots the number of defective units in each sample when the sample size is constant.
Center = np̄ (average number defective per sample). UCL and LCL = np̄ ± 3 × √[ np̄(1 − p̄) ].
Constant sample of 200: NP chart. Varying size: P chart.
A constant sample of 200 is an np chart. If the size varies, it is a p chart.
If the computed LCL is negative, set it to 0; the UCL cannot exceed n
If the computed LCL is negative, set it to 0. The UCL cannot exceed n.
Subgroup size above about 10; the standard deviation is a better spread estimate than the range
Like Xbar-R, but the second chart shows the subgroup standard deviation (S). It is used for subgroups above about 10 , where the range wastes information.
Xbar limits = X̿ ± A3 × s̄; S chart UCL = B4 × s̄, LCL = B3 × s̄; σ estimate = s̄ ÷ c4 (c4 is not in the sheet's table)
Xbar chart: UCL and LCL = X̿ ± A3 × S̄. S chart: UCL = B4 × S̄, LCL = B3 × S̄. σ estimate = S̄ ÷ c4. (c4 is not in the sheet's table, so it would have to be supplied.)
n = 10 constants from the sheet: A3 0.975, B3 0.284, B4 1.716. (c4 = 0.9727 is not in the table.)
From the sheet's table at n = 10: A3 = 0.975, B3 = 0.284, B4 = 1.716. (c4 = 0.9727 is not in the table.)
Subgroups of 15 readings call for an Xbar-S chart.
Check the sheet's S chart entry
The S chart limits are UCL = B4 × S̄ and LCL = B3 × S̄; the mean chart uses A3 × S̄. (The 2010 sheet misprinted B4 for both; version 1.4.2 is correct.)
The S chart limits are UCL = B4 × S̄ and LCL = B3 × S̄ , and the mean chart uses A3 × S̄ . (The 2010 copy of the sheet misprinted B4 for both; version 1.4.2 has it right.)
Plots cumulative deviations from a target
Plots the cumulative sum of deviations from a target. Each new point adds to the running total, so small consistent departures pile up and become visible.
Detects small, sustained shifts faster than Shewhart charts; slower for large shifts
Detects small, sustained shifts faster than a Shewhart chart (Xbar, individuals). It is slower for large, sudden shifts.
Typical starting parameters: target, reference value k (about 0.5σ), decision interval h (about 4 to 5σ). These are design choices, not fixed thresholds.
Typical starting values: a target , a reference value k (about 0.5σ ), and a decision interval h (about 4 to 5σ ). These are design choices, not fixed thresholds.
"Detect a small persistent drift": CuSum or EWMA.
When a question says "detect a small persistent drift," the answer is CuSum or EWMA.
The CuSum on the reference sheet
CuSum on the reference sheet (standardized): Sₙ = (1 ÷ σx) × Σ(xᵢ − T), the running sum of deviations from target T, in σ units

The sheet gives a standardized version: Sₙ = (1 ÷ σx) × Σ(xᵢ − T) , where T is the target and σx the process standard deviation. It is the running total of deviations from target, measured in σ units. Example: target 50, σ = 2, readings 52, 51, 53. Deviations 2, 1, 3, total 6. S = 6 ÷ 2 = 3.0.
EWMA on the reference sheet: EWMAₜ = λ·Yₜ + (1 − λ)·EWMAₜ₋₁, with λ greater than 0 and at most 1, and EWMA₀ = target or historical mean

EWMAₜ = λ × Yₜ + (1 − λ) × EWMAₜ₋₁ (this is on the reference sheet), where λ is greater than 0 and at most 1, and EWMA₀ is the target or the historical mean. Each point is a weighted average of the newest reading and all earlier ones, with recent data weighted most.
λ typically 0.05 to 0.25 (a common choice, not fixed); control limits about 3σ of the EWMA statistic
λ is typically 0.05 to 0.25 (a common choice, not fixed). Small λ gives more smoothing and better detection of small shifts. Control limits are about 3σ of the EWMA statistic.
Detects small shifts; weights recent data more heavily; fairly robust to non-normality
Detects small shifts , weights recent data more heavily, and is fairly robust to non-normality.
CuSum vs EWMA vs Shewhart: small shifts favor CuSum/EWMA.
For small shifts , favor CuSum or EWMA. For large, sudden shifts, a regular Shewhart chart is fine.
Western Electric rules: 1 point beyond 3σ; 2 of 3 beyond 2σ (same side); 4 of 5 beyond 1σ (same side); 8 in a row on one side of center
A signal is: One point beyond 3σ. Two of three points beyond 2σ (same side). Four of five points beyond 1σ (same side). Eight in a row on one side of the center line.
Nelson tests (Minitab): 1 point >3σ; 9 in a row on one side; 6 trending; 14 alternating; 2 of 3 >2σ; 4 of 5 >1σ; 15 within 1σ (stratification); 8 beyond 1σ both sides (mixture)

One point beyond 3σ. Nine in a row on one side of the center line. Six in a row steadily increasing or decreasing (a trend). Fourteen in a row alternating up and down. Two of three points beyond 2σ (same side). Four of five points beyond 1σ (same side). Fifteen in a row within 1σ of the center line (either side), which suggests stratification or limits that are too wide. Eight in a row beyond 1σ on either side, which suggests a mixture of two populations.
Common cause means leave alone and improve the system. Special cause means investigate and react.
Common cause: natural variation. Leave it alone and improve the system if the level is not acceptable. Special cause: an assignable event. Investigate and react.
Control limits are not spec limits
Control limits are not spec limits. 3σ limits give about a 0.27% false-alarm rate per independent point; using several sensitizing rules together raises the overall false-alarm rate.

Control limits come from the process. Spec limits come from the customer. A 3σ limit gives about a 0.27% false-alarm rate per independent point. Using several sensitizing rules together raises the overall false-alarm rate.
Chart selection by data type (see SG-0)
By data type and subgroup size (see the selection tree at the top of this file).
Other control methods: standard work, training, documented procedures, audits, process-owner handoff
Charts are one method. Others include standard work, training, documented procedures, audits, and handoff to the process owner.
Read the chart and choose the action
Given a chart, identify the rule violated and decide the correct action (investigate vs leave alone).
Given a chart, name the rule that was violated and decide: investigate (special cause) or leave alone (common cause).
