Anatomy: plotted statistic, center line, UCL/LCL at ±3σ of the plotted statistic, and zones A (2 to 3σ), B (1 to 2σ), C (center to 1σ) used by the sensitizing rules. σ of the data differs from σ of the statistic (σ/√n for subgroup means).

A chart has the plotted statistic , a center line , and UCL and LCL at ±3σ of the plotted statistic. The space between is divided into zones : Zone A (2 to 3σ), Zone B (1 to 2σ), and Zone C (center to 1σ). The sensitizing rules use these zones. Note that the σ of the data differs from the σ of the statistic : for subgroup means, the plotted statistic has σ ÷ √n.
Western Electric (8 in a row on one side) and Nelson/Minitab (9) are different rule systems, not contradictions. Use one set per question and do not mix them.
Western Electric (8 in a row) and Nelson or Minitab (9 in a row) are different rule systems, not contradictory. Use one set per question and do not mix them.
Minitab applies only the beyond-limits test on time-weighted charts (EWMA, CuSum)
Minitab applies only the beyond-the-limits test on time-weighted charts (EWMA and CuSum).
Do not recompute limits just because a point is out
Do not recompute limits because a point is out of control. Investigate the assignable cause; recompute only after a verified process change and a stable baseline.
Investigate the assignable cause. Recompute limits only after a verified process change and a stable baseline. Deleting points and re-limiting to make a chart look in control hides the problem.
Inside the limits is not the same as in control
A point inside the 3σ limits can still violate a run or trend rule; 'all points within limits' does not prove control
A point inside the 3σ limits can still violate a run or trend rule. "All points within limits" does not prove control.
Cost of controls versus the benefit
Compare the cost of sustaining controls (monitoring, training, audits) to the benefit of preventing regression

Controls are not free. Compare the cost of sustaining them (monitoring, training, audits, inspection, software) with the benefit of preventing the process from sliding back. A control that costs more than the loss it prevents is not worth keeping.
ROI and payback logic carried from 1.3.3
Use the same tools as in SG-1.3. ROI = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost. Payback = investment ÷ annual benefit (assuming a steady yearly benefit).
Include both hard and soft benefits, and ongoing costs
Count both hard and soft benefits , and include ongoing costs , not just the upfront cost. A control with a small purchase price and a large yearly labor cost can be more expensive than it looks.
Is a costly control justified? Compare expected savings with the cost of control.
Compare the expected savings the control protects with the total cost of the control. The expected loss without the control is the savings at risk times the chance they slip away.
Process step, characteristic (CTQ), specification/target, measurement system, sample size and frequency, control method, owner, reaction plan, document reference

For each key process step, a control plan lists: the process step the characteristic (CTQ) being controlled the specification or target the measurement system (and that it has been validated) the sample size and frequency the control method (a control chart, a poka-yoke, an SOP) the owner (who is responsible) the reaction plan (what to do when something goes wrong) a document reference (where the procedure lives)
Supporting items: SOPs, training, process owner, transition plan
SOPs , training , a named process owner , and a transition plan for the handoff from the project team.
A living document owned by the process owner
The control plan is owned by the process owner and updated as the process changes. It is not filed away at project close.
A control plan is missing a reaction plan or an owner. Identify what is wrong.
Check the list above. The most common gaps are a missing reaction plan and a missing owner.
Trigger (out-of-control signal or rule), immediate containment, who acts, investigation, corrective action, escalation, documentation, resume

A response plan covers: the trigger (an out-of-control signal or a rule violation) immediate containment (stop bad product moving on) who acts investigation to find the cause corrective action escalation if it cannot be resolved quickly documentation resuming normal operation
Decision rules for out-of-spec product disposition
The plan states the rules for handling nonconforming product: segregate it , then decide to sort, rework, scrap, or accept as is , with named authority for each decision.
Which action follows an out-of-control signal? Contain, investigate, correct, document.
Contain, investigate, correct, document. Containing comes first so that suspect product does not reach the customer.
Out of control is not out of spec

Out of control is not out of spec: a point can signal a special cause while within spec, and a stable process can still produce out-of-spec output. Response plans differ: investigate a special cause vs redesign the process.

A point can signal a special cause while still within the spec. Investigate the cause even though the part would pass. A stable process can still produce out-of-spec output if its natural variation is too wide or off target. The responses differ: investigate a special cause , versus redesign or improve the process itself.
readings: Meanings of Six Sigma

Why this matters "Six Sigma" is used three different ways, often in the same sentence. Exam questions take advantage of that. If you know which meaning a question intends, and you know the numbers behind the name, a whole family of questions becomes easy. The big idea Every process varies. No two deliveries take exactly the same time, no two bolts are exactly the same length. Customers set limits on how much variation they will accept. Six Sigma is about making the variation so small, compared with those limits, that defects almost never happen. The name comes from a Greek letter. Sigma (σ) is the symbol statisticians use for the standard deviation , the typical distance of individual results from their average. A small σ means results are tightly bunched. A large σ means they are spread out. Three meanings of "Six Sigma" A metric. A "six sigma process" produces about 3.4 defects per million opportunities (DPMO) . This is a performance level you can measure and compare. A methodology. Six Sigma is a structured way to solve problems, called DMAIC : Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control. When someone says "we ran a Six Sigma project", they mean this. A management philosophy. Six Sigma is also a way to run an organization: decisions based on data, projects chosen for their effect on customers and the business, and trained people (the "belts") who lead the work. When a question asks "what is Six Sigma?", the best answer usually includes all three. When it asks about 3.4 DPMO, it means the metric. Sigma level: how many σ fit before the limit Imagine measuring the weight of cereal boxes. The weights form a hill-shaped pattern called a normal distribution : most boxes are near the average, and fewer and fewer are far away from it. The customer (or the law) sets a specification limit , for example "no box above 56 g of air space" or "no delivery later than 5 days". The sigma level asks one question: how many standard deviations fit between the process average and the nearest specification limit? Z = (specification limit − process mean) ÷ σ That number is called Z . If the mean is 50, σ is 2 and the upper limit is 56, then Z = (56 − 50) ÷ 2 = 3 . Three standard deviations fit, so the process is at a sigma level of 3 . Upper spec limit (USL) 1σ 1σ Mean (μ) Defects 2 steps of σ fit: sigma level 2 The farther the limit is from the mean, measured in σ steps, the smaller the tail of defects beyond it. More room means fewer results land beyond the limit. Each extra σ of room cuts defects dramatically, because the tails of the normal curve shrink very fast. You can get more σ of room in two ways: reduce the variation (make σ smaller, so more of them fit), or center the process (move the mean away from the limit it is crowding). That is why the goal of Six Sigma is reducing variation and centering the process. Inspecting finished products and throwing out the bad ones does neither. It only hides the problem and adds cost. The 1.5σ shift: why 6σ means 3.4 per million Here is the part that confuses almost everyone. If a process truly had six standard deviations of room on one side, the chance of a result beyond the limit would be about 1 in a billion on that side (about 0.002 parts per million counting both sides). So why does everyone say six sigma is 3.4 per million ? Because of a convention Motorola built into the definition. Motorola observed that processes measured over a short period look better than they really are over months and years. Over time the average drifts: new material lots, new operators, tool wear, seasons. Motorola assumed the average can drift about 1.5σ toward a limit in the long run. USL Short term Long term (drifted) 1.5σ drift Many more defects Short-term data (solid) has full room to the limit. Over the long term the average drifts about 1.5σ (dashed), and many more results cross the limit. So the convention says: Long-term Z = short-term Z − 1.5 A process with 6σ of room in short-term data is expected to have only 4.5σ of room in the long run. The tail beyond 4.5σ is 3.4 per million . That is where the famous number comes from. The sigma level that people report is the short-term figure (the 6). The DPMO they quote with it is the long-term expectation (the 3.4). The anchor table These are worth memorizing. They all include the 1.5σ shift. Sigma level Long-term Z DPMO (defects per million opportunities) Yield 2 0.5 308,538 69.1% 3 1.5 66,807 93.3% 4 2.5 6,210 99.38% 5 3.5 233 99.977% 6 4.5 3.4 99.99966% Notice how fast the defect rate falls. Going from 3 sigma to 4 sigma cuts defects by more than 10 times. Going from 5 to 6 cuts them by almost 70 times. For contrast, with no shift (pure statistics), the area outside ±3σ is 0.27% (2,700 per million), outside ±4σ about 63 per million , and outside ±6σ about 0.002 per million . Connecting sigma level to Cpk You will meet a capability index called Cpk in Measure (2.4). It measures the same "room to the nearest limit", but in units of 3σ instead of σ: Cpk = Z ÷ 3, so Z = 3 × Cpk So Cpk 1.0 = 3 sigma , Cpk 1.33 = 4 sigma , Cpk 2.0 = 6 sigma . A Cpk of 1.33 therefore corresponds to about 6,210 DPMO in the long term (using the shift). The IASSC Reference Document states this relationship for attribute data as Cpk = (1.5 + Z of the long-term yield) ÷ 3, which is the same idea written the other way round: long-term Z plus 1.5 gives the short-term sigma level, and dividing by 3 gives Cpk. Worked example A trucking terminal loads trailers. The time to load has a mean of 40 minutes and a standard deviation of 4 minutes (from two weeks of data, so treat it as short-term). Dispatch needs every trailer loaded within 52 minutes. Room to the limit: 52 − 40 = 12 minutes. In σ units: Z = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 . The process is at a 3 sigma level . Long-term expectation using the convention: long-term Z = 3 − 1.5 = 1.5. From the anchor table, about 66,807 late loads per million , or roughly 6.7%. Without the shift: the one-sided tail beyond Z = 3 is about 0.135%, or 1,350 per million . That is what the next two weeks would look like if nothing drifts. Which answer is right? Both, under different assumptions. If a question uses words like "sigma level", "long-term" or "DPMO" and gives the 3.4 / 6,210 style numbers, use the shift. If it simply gives a mean, σ and a limit and asks for the expected fraction beyond the limit, use the Z table directly with no shift. How to reach 4 sigma: you need Z = 4, so 12 ÷ σ = 4, giving σ = 3 minutes. Alternatively, keep σ = 4 and move the mean to 52 − 16 = 36 minutes. Usually a project does some of each. Common mistakes and exam traps Mixing the two "six sigmas". "Six sigma = 3.4 DPMO" includes the shift. "Six sigma = ±6σ, about 0.002 ppm" does not. Read which one the question is using. Adding the shift when you should not. If the question gives short-term σ and asks for expected defects without mentioning a shift or sigma level, use the Z table with no 1.5. Thinking Six Sigma means inspecting harder. Inspection catches defects after they are made. Six Sigma reduces variation so they are not made. Forgetting the nearest limit. With two limits, the sigma level is set by the closer one, because that is where the defects come from. Check yourself Name the three meanings of Six Sigma. A process has mean 100, σ = 5, and an upper limit of 115 (no lower limit). What is its sigma level? Why is a six sigma process said to make 3.4 DPMO instead of about 0.002 ppm? A process runs at 6,210 DPMO. What sigma level is that, and what Cpk? Two teams improve the same process. One cuts σ in half. The other moves the mean away from the limit by 1σ. Which gains more sigma level if the process started at Z = 3? Show answers A metric (3.4 DPMO), a methodology (DMAIC), and a management philosophy (data-driven, project-based improvement). Z = (115 − 100) ÷ 5 = 3, so a 3 sigma level. The convention assumes the long-term mean drifts 1.5σ toward the limit, so a short-term 6σ process has 4.5σ of long-term room, and the tail beyond 4.5σ is 3.4 per million. 4 sigma, and Cpk = 4 ÷ 3 ≈ 1.33. Halving σ doubles Z from 3 to 6, a gain of 3. Moving the mean 1σ gains only 1 (Z = 4). Cutting variation is far more powerful here. Key takeaways Six Sigma is a metric, a method (DMAIC), and a philosophy. Sigma level = how many σ fit between the mean and the nearest spec limit. The 1.5σ shift convention turns a short-term 6σ into 3.4 DPMO long-term. Memorize: 2σ = 308,538; 3σ = 66,807; 4σ = 6,210; 5σ = 233; 6σ = 3.4 DPMO. Cpk = Z ÷ 3, so Cpk 1.33 = 4σ. The goal is less variation and better centering, not more inspection.
General History of Six Sigma and Continuous Improvement

Why this matters Six Sigma did not appear from nowhere. Almost every tool in it was invented by someone between the 1920s and the 1990s. The exam asks matching questions: which person gave us which idea, and what came first. Learning the story makes these easy, because each idea grew out of the one before. The big idea The history has three strands that eventually merged: Statistical quality control (Shewhart, Deming): use statistics to understand and reduce variation. Quality management (Juran, Feigenbaum, Crosby, Ishikawa, Taguchi): make quality a management responsibility and count what poor quality costs. Lean (Toyota: Toyoda, Ohno, Shingo): remove waste and make work flow. Motorola combined strand 1 and 2 into Six Sigma in 1986. In the 2000s, companies merged it with strand 3 to make Lean Six Sigma. The quality pioneers, in order Walter Shewhart (1920s, Bell Laboratories). Shewhart realized that all processes vary, and that there are two kinds of variation: the routine background kind that is always present, and unusual variation that has a specific cause. In 1924 he invented the control chart to tell them apart. He also described a cycle of learning (plan, do, check, act) that later became famous. Shewhart is the father of statistical quality control. W. Edwards Deming (1950s onward). A student of Shewhart's ideas, Deming taught statistical quality methods to Japanese industry from 1950, and Japan's quality revolution followed. He popularized the PDCA cycle (he preferred PDSA : Plan, Do, Study, Act), named the two kinds of variation common cause and special cause , and wrote 14 Points for Management , which say that most quality problems come from the system that management designs, not from the workers. Japan's top quality award is the Deming Prize. Joseph Juran (1950s onward). Juran wrote the Quality Control Handbook (1951) and focused on management. His Quality Trilogy says quality takes three processes: quality planning , quality control , and quality improvement . He applied the Pareto principle to quality (the "vital few and trivial many") and pushed companies to measure the cost of poor quality in money, the language executives understand. Armand Feigenbaum (1950s). Feigenbaum coined Total Quality Control : quality is everyone's job across the whole company, from design to sales, not just the inspection department. He also described the "hidden plant", the share of a factory's capacity spent fixing mistakes. Kaoru Ishikawa (1950s to 1960s, Japan). Ishikawa created the cause-and-effect diagram , also called the fishbone or Ishikawa diagram, and promoted quality circles : small groups of workers who meet to solve problems in their own area. He also championed the "seven basic quality tools" for everyday problem solving. Philip Crosby (1979). Crosby wrote Quality Is Free , arguing that preventing defects costs less than fixing them, so quality pays for itself. He promoted zero defects as a performance standard and defined quality as conformance to requirements . Genichi Taguchi (1960s to 1980s, Japan). Taguchi introduced the quality loss function : any deviation from the target value causes some loss, even inside the specification limits, and the loss grows quickly the farther you go. He also developed robust design : designing products and processes that perform well even when conditions vary. Toyota and the roots of Lean Sakichi Toyoda built automatic looms in the early 1900s that stopped by themselves when a thread broke . This idea, building quality into the machine so it never produces defects silently, is called jidoka . Taiichi Ohno developed the Toyota Production System (TPS) from the late 1940s through the 1970s: just-in-time production, pull systems, kanban and waste elimination. Shigeo Shingo worked with Toyota on SMED (single-minute exchange of die, fast changeovers) and poka-yoke (mistake-proofing). Lean is covered in depth in 1.4. Motorola invents Six Sigma In the early 1980s Motorola was losing market share to higher-quality Japanese competitors. CEO Bob Galvin demanded dramatic improvement. In 1986 engineer Bill Smith proposed the Six Sigma standard (3.4 defects per million opportunities), and Mikel Harry developed much of the structured, statistics-based problem-solving approach and the belt training system. Motorola won the first Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award in 1988 , which made its methods famous. AlliedSignal and GE scale it up Larry Bossidy brought Six Sigma to AlliedSignal in the early 1990s. Jack Welch made it company-wide at General Electric from 1995 , tying managers' bonuses to it and publicizing large savings. GE's success turned Six Sigma into a global business movement. Lean Six Sigma and standards In the late 1990s and 2000s companies combined Six Sigma (variation and defects) with Lean (waste and speed) into Lean Six Sigma . In 2011 the international standard ISO 13053 described the DMAIC methodology, giving it a formal reference. It is rarely tested. A timeline to remember When Who What Early 1900s Sakichi Toyoda Self-stopping loom (jidoka) 1924 Shewhart Control chart 1950s Deming PDCA/PDSA, 14 points, Japan 1951 Juran Quality handbook, trilogy, cost of quality 1950s Feigenbaum Total Quality Control 1950s to 60s Ishikawa Fishbone, quality circles 1950s to 70s Ohno, Shingo Toyota Production System, SMED, poka-yoke 1979 Crosby Quality Is Free , zero defects 1980s Taguchi (in the West) Loss function, robust design 1986 Motorola (Smith, Harry, Galvin) Six Sigma 1988 Motorola First Baldrige Award 1995 GE (Welch) Six Sigma company-wide 2011 ISO ISO 13053 Memory hooks Shewhart = Sheets of control charts. The first statistician of quality. Deming = Do (PDSA) and Doctrine (14 points). Juran = Journey of three (trilogy) and Junk costs (cost of poor quality). Crosby = Costs nothing ("Quality Is Free"), zero defects. Ishikawa = Image of a fish. Taguchi = Target (loss grows away from target). Feigenbaum = Full company (total quality control). Common mistakes and exam traps Deming vs Shewhart on PDCA. Shewhart described the cycle; Deming popularized it (as PDSA). If asked who is associated with PDCA, Deming is the usual answer. Juran vs Pareto. Vilfredo Pareto was an economist who noticed that 80% of land was owned by 20% of people. Juran applied the idea to quality problems. Motorola vs GE. Motorola created Six Sigma (1986). GE did not invent it; GE scaled it. Crosby vs Deming on zero defects. Zero defects is Crosby. Deming actually criticized slogans and targets like that. Check yourself Who invented the control chart, and where? What are the three parts of Juran's trilogy? Which pioneer said any deviation from target creates loss, even within specification? Put in order: GE adopts Six Sigma, Shewhart's control chart, Motorola creates Six Sigma, Baldrige Award to Motorola. What is jidoka, and who started it? Show answers Walter Shewhart, at Bell Laboratories in the 1920s (1924). Quality planning, quality control and quality improvement. Genichi Taguchi (the quality loss function). Shewhart's control chart (1924), Motorola creates Six Sigma (1986), Baldrige Award to Motorola (1988), GE adopts Six Sigma (1995). Building quality in by making a machine stop automatically when something goes wrong. Sakichi Toyoda's self-stopping loom. Key takeaways Statistical control (Shewhart, Deming) + quality management (Juran, Feigenbaum, Crosby, Ishikawa, Taguchi) + Lean (Toyota) = Lean Six Sigma. Shewhart: control chart. Deming: PDSA, 14 points, common vs special cause. Juran: trilogy, Pareto, cost of quality. Crosby: zero defects. Ishikawa: fishbone. Taguchi: loss function. Feigenbaum: total quality control. Motorola 1986 (Bill Smith, Mikel Harry), Baldrige 1988; AlliedSignal (Bossidy) and GE (Welch, 1995) scaled it.
Deliverables of a Lean Six Sigma Project

Why this matters A Six Sigma project is not "work on the problem until it feels fixed". It moves through five phases, and each phase must produce specific outputs, called deliverables , before the next phase starts. Knowing what belongs where keeps a project honest, and the exam asks it directly. The big idea DMAIC works like a funnel of evidence: Define says what the problem is and why it matters. Measure says how big it really is, with trustworthy data. Analyze proves what is causing it. Improve fixes the proven causes and shows the fix works. Control makes sure it stays fixed after the team walks away. Skipping a phase is the most common way projects fail. Teams that jump from Define straight to Improve end up fixing what they guessed, not what the data shows. Deliverables, phase by phase Define: agree on the problem. Project charter , signed by the sponsor: business case, problem statement, goal, scope, team, timeline (see 1.3.1). SIPOC : a one-page, high-level map of Suppliers, Inputs, Process steps, Outputs and Customers (see 2.1.2). Voice of the customer (VOC) and the list of CTQs (critical-to-quality requirements) it produces (see 1.1.5 and 1.2.2). Stakeholder map : who is affected, who must support it. Measure: get the facts. Data collection plan : what to measure, how, how often, by whom. Validated measurement system (MSA) : proof that the measurements themselves are trustworthy (see 2.3). Baseline performance : how the process performs today (for example DPMO, yield, cycle time). Baseline capability : how well today's process fits the customer's limits (Cp, Cpk, sigma level, see 2.4). Analyze: find and prove the root causes. List of potential causes (from fishbones, process maps, brainstorming). Statistically validated root causes : the "vital few X's" proven with data, using hypothesis tests, regression and similar tools (see Domain 3). Improve: fix the causes and prove the fix. Selected solutions that address the proven causes. Pilot results : the solution tested on a small scale, with before-and-after data. Updated FMEA : risks of the new process reviewed (see 2.1.4). Implementation plan for full rollout. Control: lock in the gain. Control plan : what will be monitored, how, how often, by whom (see 5.3). Response plan : what to do if the process drifts. Standard work and training updated. Handoff to the process owner , who now owns the improved process. Financial sign-off of the benefits and project closure. Tollgate reviews At the end of each phase the team meets the sponsor or champion in a tollgate review (sometimes called a phase-gate). The team presents the deliverables. The sponsor decides: proceed, revisit, or stop. A phase is finished only when its deliverables are accepted. Tollgates keep management involved, catch weak evidence early, and let the organization stop projects that are no longer worth doing. Hard and soft benefits at closure When the project closes, benefits are reported in two kinds: Hard benefits : money that shows up on the financial statements, such as lower scrap, less overtime or fewer freight claims. Soft benefits : real but harder to put in the bank, such as freed-up capacity, better customer satisfaction, cost avoidance or improved safety. More in 1.3.3. Worked example A carrier wants to reduce damaged freight claims. Which phase does each item belong to? Item Phase Why "Claims cost $480k last year; goal is to halve them by Q4" Define Part of the charter (business case and goal) Gauge study confirming dock inspectors classify damage consistently Measure Validating the measurement system Current rate of 3.1 claims per 1,000 loads Measure Baseline performance Regression showing claims rise with trailers loaded in under 25 minutes Analyze Statistically validated root cause New load-securing procedure trialed at one terminal for 6 weeks Improve Pilot Weekly chart of claims per 1,000 loads with a reaction plan Control Control and response plan Common mistakes and exam traps Baseline capability belongs to Measure, not Define. Define says the problem exists and matters. Measure quantifies it. "Root causes" are Analyze deliverables only when validated with data. A brainstormed fishbone alone is a list of suspects, not proof. The pilot is Improve, not Control. Control comes after the solution is proven and rolled out. The process owner takes over in Control. The Green Belt does not keep running the process. Check yourself In which phase do you validate the measurement system? What is a tollgate review, and who decides whether the project passes? A team presents a fishbone diagram with 25 possible causes. Has it completed Analyze? Name two Control-phase deliverables. Is "reduced overtime, saving $60k this year" a hard or soft benefit? Show answers Measure. A review at the end of each phase where the team presents its deliverables; the sponsor or champion decides to proceed, revisit or stop. No. It has potential causes. Analyze ends only when the vital few causes are validated with data. Any two of: control plan, response plan, updated standard work and training, handoff to the process owner, financial sign-off. Hard. It is real money on the financial statements. Key takeaways Define: charter, SIPOC, VOC/CTQs, stakeholders. Measure: data collection plan, validated measurement system, baseline performance and capability. Analyze: statistically validated root causes. Improve: piloted solution, updated FMEA, implementation plan. Control: control plan, response plan, handoff, financial sign-off. A phase ends when the sponsor accepts its deliverables at a tollgate.
The Problem Solving Strategy Y = f(x)

Why this matters "Y = f(X)" is the single idea that ties all of Six Sigma together. Every phase of DMAIC is a step in finding and controlling the X's that drive a Y. Once you see a process this way, the tools make sense: each one either measures the Y, finds the X's, or controls them. The big idea Any result you care about depends on the things that go into producing it. Y = f(X₁, X₂, X₃, …, Xₙ) + error Read it as: the output (Y) is a function of the inputs (X's), plus some leftover variation we cannot explain. Think about a truck's fuel economy. That is your Y . What does it depend on? Speed, tire pressure, load weight, idling time, route terrain, weather, the engine's condition and the driver's habits. Those are the X's . If fuel economy is bad, staring at the fuel gauge will not fix it. You have to find which X's are responsible and change them. Vocabulary for Y and X The same two ideas have many names. Learn them as pairs: The Y The X Output Input Response Factor, driver Effect Cause Dependent variable Independent variable CTQ (what the customer cares about) Process variable Symptom Root cause The vital few A process may have dozens of X's, but usually only a few of them cause most of the variation in Y. These are the vital few ; the rest are the trivial many . Much of the Measure and Analyze work is narrowing a long list of suspect X's down to the vital few, using data. This is the same 80/20 thinking as the Pareto principle (see 1.2.4). Monitor the Y, control the X's If Y depends on the X's, then the way to control Y is to control the X's. Measuring Y tells you whether there is a problem. Controlling the X's prevents it. A thermostat does not control your comfort directly; it controls the furnace (an X), and comfort (the Y) follows. Checking every trailer's damage at delivery (Y) finds damage after the fact. Controlling load securing and driving behavior (X's) prevents it. This is why the Control phase sets up controls on the critical X's, while still watching Y to confirm it stays good. Four steps from problem to solution Six Sigma moves a problem through a statistical "translation" and back: Practical problem: "Too many late deliveries." Statistical problem: "On-time rate is 87% with high day-to-day variation; the target is 97%." Statistical solution: "Data shows 70% of late deliveries are explained by departure delays at two terminals and by route length over 400 miles." Practical solution: "Change dock scheduling at those two terminals and add a relay point on long routes." The middle two steps are where data replaces opinion. Types of inputs: C, N, P and X When teams list inputs (on a process map or fishbone), they often tag each one: C, controllable: you can set it and hold it, such as oven temperature or dispatch time. N, noise: it affects Y but is hard or too expensive to control, such as weather, traffic or humidity. You design around it instead. P, procedural (SOP): controlled by a written procedure, such as "inspect straps before departure". X, critical: an input proven by data to be one of the vital few. (Some materials use "X" for any input; in this classification it marks the critical ones.) Worked example A distribution center's problem: picking errors (wrong item shipped). The team lists these candidates. Which is the Y, and how would you tag the inputs? Number of picking errors per 1,000 order lines Picker experience (months) Shelf label layout Lighting in the aisle Daily order volume The written pick-and-check procedure The Y is picking errors per 1,000 order lines. It is the measurable outcome the customer feels. Inputs: picker experience (C, the company controls hiring and training), shelf label layout (C), aisle lighting (C), daily order volume (N, set by customers, not controllable), pick-and-check procedure (P). After analysis, if regression shows label layout and experience explain most of the errors, those two become the critical X's . Common mistakes and exam traps Picking a cause as the Y. In "which is the Y?" questions, the Y is the measurable outcome (errors, time, cost, satisfaction), not something that causes it. Trying to fix the Y directly. Rework, inspection and expediting attack the Y. Lasting fixes change the X's. Treating noise as controllable. You cannot control the weather; you can make the process robust to it. Check yourself In Y = f(X), which one is the dependent variable? A bakery's complaint rate depends on oven temperature, flour supplier, humidity and baking time. Which of these is most likely noise? Why does Six Sigma say "control the X's" instead of "inspect the Y"? Put in order: statistical solution, practical problem, practical solution, statistical problem. A hospital measures patient wait time. Is "number of nurses on shift" a Y or an X? Show answers Y. Humidity, because it affects results but is hard to control. Because Y is the result of the X's. Controlling the inputs prevents problems; inspecting the output only finds them after they happen. Practical problem, statistical problem, statistical solution, practical solution. An X: it is an input that influences wait time. Key takeaways Y = f(X) + error: outputs depend on inputs. Y = output, effect, response, CTQ. X = input, cause, factor. A few X's (the vital few) drive most of the variation. Monitor the Y, control the X's. Practical problem, statistical problem, statistical solution, practical solution. Inputs: controllable, noise, procedural, and critical (proven vital few).
Voice of the Customer, Business and Employee

Why this matters A project that improves something the customer does not care about is wasted effort. Six Sigma starts by listening: to customers, to the business, and to the people doing the work. Then it turns what they say, which is usually vague, into measurable requirements. The big idea There are three "voices" a project must hear: Voice of the Customer (VOC): what the external customer needs and expects. "My delivery has to arrive on the day you promised." Voice of the Business (VOB): what the organization needs: profit, cost, growth, regulatory compliance, return on investment. "We must cut fuel cost per mile by 8%." Voice of the Employee (VOE): what the people doing the work need: safety, tools, training, reasonable workload. "We cannot meet the schedule with two forklifts down." A good project balances all three. Satisfying customers in a way that bankrupts the business, or burns out employees, is not a success. Where VOC comes from There are two styles of listening: Reactive sources : information that arrives on its own, usually when something went wrong. Complaints, returns, warranty claims, credit notes, customer service calls, online reviews. Cheap to collect, but biased: you mainly hear from unhappy customers, and only about problems they notice. Proactive sources : information you go out and get. Surveys : reach many customers; good for measuring how many feel a certain way. Interviews : one-to-one, deep understanding of needs and reasons. Focus groups : small group discussion; good for exploring ideas. Observation / gemba walks : watching customers use the product or service where it happens ("gemba" means "the real place"). Reveals needs customers never say. CRM and transaction data : what customers actually do, not what they say. The best VOC combines both: reactive data shows where pain is, proactive methods explain why. Turning a vague voice into a CTQ Customers speak in general terms: "fast", "easy", "reliable", "friendly". You cannot measure "fast". So the team translates each statement in three steps, using a CTQ tree : Need : the general want. "Fast delivery." Drivers : what "fast" means to them, broken into specifics. "Order ships the same day", "Truck arrives on the promised day". CTQ : a measurable requirement with a target and a limit. "Order placed by 2 p.m. ships the same day (target 100%, at least 98%)"; "Delivery within the promised day (no later than 6 p.m.)". A CTQ has a measure , a target and a limit . More on CTQs in 1.2.2. The Kano model: not all needs are equal Professor Noriaki Kano showed that customer needs behave differently. Picture a chart: the horizontal axis is how well you deliver a feature, the vertical axis is customer satisfaction. Must-be (basic) needs. Expected so completely that customers do not even mention them: brakes that work, freight that is not damaged, an invoice with the right price. Delivering them perfectly earns no praise ; failing them causes strong dissatisfaction . They can only stop customers being unhappy. One-dimensional (performance) needs. More is better, less is worse, in a roughly straight line: faster delivery, lower price, better fuel economy. Customers talk about these openly and compare competitors on them. Attractive (delighter) needs. Customers do not expect them, so their absence causes no dissatisfaction, but their presence delights: live GPS tracking with a photo at delivery, a driver who calls ahead unasked. These create loyalty. Two more categories exist: Indifferent : customers do not care either way. Reverse : some customers actively dislike it (for example, too many notification texts). Needs move over time. Yesterday's delighter becomes today's performance need and tomorrow's must-be. Shipment tracking delighted customers once; now it is expected. QFD and the House of Quality Quality Function Deployment (QFD) is a structured way to connect customer requirements ("whats") to technical design characteristics ("hows"). Its main chart, the House of Quality , is a matrix with customer needs down the side, technical characteristics across the top, relationship strengths inside, and a triangular "roof" showing how the technical characteristics affect each other. It is mostly used in product design and is lightly tested. Worked example A freight broker surveys shippers. Classify each statement with Kano: Statement Kano category Why "The truck must show up." Must-be Expected; failure is a disaster, success earns nothing "The cheaper the rate, the better." One-dimensional Satisfaction rises steadily as price falls "I loved that you texted a photo of the signed delivery receipt." Attractive Unexpected, creates delight "I don't care which brand of truck you use." Indifferent No effect on satisfaction Now translate "I want to know where my freight is" into a CTQ. Need: visibility. Driver: location updates while in transit. CTQ: "Location update posted at least every 2 hours while the load is moving (target: 100% of loads)". Common mistakes and exam traps Over-delivering a must-be. Making must-be quality even better does not create delight; it only prevents dissatisfaction. Spend effort on performance and attractive needs once basics are reliable. Treating complaints as complete VOC. Complaints are reactive and biased toward unhappy, vocal customers. Stopping at the vague voice. "Fast" is not a CTQ. It needs a measure, a target and a limit. Forgetting VOB and VOE. A solution customers love but the business cannot afford is not acceptable. Check yourself What are the three voices, and give one example of each. Is analyzing returned products a reactive or proactive VOC source? A hotel guest is not pleased by clean sheets, but is furious if they are dirty. Which Kano category? What three elements does a well-written CTQ contain? Why might a delighter stop delighting? Show answers VOC (customer: on-time delivery), VOB (business: lower cost per mile), VOE (employees: working equipment and safety). Reactive. Must-be (basic). A measure, a target and a limit (specification). Customers get used to it, so it becomes expected (a performance or must-be need). Key takeaways VOC = customer, VOB = business, VOE = employees; balance all three. Reactive sources (complaints, returns) vs proactive sources (surveys, interviews, observation). Translate vague needs into measurable CTQs: need, then drivers, then CTQ. Kano: must-be (only dissatisfies), one-dimensional (more is better), attractive (only delights); plus indifferent and reverse. Needs drift over time from delighter to must-be.
Six Sigma Roles and Responsibilities

Why this matters Improvement projects fail more often for organizational reasons (no time, no resources, no support) than technical ones. Six Sigma assigns clear roles so that someone owns every part of making a project succeed. The exam asks who does what, especially who to go to when the team is blocked. The big idea Think of a project like a long-haul delivery: The shipper (sponsor) pays for it and cares about the result. Dispatch (champion) clears the way: permits, routes, problems with other departments. The driver (belt) does the work. The receiver (process owner) takes ownership at the end. A trainer (Master Black Belt) taught the driver and helps on hard routes. The roles Executive leadership. Sets the strategy, decides that the organization will use Six Sigma, and makes it part of how the business is run. Without visible executive support, programs fade. Sponsor. A senior manager who owns the business result the project affects. The sponsor funds the project, provides resources, signs the charter , and accepts the deliverables at tollgates. The sponsor is accountable for the result. Champion. A manager who links projects to strategy and removes organizational barriers : getting people released from other duties, resolving conflicts with other departments, getting decisions made. In many organizations the sponsor and champion are the same person; when they are separate, the champion often oversees several projects and helps choose them. Process owner. The person who owns the process day to day . They help define the problem, and at the end they take over the improved process and its control plan . If the process owner is not involved, improvements tend to disappear after the team leaves. Master Black Belt (MBB). The organization's Six Sigma expert. Trains and coaches Black Belts and Green Belts , helps with difficult statistics, reviews project quality, and often helps run the overall program. Black Belt (BB). Usually full-time on improvement. Leads larger, cross-functional projects, uses advanced statistics, and mentors Green Belts. Green Belt (GB). Usually part-time : keeps their regular job and leads smaller projects within their own area , or works on a Black Belt's team. Knows the core tools of DMAIC and basic statistics. Yellow Belt and White Belt. Basic awareness. Yellow Belts usually serve as team members, collect data and help with tasks; White Belts know the vocabulary and support local improvements. Team members. People who work in the process. They bring knowledge of how the work really happens, which no expert can replace. Summary table Role Time on projects Main job Sponsor Part Owns the result, funds it, signs the charter Champion Part Removes barriers, aligns to strategy Process owner Part Owns the process, takes over at the end Master Black Belt Full Trains, coaches, runs the program Black Belt Full Leads big projects, advanced analysis Green Belt Part Leads smaller projects in own area Yellow / White Belt Part Team support, basic tools Worked example A Green Belt's project to reduce invoice errors needs two people from the billing department for four hours a week, but the billing manager refuses to release them. Who should solve this? Not the Green Belt: they have no authority over another department's staff. This is an organizational barrier, so it goes to the champion (or sponsor), who can negotiate with the billing manager or escalate. After the project, who makes sure invoice errors stay low? The process owner for invoicing, using the control plan the team hands over. Common mistakes and exam traps "Who removes the roadblock?" The champion or sponsor, never the Green Belt. "Who signs the charter?" The sponsor (often with the champion and process owner). "Who owns the process after the project?" The process owner, not the belt. Black Belt vs Green Belt. Full-time vs part-time; cross-functional vs own area; advanced vs core statistics. Check yourself Who trains and mentors Black Belts? Which role usually works on improvement part-time while keeping their regular job? Who takes over the control plan at project closure? A team cannot get access to data held by another department. Who should they escalate to? What is the difference between a sponsor and a process owner? Show answers The Master Black Belt. The Green Belt. The process owner. The champion (or sponsor). The sponsor owns the business result and funds the project; the process owner runs the process day to day and keeps the improvement in place afterward. Key takeaways Sponsor: owns results, funds, signs the charter. Champion: removes barriers, aligns to strategy. Process owner: owns the process and its control plan after the project. MBB trains and coaches; BB leads big projects full-time; GB leads smaller projects part-time in their own area. Escalate organizational roadblocks to the champion or sponsor.
Defining a Process

Why this matters You cannot improve something you cannot describe. Before measuring anything, a team has to agree on exactly what process it is working on: where it starts, where it ends, who feeds it and who receives what it produces. Most "scope creep" and wasted effort comes from skipping this. The big idea A process is a series of activities that turns inputs into outputs for a customer . Inputs: materials, information, people's time, equipment, energy. Activities: the steps that transform them. Outputs: the product, service or information that comes out. Every job is a process, not just factory work. Dispatching a load is a process: inputs are the customer order, available trucks and drivers; activities are matching, scheduling and communicating; output is a dispatched truck with a confirmed plan. Boundaries: where does it start and stop? A process for a project needs a defined start point (the first step, triggered by something) and stop point (the last step, ending in an output). Everything between them is in scope . Everything outside is out of scope . For example, "order to delivery": Start: customer order received. Stop: delivery receipt signed. In scope: order entry, dispatch, loading, transport, unloading. Out of scope: invoicing and payment (they happen after the stop point), the customer's own purchasing (before the start). Clear boundaries stop a project from growing until it tries to fix the whole company (often called "boiling the ocean"). Suppliers and customers: internal and external External customers pay for the output: the shipper, the consignee. Internal customers are the next step or department inside the organization: the loading dock is dispatch's internal customer, billing is the driver's internal customer for paperwork. External suppliers are outside companies that provide inputs: fuel vendors, equipment lessors. Internal suppliers are departments providing inputs to your step: dispatch supplies the driver with a load plan. Thinking of the next step as a customer is powerful: if billing keeps getting incomplete paperwork, the driver's process has a quality problem, even if the external customer never sees it. Value-added, necessary, and waste Every step in a process falls into one of three types: Value-added (VA): the customer would willingly pay for it. It changes the product or service in a way the customer wants, and it is done right the first time. Driving the load toward the destination is value-added. Non-value-added but necessary (business value-added): the customer would not pay for it, but it cannot be removed today because of law, safety or business needs. Logging hours of service, pre-trip inspections and invoicing are examples. Non-value-added (pure waste): neither the customer nor the business needs it. Waiting at the dock, re-entering the same data twice, searching for paperwork. In most processes, value-added steps are a small fraction of the total time. Lean (1.4) focuses on removing pure waste and minimizing necessary non-value-added work. Manufacturing vs transactional processes Manufacturing processes make physical things. Defects are often visible and easy to count. Transactional (service) processes move information or provide services: billing, dispatch, customer service, hiring. Their "defects" (wrong invoice amount, missed callback) are often invisible until someone complains, and the work itself is hard to see, so mapping and measuring take more effort. Six Sigma works for both. Transactional processes often have more waste because nobody can see the work piling up. Worked example A team is told to "fix late invoices". Narrative: "A driver delivers, scans the signed bill of lading, and billing creates the invoice. Customers then pay within 30 days. Late invoices delay payment." Good scope: Start: signed delivery receipt. Stop: invoice sent to the customer. In scope: scanning, document transfer, invoice creation, review. Out of scope: the delivery itself and the customer's payment behavior. Why not include customer payment? The team cannot control when customers pay, and the problem as stated is late invoices , not late payments. Common mistakes and exam traps Choosing boundaries too wide. If the start or stop point includes things the team cannot influence, the project becomes unmanageable. Calling necessary steps value-added. Inspection, approvals and compliance paperwork are usually necessary non-value-added. Forgetting internal customers. The next step in the process is a customer too. Check yourself Define a process in one sentence. Is a pre-trip safety inspection value-added, necessary non-value-added, or waste? Who is the internal customer of a warehouse's picking step? Why do projects need a stop point? Give one reason defects are harder to see in transactional processes. Show answers A series of activities that turns inputs into outputs for a customer. Necessary non-value-added: required by law and safety, but the customer does not pay for it. The next step, typically packing (or shipping). To keep the scope manageable and prevent it from expanding into areas the team cannot control. The work is information, not physical items, so errors are not visible until someone complains or checks. Key takeaways Process = inputs, activities, outputs, customer. Define start and stop points; in scope vs out of scope. Customers and suppliers can be internal or external. Steps are value-added, necessary non-value-added, or waste. Six Sigma applies to manufacturing and transactional processes alike.
Critical to Quality Characteristics (CTQs)

Why this matters Customers speak in vague words like "fast" or "accurate". A project needs something it can measure, set a target for and judge success by. The CTQ is that bridge. A project without a clear CTQ cannot prove it succeeded. The big idea A CTQ (critical to quality) is a measurable characteristic of a product or service that is critical to customer satisfaction . It has three parts: A measure : what you count or measure, in what unit (hours, percent, defects). A target : the ideal value. A specification limit : the boundary between acceptable and unacceptable. "Fast delivery" is a need. "Delivered within 48 hours of order, target 24 hours" is a CTQ. The CTQ tree The CTQ tree breaks a general need into specific, measurable requirements in three levels: Need Fast delivery Ships the same day Order by 2 p.m. ships same day, at least 98% Arrives on promised day Delivered by 6 p.m. on promised day, at least 97% Easy to track Location update at least every 2 h in transit Need Drivers CTQs (measure, target, limit) From a vague need, through what it means to the customer, to measurable CTQs. Need : the customer's general want, in their words. Drivers : what the need means more specifically; the things that, if done well, satisfy it. CTQs : each driver turned into a measure, target and limit. You get the drivers from VOC work (1.1.5): interviews, surveys and complaints tell you what "fast" actually means to this customer. The CTx family CTQ is often used loosely for all customer requirements, but there are related terms: CTQ, critical to quality : product or service performance (accuracy, defects, damage). CTC, critical to cost : the customer's cost (price, fees, total cost of ownership). CTD, critical to delivery : timing and availability (lead time, on-time rate). Some materials add CTS (safety) or CTP (process). The idea is the same: a measurable requirement the customer cares about. Operational definitions Even a well-written CTQ can be measured differently by different people. "Delivered on time": on time according to which clock? The appointment window? Arrival at the gate, or at the dock door? An operational definition states exactly how the characteristic is measured, so that two people measuring the same thing get the same answer: What is measured (arrival at the dock door, from the electronic logging device timestamp). How (compare with the appointment start time). What counts as a pass ("on time" = no more than 15 minutes after the appointment start). Without operational definitions, data from different people or sites cannot be compared, and the measurement system will fail its analysis in Measure. Worked example Which is the best-written CTQ for "quick quotes"? A. Quotes should be fast. B. Respond to quote requests promptly and accurately. C. Quote sent within 4 business hours of the request (target 2 hours). D. Reduce quote time. Answer: C. It has a measure (time from request to quote sent), a unit (business hours), a limit (4) and a target (2). A and B have no number. D is a goal direction, not a requirement. Common mistakes and exam traps No number, no CTQ. The correct answer to "which is the best CTQ?" is the one with a measure, a unit and a limit. Confusing the need with the CTQ. "Reliable service" is a need. The CTQ is how reliability is measured. Skipping the operational definition. Two sites can report different on-time rates for identical performance if they define "on time" differently. Check yourself What three parts does a complete CTQ have? Put in order: CTQ, need, driver. "Billing accuracy" is a driver. Write a CTQ for it. What does CTD stand for? Why does an operational definition matter? Show answers A measure, a target and a specification limit. Need, driver, CTQ. For example: "Invoices with zero errors in price, weight or address, at least 99.5% of invoices per month." Critical to delivery. So everyone measures the characteristic the same way and the data is consistent and comparable. Key takeaways CTQ = measurable characteristic critical to customer satisfaction, with a measure, target and limit. CTQ tree: need, drivers, CTQs. CTx family: CTQ (quality), CTC (cost), CTD (delivery). An operational definition says exactly how to measure it.
Cost of Poor Quality (COPQ)

Why this matters Executives decide with money. A team that says "we have many defects" gets polite nods. A team that says "defects cost us $1.2 million a year" gets resources. Cost of poor quality turns quality problems into dollars. The big idea Doing things wrong costs money in many ways, and most of those costs are hidden in normal budgets: overtime, extra staff, expediting, write-offs. Cost of poor quality (COPQ) collects them so they can be seen and attacked. Quality-related costs fall into four buckets, often called the PAF model (prevention, appraisal, failure): The four categories 1. Internal failure costs: defects found before the customer gets the product. Scrap, rework, re-inspection after rework, retesting. Downtime caused by quality problems. Re-delivering a load that was loaded to the wrong trailer before it left. 2. External failure costs: defects the customer finds. Warranty repairs, returns, refunds, credits. Freight damage claims, chargebacks. Complaint handling, recalls. Lost future sales and reputation (real, but very hard to measure). External failures are usually the most expensive, because the cost includes the customer relationship. 3. Appraisal costs: checking whether things are right. Inspection, testing, audits. Calibrating measuring equipment. Checking invoices before they are sent. 4. Prevention costs: stopping defects from happening. Training, process planning, quality planning. FMEA, mistake-proofing, preventive maintenance. Statistical process control. How the money moves The four categories are connected. Spending a little more on prevention usually reduces appraisal and failure costs by much more. Spending on appraisal alone just catches failures earlier; it does not stop them being made. The cheapest defect is the one never made. A common rule of thumb is that the cost of a defect grows roughly tenfold at each stage it escapes: cheap to prevent, more to catch in inspection, much more to fix inside, far more if the customer finds it. Two conventions, read the question Sources group these costs differently: ASQ-style: cost of good quality = prevention + appraisal (money spent to get it right); cost of poor quality = internal + external failure (money lost because it went wrong). PAF-style, common in training material: all four categories together are "cost of quality", and sometimes all four are called COPQ. If a question forces you to choose what is "definitely COPQ", the failure costs (internal and external) are the safe core under every convention. The hidden factory and the iceberg Picture an iceberg. Above the water are visible costs: scrap, warranty, rework that is tracked. Below the water, much larger, are hidden costs: extra inventory held "just in case", expediting, overtime to recover, engineering time spent firefighting, lost customers, management time in meetings about problems. The hidden factory is the part of an operation's capacity spent fixing, redoing and chasing things. Many organizations find that 15% to 25% of their revenue goes to poor quality once hidden costs are included. Worked example Classify these costs at a trucking company: Cost Category Driver training on load securing Prevention Dock supervisor checking straps before departure Appraisal Re-stacking a pallet that fell inside the trailer before departure Internal failure Paying a damage claim to a customer External failure Preventive maintenance program for reefers Prevention Auditing invoices before sending Appraisal Credit issued for a billing error the customer caught External failure If the claims (external failure) total $300,000 a year and a $40,000 training program (prevention) cuts them in half, the company saves $150,000 for $40,000 spent. Common mistakes and exam traps Rework is internal failure; inspection is appraisal. These two are swapped often. Training and FMEA are prevention. Not appraisal. The customer found it, so it is external. Even a small credit for an error the customer noticed is external failure. Whether appraisal and prevention count as COPQ depends on the source. Read the wording. Check yourself Name the four categories of quality cost. A warehouse re-counts inventory because counts are often wrong. Which category? Which category is usually most expensive per defect, and why? Under the ASQ convention, which two categories make up COPQ? What is the hidden factory? Show answers Prevention, appraisal, internal failure, external failure. Appraisal (checking). If the re-count is needed because the first count was wrong, the re-counting is arguably internal failure; questions usually treat routine counting and checking as appraisal. External failure, because it adds claims, credits and lost customers to the cost of fixing the defect. Internal failure and external failure. The hidden share of capacity and cost spent fixing, redoing and chasing problems. Key takeaways Four buckets: prevention, appraisal, internal failure, external failure. Prevention is cheapest; external failure is most expensive. ASQ-style: COPQ = internal + external failure. Some sources count all four. Most COPQ is hidden (the iceberg, the hidden factory).
Pareto Analysis (80:20 Rule)

Why this matters Teams cannot fix everything at once. Pareto analysis shows where to focus first, using data instead of opinion. It is one of the most used charts in all of Six Sigma. The big idea The Pareto principle says that a few causes produce most of the effect . Roughly 80% of problems come from 20% of causes. The numbers are a rule of thumb, not a law: it might be 70/30 or 90/10. The point is the imbalance: there are vital few causes and trivial many . The economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed that a small share of people owned most of the land in Italy. Joseph Juran recognized the same pattern in quality problems and named it the Pareto principle. How to build a Pareto chart Collect counts by category. For example, the reason for every late load last quarter. Sort categories from largest to smallest. Put small ones together as "Other" at the far right, even if "Other" is bigger than some named categories. Draw bars in that order. Add a cumulative percentage line. For each bar, add its count to all the bars before it and divide by the total. Draw an 80% reference line (optional) to see where the vital few end. 0 25 50 0% 50% 100% 80% 46 Dock delay 22 Traffic 12 Paperwork 8 Weather 6 Breakdown 6 Other Late loads (count) Cumulative 100 late loads. The first three causes (dark bars) account for 80% of them. Reading the chart In the example, the cumulative line reaches 46%, 68%, then 80% at the third bar. Dock delay, traffic and paperwork are the vital few: fixing them addresses 80% of late loads. Weather, breakdowns and "other" are the trivial many for now. Frequency vs cost: the same data can rank differently Counting how often something happens is not the same as how much it hurts. Suppose: Defect Count Cost each Total cost Wrong address label 120 $15 $1,800 Damaged freight 30 $400 $12,000 Late pickup 80 $50 $4,000 By frequency , wrong labels lead. By cost , damaged freight is the biggest problem by far. When causes have very different impacts, build the Pareto on cost (or another weighted impact) before choosing what to fix. Using Pareto in a project Define/Measure: decide which problem area to target. Analyze: narrow causes; you can also build a second-level Pareto that breaks the top bar into its own causes (why are there dock delays?). After Improve: run it again. If the fix worked, the old top bar shrinks and a different cause becomes the leader. That is how continuous improvement continues. Worked example A call center logs 200 complaints: billing error 84, long hold 50, rude agent 26, wrong information 20, other 20. Cumulative: 84 (42%), 134 (67%), 160 (80%), 180 (90%), 200 (100%). The vital few are billing error, long hold and rude agent, at 80%. If the team can only work on one cause, billing errors give the biggest single reduction (42%). If billing errors cost $5 each to fix and rude-agent complaints risk losing $2,000 accounts, the cost-weighted chart may rank them differently. Common mistakes and exam traps Not sorting. A Pareto chart is always sorted largest to smallest, with "Other" last. Assuming the frequency leader is the best target. Weight by cost or impact when severity differs. Expecting exactly 80/20. The principle is about imbalance, not a precise ratio. Stopping after one Pareto. Drill down with second-level Paretos, and re-run after improvement. Check yourself Who applied the Pareto principle to quality? Where does "Other" go on a Pareto chart? Counts are 50, 30, 10, 6, 4. Which categories make up about 80%? Why might you build a Pareto by cost instead of count? What should happen to the chart after a successful improvement? Show answers Joseph Juran. At the far right, regardless of its size. The first two: 50 + 30 = 80 out of 100, exactly 80%. Because a rare but expensive problem can matter more than a common, cheap one. The improved category's bar shrinks, and a different category may become the top priority. Key takeaways A few causes produce most of the effect (vital few vs trivial many). Sort bars largest to smallest, "Other" last, add a cumulative percentage line. The vital few are the bars up to about 80% cumulative. Frequency and cost Paretos can disagree; weight by impact when severity differs. Drill down and re-run after improvement.
Basic Six Sigma Metrics

Why this matters Six Sigma runs on numbers. These metrics are how you describe how good a process is, compare it with others, and prove improvement. They are also some of the most frequently tested calculations on the exam. The big idea There are two families of metrics: Quality metrics : how often things go wrong (DPU, DPO, DPMO, yields). Speed and flow metrics : how long things take and how work moves (cycle time, lead time, takt time, throughput, process cycle efficiency, Little's Law). Defects vs defectives A defect is a single nonconformance: one thing wrong. A defective is a unit that has one or more defects. It counts as one, no matter how many defects it has. An invoice with a wrong price and a wrong address has two defects but is one defective invoice. Mixing these up is the most common source of wrong answers. Units and opportunities A unit is the thing being produced: an invoice, a load, a part. An opportunity is a distinct chance for a defect: a specific type of defect or a specific location where something can go wrong. An invoice might have 5 opportunities: customer name, address, weight, rate, total. Opportunities must be defined in advance and stay fixed. Changing the count changes DPMO without changing real quality, so inflating the number of opportunities makes a process look better than it is. DPU, DPO and DPMO DPU = defects ÷ units DPO = defects ÷ (units × opportunities per unit) DPMO = DPO × 1,000,000 DPU (defects per unit): average number of defects on each unit. DPO (defects per opportunity): the chance that any single opportunity is a defect. DPMO (defects per million opportunities): DPO scaled to a million, so very different processes can be compared. DPMO converts to a sigma level with the anchor table in 1.1.1. Yield First time yield (FTY) , also called first pass yield, is the fraction of units that come through a step right the first time, with no rework : FTY = units passing the first time ÷ units entering the step Under a specific assumption, that defects occur randomly and independently (a Poisson process), FTY can be estimated from DPU: FTY ≈ e^(−DPU) where e ≈ 2.718. If DPU = 0.1, FTY ≈ e^(−0.1) ≈ 0.905, about 90.5%. The direct fraction is the general definition; use e^(−DPU) only when the question gives DPU and expects the Poisson link. Rolled throughput yield (RTY) Most processes have several steps. Rolled throughput yield is the probability that a unit gets through every step right the first time. It is the product of the step FTYs: RTY = FTY₁ × FTY₂ × … × FTYₙ Pick FTY 95% Pack FTY 90% Load FTY 98% 100 orders in RTY = 0.95 × 0.90 × 0.98 = 0.838 Only about 84 of 100 orders get through every step right the first time, even though the final yield may be 100%. Even good individual steps multiply into a much lower overall first-time yield. Because you multiply numbers less than 1, RTY is always less than or equal to the lowest step FTY . Long processes with many steps lose yield quickly: ten steps at 95% each give RTY = 0.95¹⁰ ≈ 60%. Normalized yield is the average yield per step: RTY^(1/n). For the example above, 0.838^(1/3) ≈ 0.943. It is useful for comparing processes with different numbers of steps. The hidden factory again A step can show 100% final yield because every bad unit was reworked before moving on, while its first time yield is only 80%. Traditional "final yield" hides the rework. RTY uses first-time yields, which is why it exposes the hidden factory. Speed and flow metrics Cycle time : the time to complete one unit at one step (or the time between units coming out). Lead time (also throughput time): the total time from when a customer request enters the process to when it is completed, including all waiting. Throughput : how many units the process completes per unit of time (loads per day). Takt time : the pace needed to meet customer demand. Takt time = available working time ÷ customer demand If a cross-dock has 450 minutes of working time a shift and customers need 90 trailers unloaded, takt = 450 ÷ 90 = 5 minutes per trailer . If unloading takes 6 minutes, the dock cannot keep up. Process cycle efficiency (PCE) : the share of lead time that adds value. PCE = value-added time ÷ total lead time If a shipment spends 3 hours being handled in ways the customer values out of a 30-hour lead time, PCE = 10%. Low PCE means lots of waiting and waste, which is typical. Little's Law Little's Law connects work in process, throughput and lead time: Lead time = work in process (WIP) ÷ throughput rate If a claims department has 120 claims open and closes 20 a day, the average claim takes 120 ÷ 20 = 6 days . To cut lead time you either cut WIP (fewer things waiting) or raise throughput. Cutting WIP is often easier, which is why Lean limits work in process. Worked example: DPMO A carrier audits 400 delivery documents. Each has 5 opportunities for error (name, address, weight, piece count, signature). The audit finds 30 errors, on 22 documents. DPU = 30 ÷ 400 = 0.075 defects per document . DPO = 30 ÷ (400 × 5) = 30 ÷ 2,000 = 0.015 . DPMO = 0.015 × 1,000,000 = 15,000 . Defective rate = 22 ÷ 400 = 5.5% of documents have at least one error. Sigma level: 15,000 DPMO falls between 4σ (6,210) and 3σ (66,807), so roughly 3.7σ . Worked example: RTY Orders go through entry (FTY 97%), credit check (92%) and scheduling (95%). RTY = 0.97 × 0.92 × 0.95 = 0.848 . About 85 of every 100 orders get through without any rework. The credit check, at 92%, is the weakest step and the best place to start. Common mistakes and exam traps Defects vs defectives : DPU and DPMO use defects; percent defective uses defective units. Opportunity counting : count only defined, independent chances for a defect; do not inflate them. Hidden rework : always use first-time yield in RTY, not final yield. RTY is a product, not an average. Takt time is demand-driven : it does not depend on how fast the process actually is. Check yourself 500 units, 3 opportunities each, 45 defects. What are DPU, DPO and DPMO? A unit has 3 defects. How many defectives is that? Three steps have FTY of 90%, 95% and 99%. What is RTY? Available time is 480 minutes and demand is 120 units. What is takt time? A help desk has 60 open tickets and closes 15 an hour. What is the average lead time? Show answers DPU = 45 ÷ 500 = 0.09. DPO = 45 ÷ 1,500 = 0.03. DPMO = 30,000. One defective. 0.90 × 0.95 × 0.99 ≈ 0.846, about 84.6%. 480 ÷ 120 = 4 minutes per unit. 60 ÷ 15 = 4 hours. Key takeaways Defect = one nonconformance; defective = a unit with at least one. DPU = defects ÷ units; DPO = defects ÷ (units × opportunities); DPMO = DPO × 10⁶. FTY = right first time ÷ entering; FTY ≈ e^(−DPU) under the Poisson assumption. RTY = product of FTYs, never more than the worst step. Takt = available time ÷ demand; PCE = VA time ÷ lead time; Little's Law: lead time = WIP ÷ throughput.
Building a Business Case and Project Charter

Why this matters The charter is the contract between the project team and the business. It says what problem will be solved, why it matters, what success looks like, and what is in and out of bounds. A weak charter is the most common root cause of failed projects: unclear goals, endless scope, no support. On the exam, charter questions usually ask you to spot a badly written problem or goal statement. The big idea Before any data is collected, the team and the sponsor agree in writing on the answers to six questions: Why does this matter to the business? (business case) What exactly is wrong? (problem statement) What will we achieve, by when? (goal statement) What are we working on, and not working on? (scope) Who is involved? (team and roles) When will it be done, and with what? (timeline, resources) The sponsor signs the charter. From then on, it is the reference point for every tollgate review. Elements of a charter Business case. Why this project, why now, in business terms: cost, revenue, customer, strategy, compliance. "Damage claims cost $480,000 last year and our largest customer has said claims are the main reason it is reviewing our contract." Problem statement. A factual description of the problem: what is wrong, where , when (since when, how often), and how big (the extent, with numbers). It contains no cause, no solution and no blame . Goal statement. What the project will achieve, written SMART : S pecific, M easurable, A chievable, R elevant, T ime-bound. It usually states the baseline , the target and the deadline : "Reduce damage claims from 3.1 to 1.5 per 1,000 loads by December 31." Scope. The process boundaries (start and stop points, see 1.2.1) and what is explicitly in scope and out of scope : which sites, products, customers, steps. Team and roles. Sponsor, champion, process owner, belt leading the project, team members, and how much time each gives. Timeline and milestones. Target dates for each DMAIC tollgate. Resources, constraints and assumptions. Budget, data access, people, and limits such as "no capital spending" or "no changes to the union agreement". Risks. What might stop the project, and how the team will handle it. Sign-off. Signatures of the sponsor and key stakeholders. Writing a good problem statement Use this checklist: what, where, when, how big, and what impact . Bad: "Drivers are careless and we need a new load-securing system." Blames people ("careless"). Jumps to a solution ("new system"). No numbers, no time frame, no location. Good: "Since January, damage claims at the Dallas and Memphis terminals have averaged 3.1 per 1,000 loads, versus 1.2 at other terminals, costing $40,000 a month in claims." What: damage claims. Where: Dallas and Memphis. When: since January. How big: 3.1 per 1,000, $40,000 a month. No cause, no solution, no blame. A problem statement that names the cause or the fix assumes the answer. If the team is wrong about the cause, the whole project is pointed the wrong way. Scope and "boiling the ocean" A project that tries to fix too much ("improve all customer service across the company") will not finish. A Green Belt project should normally be completable in about 3 to 6 months by a small team. If the scope is too large, break it into several projects. Scope creep is when the project quietly grows: new sites, new problems, new requests. The charter is the defense: anything outside the agreed scope needs the sponsor's approval to add. Stakeholders and communication Stakeholder analysis lists everyone affected by or able to affect the project and rates their current and needed support (for example, from "strongly against" to "strongly supportive"), so the team knows whom to win over. RACI chart : for each task, who is R esponsible (does it), A ccountable (owns the outcome, only one person), C onsulted (gives input before) and I nformed (told after). Communication plan : who gets what information, how, and how often. Choosing the right projects Organizations have more possible projects than people to run them. Common selection tools: Strategic alignment : does it support the organization's goals? Impact/effort matrix (also called a PICK chart): plot each idea by benefit and difficulty. High benefit, low effort first; low benefit, high effort never. Benefit vs resources : expected savings or customer impact compared with the people, time and money needed. Data availability : Six Sigma needs data. A project with no way to measure the Y is a poor candidate. Known solution? If the fix is already known and just needs doing, it is a "just do it" task, not a DMAIC project. Worked example Evaluate this draft goal: "Improve on-time delivery significantly." Specific? No: improve how? Measurable? No: no number. Time-bound? No: no date. Rewrite: "Increase on-time delivery for the Southeast region from 88% to 95% by June 30." It now has a scope (Southeast), a baseline (88%), a target (95%) and a deadline (June 30). Common mistakes and exam traps A problem statement with a solution in it is wrong. "We need new software" belongs nowhere in a problem statement. A problem statement with a cause in it is wrong. "Late deliveries caused by new drivers" assumes what Analyze should prove. A goal without a baseline or deadline is not SMART. The sponsor signs the charter , not the belt alone. Too-big scope is a selection mistake, not a sign of ambition. Check yourself Name four elements of a project charter. What four things should a problem statement state, and what three things should it never contain? Rewrite as SMART: "Reduce invoice errors." In a RACI chart, how many people can be Accountable for a task? A sponsor asks you to "also look at the Atlanta terminal" halfway through. What is this, and what should happen? Show answers Any four of: business case, problem statement, goal statement, scope, team and roles, timeline, resources, constraints and assumptions, risks, sign-off. What, where, when and how big (extent). Never a cause, a solution or blame. For example: "Reduce invoice errors from 4.2% to under 1% of invoices by September 30." One. Scope creep. It should be evaluated and formally added to the charter (with timeline and resources adjusted), or handled as a separate project. Key takeaways The charter is the signed agreement: business case, problem, goal, scope, team, timeline, resources, risks. Problem statement: what, where, when, how big; no cause, solution or blame. Goal statement: SMART, with baseline, target and deadline. Control scope; break oversized projects up. Choose projects by strategic fit, impact versus effort, and data availability.
Developing Project Metrics

Why this matters A project is judged by its metrics. Pick the wrong one and you can "succeed" while the business gets worse: faster deliveries with more damage, lower costs with angrier customers. Good metrics define success honestly and catch side effects. The big idea Every project has three kinds of metrics: Primary metric : the main measure of success. It is the project's Y , tied directly to the problem statement. There should be one. Secondary metrics : other measures that help explain or support the primary, such as the components of the Y. Consequential (balancing) metrics : measures that could get worse because of the project. They guard against sub-optimization: improving one thing by hurting another. Example, a project to cut loading time: Primary: average minutes to load a trailer. Secondary: minutes waiting for a door, minutes waiting for freight. Balancing: damage claims per 1,000 loads, injuries. If loading gets faster but damage rises, the project has not truly succeeded. Defining a metric properly Each metric needs: An operational definition (exactly what is measured and how, see 1.2.2). A baseline : current performance, measured in the Measure phase. A target : the goal from the charter. A data type : Continuous (variable) data can take any value on a scale: time, weight, cost, temperature. It carries more information, so smaller samples are needed. Discrete (attribute) data comes in categories or counts: pass/fail, number of defects, on time or late. It is easier to collect but needs larger samples. Choosing continuous data when possible makes analysis much more powerful. "Minutes late" tells you more than "late yes/no". Process vs outcome, leading vs lagging Outcome metrics measure the result the customer sees: on-time delivery rate, claims, satisfaction. Process metrics measure how the work is done: dock door wait time, percent of loads with complete paperwork at departure. Lagging indicators report what already happened: last month's claims. Reliable, but too late to prevent anything. Leading indicators predict future results: percent of trailers inspected for securing before departure. They let you act before the outcome suffers. Good projects watch the outcome (the Y) and manage the process and leading indicators (the X's). That is "monitor the Y, control the X's" from 1.1.4.
