Typical Six Sigma metrics Quality : DPMO, defect rate, first time yield, rolled throughput yield (1.2.5). Capability : Cp, Cpk, sigma level (2.4, 1.1.1). Speed : cycle time, lead time, on-time rate. Cost : cost of poor quality (1.2.3), cost per unit. Customer : satisfaction scores, complaints, net promoter score. Worked example A project charter says: "Reduce time to issue customer credits from 9 days to 3 days." Suggest metrics. Primary : days from credit approval to credit issued (continuous). Secondary : days waiting for manager approval; days in accounting queue. Balancing : percentage of credits issued in error (speed must not cause wrong credits); customer complaints about credits. Leading indicator : number of credits waiting more than 2 days in any queue. Common mistakes and exam traps No balancing metric. A project that speeds up a process can damage quality. The balancing metric catches it. Several primary metrics. One primary metric keeps the project focused. Discrete when continuous is available. "Late or not" throws away how late. Only lagging indicators. You see problems only after they have hurt customers. Check yourself What is the purpose of a consequential (balancing) metric? Is "number of late loads" continuous or discrete? What continuous alternative is there? Classify: "monthly customer complaints" as leading or lagging. A project's primary metric is hold time in a call center. Name a balancing metric. Why prefer continuous data? Show answers To detect if improving the primary metric makes something else worse (sub-optimization). Discrete (a count). Continuous alternative: minutes late for each load. Lagging. For example, first-call resolution rate or customer satisfaction, because rushing calls could hurt them. It contains more information, so it needs smaller samples and supports more powerful analysis. Key takeaways Primary (the Y), secondary (supporting), consequential/balancing (side effects). Each metric needs an operational definition, baseline, target and data type. Continuous data is more informative than discrete. Outcome vs process metrics; lagging vs leading indicators.
Financial Evaluation and Benefits Capture

Why this matters Companies fund projects that pay off. Being able to estimate and classify a project's financial benefit is how you win approval and prove success. The exam asks you to classify benefits and compute ROI and payback, and sometimes to choose which project to fund. The big idea Benefits come in two kinds, and the difference is whether money actually moves: Hard savings : real cash that shows up on the profit and loss statement (P&L). Budgets can be reduced, or revenue goes up. Soft savings : real value that does not directly change the P&L: freed capacity, avoided future costs, time saved, better satisfaction. Hard vs soft, with examples Benefit Hard or soft Why Overtime cut by $60k a year Hard Payroll spending actually falls Damage claims cut by $120k a year Hard Cash paid out falls Fuel cost reduced by $0.04 a mile Hard Fuel bills fall Dispatchers save 10 hours a week, but no one is let go or reassigned Soft Capacity freed, but costs unchanged Avoided buying a second forklift next year Soft (cost avoidance) Money never spent, but no budget line falls Customer satisfaction up 8 points Soft Valuable, but not cash Soft savings can become hard when the freed capacity is actually used: the saved dispatcher hours absorb growth so no new hire is needed, or a contractor is released. Ways projects create value Cost reduction : spend less on something you already spend on (hard). Revenue growth : sell more, keep customers, charge for better service (hard if it can be traced). Cost avoidance : prevent a future cost that would otherwise occur (usually soft). Return on investment (ROI) ROI compares net benefit with cost: ROI = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost A project costs $25,000 (training, equipment, team time) and saves $100,000 in its first year. ROI = (100,000 − 25,000) ÷ 25,000 = 3.0 , or 300%. Payback period Payback is how long it takes for the benefits to repay the investment. When the yearly benefit is constant: Payback period = investment ÷ annual benefit A $40,000 dock leveler that saves $16,000 a year pays back in 40,000 ÷ 16,000 = 2.5 years . When benefits are uneven, add them year by year until the total reaches the investment. Investment $50,000; savings of $10,000, $20,000, $30,000 in years 1 to 3. Cumulative: $10k, $30k, $60k. Payback happens during year 3: after year 2, $20,000 is still needed out of year 3's $30,000, so payback is 2 + 20/30 ≈ 2.67 years . NPV and IRR (awareness only) A dollar next year is worth less than a dollar today. Net present value (NPV) discounts future benefits back to today's value and subtracts the cost. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the company's required return. Internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate at which NPV equals zero. Green Belts mostly need to know what these are; finance usually calculates them. Capturing the benefits Finance validation : many companies require the finance department to agree on the baseline and verify savings before they are claimed. Tracking : benefits are typically tracked for about 12 months after the project closes, to confirm they last. This is common company practice, not an IASSC rule. Ownership : the process owner keeps the gains; the control plan protects them. Worked example: which project to fund? Project A Project B Cost $20,000 $60,000 Annual hard savings $30,000 $45,000 Payback 0.67 years 1.33 years First-year ROI 0.5 (50%) −0.25 (−25%) If money is tight and the goal is a quick return, A wins: faster payback, positive first-year ROI. B saves more per year, so over a long horizon B produces more total savings; a judgment call might still fund B if it supports a strategic goal. Questions at the "Evaluate" level expect you to weigh payback, ROI, strategic fit and risk together. Common mistakes and exam traps Calling freed capacity hard savings. It is soft unless costs actually fall. Cost avoidance is soft. Nothing in the current budget goes down. ROI uses net benefit (benefit minus cost) on top. Benefit ÷ cost alone is a benefit-cost ratio, not ROI. Payback with uneven cash flows needs a cumulative total, not a single division. Check yourself Is "avoided hiring a planned second shift supervisor" hard or soft? A project costs $15,000 and saves $45,000. What is ROI? A $90,000 system saves $30,000 a year. What is payback? Investment $30,000; savings $5,000, $15,000, $20,000 in years 1 to 3. When does it pay back? Why might finance need to validate savings? Show answers Soft (cost avoidance): no current budget line falls. (45,000 − 15,000) ÷ 15,000 = 2.0, or 200%. 90,000 ÷ 30,000 = 3 years. Cumulative: 5k, 20k, 40k. After year 2, 10k is still needed out of year 3's 20k, so 2.5 years. To make sure the baseline and claimed savings are real and agreed, so the numbers are credible. Key takeaways Hard savings change the P&L; soft savings (capacity, cost avoidance, satisfaction) do not directly. ROI = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost. Payback = investment ÷ annual benefit when constant; use cumulative totals when uneven. NPV and IRR account for the time value of money; awareness level. Finance validates savings; benefits are commonly tracked for about a year.
Understanding Lean

Why this matters Six Sigma makes processes consistent. Lean makes them fast and free of waste. Many problems in real operations, from long lead times to piles of work waiting, are Lean problems, not variation problems. Knowing Lean's principles and vocabulary lets you recognize which kind of problem you face. The big idea Lean starts from one question: what does the customer actually value? Everything else in the process is either necessary support or waste . Lean removes the waste so that value flows to the customer quickly, smoothly, and only when it is needed. Most processes are shockingly slow when you look closely. A shipment might take 30 hours from order to delivery, but only about 3 hours of that is something the customer values: picking, loading, driving, unloading. The rest is waiting. 0 h 10 h 20 h 30 h Total lead time: 30 hours Dark = value-added (load, drive, unload) = 3 hours Light = waiting in the yard, at the dock, for paperwork Process cycle efficiency = 3 ÷ 30 = 10% Only the dark slivers are value-added. Lean attacks the light part. The five Lean principles James Womack and Daniel Jones summarized Lean in five principles ( Lean Thinking , 1996): Specify value : define value from the customer's point of view: what they want, when, at what price. Not what is convenient for us to make. Map the value stream : identify every step, for one product or service, from request to delivery. Mark which steps create value and which do not. Create flow : make the value-creating steps happen one after another without stopping, waiting or batching. Establish pull : produce only when the customer (or the next step) asks for it, instead of pushing work through on a forecast. Pursue perfection : repeat the cycle forever. Each round exposes more waste. Value-added and non-value-added Recall from 1.2.1: Value-added (VA) : the customer would pay for it; it changes the product or service toward what they want; done right the first time. Necessary non-value-added (NNVA) : the customer would not pay for it, but it is required for now (regulation, safety, accounting). Non-value-added (NVA) : pure waste. Remove it. Push vs pull, flow vs batch Push: each step makes what the schedule says Step A pile Step B pile Step C Pull: each step makes only what the next one used Step A Step B Step C Dashed arrows: signal (kanban) sent back upstream Customer demand starts it Push builds piles between steps; pull keeps work moving only as fast as it is used. Push : each step works to a schedule or forecast and sends its output on, whether or not the next step is ready. Result: inventory piles up, lead time grows, and problems hide in the piles. Pull : a step produces only when the next step (ultimately the customer) signals it has used something. A kanban (signal card, empty bin, electronic signal) carries that signal upstream. Batch processing : do a big batch at one step, then move the whole batch to the next. Every item waits for its whole batch at every step. One-piece flow (single-piece or continuous flow): each item moves to the next step as soon as it is done. Lead time drops dramatically, and a defect is noticed after one piece instead of after a whole batch. Muda, mura and muri Toyota describes three enemies of a smooth process: Muda (waste) : activity that adds no value. The seven (or eight) wastes in 1.4.4. Mura (unevenness) : irregular workload, such as 40 trailers arriving Monday and 5 on Friday. Unevenness causes waste because capacity must be sized for the peak. Muri (overburden) : pushing people or equipment beyond what they can sustain. It causes breakdowns, injuries and mistakes. Leveling the work (removing mura) prevents overburden (muri), which in turn reduces waste (muda). Lean vocabulary Learn one line for each: Takt time : available time ÷ customer demand; the beat the process must keep (see 1.2.5). Kaizen : continuous, incremental improvement, often in short focused events ("kaizen events" or "kaizen blitzes"). Gemba : "the real place", where the work happens. Going to see it is a "gemba walk". SMED (single-minute exchange of die) : methods to make changeovers very fast, which makes small batches affordable. TPM (total productive maintenance) : operators take part in routine care of their equipment to prevent breakdowns. Jidoka : automation with a human touch; machines or processes stop automatically when a problem occurs, so defects are never passed on. Heijunka : leveling production by volume and mix over time. Andon : a visual signal (light, board, cord) showing status and calling for help when there is a problem. Standard work : the current best, documented way to do a task, including sequence, timing and inventory. It is the baseline for improvement. Poka-yoke : mistake-proofing (5.1). Kanban : a signal that authorizes production or movement in a pull system. The two pillars Toyota's approach rests on continuous improvement (always finding and removing waste) and respect for people (the people doing the work are the experts, and improvement is done with them, not to them). Tools without respect for people do not last. Worked example A trailer repair shop takes 9 days on average to return a trailer, but total hands-on repair time is 6 hours. Value-added time: 6 hours. Lead time: 9 days = 216 hours. Process cycle efficiency = 6 ÷ 216 ≈ 2.8% . Value stream walk: trailers wait for inspection (1 day), wait for a parts order (4 days), wait in queue for a bay (3 days). Lean responses: inspect on arrival (flow), stock the most common parts with a kanban (pull), level the arrival schedule with the fleet team (heijunka). Common mistakes and exam traps Value is defined by the customer , not by the company or the engineer. Lean is not just cost cutting. It is about flow and lead time; cost falls as a result. Pull is not "make to order only". It means producing in response to actual use, often with small buffers controlled by kanban. Kaizen means incremental improvement , not a one-time big project. Check yourself List the five Lean principles in order. What is the difference between push and pull? Which of muda, mura and muri describes a workload of 40 trailers Monday and 5 Friday? What is jidoka? Lead time is 20 days; value-added time is 4 hours. What is the process cycle efficiency? Show answers Specify value, map the value stream, create flow, establish pull, pursue perfection. Push produces to a schedule regardless of need; pull produces only when the next step signals it has used something. Mura (unevenness). Stopping automatically when a problem occurs so defects are not passed on ("automation with a human touch"). 4 ÷ (20 × 24) = 4 ÷ 480 ≈ 0.8%. Key takeaways Five principles: value, value stream, flow, pull, perfection. Value is defined by the customer; most lead time is waiting. Pull and one-piece flow beat push and batches for lead time and quality. Muda (waste), mura (unevenness), muri (overburden). Pillars: continuous improvement and respect for people.
The History of Lean

Why this matters Like 1.1.2, this is a matching topic: who developed which idea. The story is short and memorable because it follows one company, Toyota, with a few key people. The story Before Toyota: Henry Ford (1910s). Ford's moving assembly line (1913) made the Model T in a continuous flow, slashing the time and cost to build a car. Ford is a precursor to Lean: he understood flow. But his system relied on huge volumes of one product ("any color so long as it is black") and big inventories. Sakichi Toyoda (around 1900 to the 1920s). Founder of the Toyoda family business, Sakichi invented power looms that stopped automatically when a thread broke . One worker could tend many machines, and no defective cloth was made. This is the origin of jidoka : building quality in by stopping at the first sign of a problem. Kiichiro Toyoda (1930s). Sakichi's son started Toyota's car business and promoted the idea of just-in-time : making only what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed. Taiichi Ohno (late 1940s to 1970s). Toyota's production engineer and executive who built the Toyota Production System (TPS) . Post-war Japan had little money, little space, and a market that wanted many models in small quantities, so mass production would not work. Ohno developed just-in-time and pull production, kanban , and the idea of the seven wastes . He was inspired partly by American supermarkets, where shelves are restocked only when customers take items. Shigeo Shingo (1950s to 1970s). An industrial engineer and consultant who worked with Toyota. He developed SMED (quick changeover) and poka-yoke (mistake-proofing), and wrote some of the first books explaining TPS to the West. How "Lean" got its name In the late 1980s, MIT's International Motor Vehicle Program studied car makers worldwide. Researcher John Krafcik coined the term "lean" (1988) for Toyota's approach, because it used less of everything: less space, inventory, effort and time. James Womack, Daniel Jones and Daniel Roos published the program's findings in The Machine That Changed the World (1990), which made Lean famous. Womack and Jones then wrote Lean Thinking (1996), which set out the five principles. Timeline When Who What 1913 Henry Ford Moving assembly line (flow) ~1900 to 1920s Sakichi Toyoda Self-stopping loom (jidoka) 1930s Kiichiro Toyoda Just-in-time idea at Toyota 1940s to 1970s Taiichi Ohno Toyota Production System, kanban, pull, seven wastes 1950s to 1970s Shigeo Shingo SMED, poka-yoke 1988 John Krafcik Coined "lean" 1990 Womack, Jones, Roos The Machine That Changed the World 1996 Womack, Jones Lean Thinking , five principles Common mistakes and exam traps Ohno vs Shingo. Ohno: TPS, kanban, just-in-time, seven wastes. Shingo: SMED and poka-yoke. Toyoda vs Toyota. The family name is Toyoda; the company became Toyota. Ford was a precursor , not the inventor of Lean. He had flow, but not pull or flexibility. Krafcik named it; Womack and Jones popularized it. Check yourself Who developed SMED? What did Sakichi Toyoda's loom contribute to Lean? Which book introduced "lean production" to a wide audience, and when? What inspired Ohno's pull system? Put in order: Lean Thinking , Ford's moving line, Krafcik coins "lean", TPS developed. Show answers Shigeo Shingo. Jidoka: stopping automatically when a problem occurs. The Machine That Changed the World (1990), by Womack, Jones and Roos. American supermarkets, which restock shelves as customers take items. Ford's moving line (1913), TPS developed (1940s to 70s), Krafcik coins "lean" (1988), Lean Thinking (1996). Key takeaways Ford: flow. Sakichi Toyoda: jidoka. Kiichiro Toyoda: just-in-time idea. Ohno: TPS, pull, kanban, seven wastes. Shingo: SMED, poka-yoke. Krafcik coined "lean"; Womack and Jones popularized it (1990, 1996).
Lean and Six Sigma

Why this matters Organizations today mostly use the combination, Lean Six Sigma. Knowing what each half is good at tells you which tools to pick for a given problem, and exam scenarios often ask exactly that. The big idea They attack different enemies: Lean Six Sigma Enemy Waste Variation Main goal Speed, flow, short lead time Consistency, few defects Key question "Why does this take so long?" "Why is this so inconsistent?" Typical tools Value stream map, 5S, kanban, SMED, standard work Statistics, MSA, hypothesis tests, regression, SPC Typical results Shorter lead time, less inventory, less space Fewer defects, higher capability, lower COPQ Both are customer-focused and data-driven , and they need each other. A fast process that makes defects just makes defects faster. A consistent process full of waiting is reliably slow. Why they fit together Waste hides variation: piles of inventory mask defects and erratic steps. Lean removes the piles so variation becomes visible. Variation creates waste: inconsistent output forces safety stock, rework and inspection. Six Sigma reduces variation so Lean flow can work. Lean tools fit inside DMAIC: Define : SIPOC, VOC. Measure : value stream map, takt time, process cycle efficiency. Analyze : the seven wastes, constraint analysis. Improve : 5S, SMED, kanban, flow cells, mistake-proofing. Control : standard work, visual management. Which to use Symptoms like "slow", "waiting", "long lead time", "too much inventory", "piles of work", "handoffs" point to Lean . Symptoms like "inconsistent", "variable", "defects", "out of specification", "rework rate", "customer complaints about errors" point to Six Sigma . Many real problems have both. Lean Six Sigma uses both tool sets inside one DMAIC project. If the solution is already known and simple, neither a DMAIC project nor a big Lean event is needed: just do it. Worked example Classify the main approach for each: "Claims take 42 days to resolve; each spends most of that in someone's inbox." Lean : waiting and flow. "Trailer weights at the scale vary widely, and 6% are overweight." Six Sigma : variation against a specification. "Invoices take 10 days and 8% have errors." Both : Lean for the 10 days, Six Sigma for the 8%. Common mistakes and exam traps Lean = waste/speed; Six Sigma = variation/defects. Look for those words in scenarios. They are complementary , not competing. Lean tools are used inside DMAIC , not in a separate method. Check yourself What is the main enemy of Lean? Of Six Sigma? A process has huge queues between steps but very few defects. Which approach first? Name a Lean tool used in the Improve phase. Why does waste hide variation? What do Lean and Six Sigma have in common? Show answers Lean: waste. Six Sigma: variation. Lean, because the problem is flow and waiting. Any of: 5S, SMED, kanban, one-piece flow, mistake-proofing, standard work. Inventory and queues absorb and hide erratic performance and defects, so problems are not seen. Both are customer-focused, data-driven and aimed at continuous improvement. Key takeaways Lean: waste, flow, speed. Six Sigma: variation, defects, consistency. Complementary: waste hides variation; variation creates waste. Lean tools sit inside DMAIC phases. Scenario words: delay and waiting point to Lean; inconsistency and defects point to Six Sigma.
The Seven Elements of Waste

Why this matters You cannot remove waste you cannot see. The seven wastes give you a checklist for "learning to see". Classification questions, "which waste is this?", are very common on the exam. The big idea Taiichi Ohno identified seven categories of waste (muda): activities that use time, effort or money but add nothing the customer values. IASSC names them: Overproduction Correction Inventory Motion Overprocessing Conveyance Waiting Many other materials use different names for two of them, with the memory aid TIMWOOD : Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Overproduction, Overprocessing, Defects. The cross-walk: Correction = Defects Conveyance = Transportation Each waste explained Overproduction: making more, or sooner, than the customer needs. Printing and staging all of tomorrow's paperwork today; loading trailers "just in case" before orders confirm; producing to forecast. It is often called the worst waste because it causes the others : extra product must be stored (inventory), moved (conveyance), handled (motion), and may become damaged or obsolete (correction). Correction (defects): fixing mistakes. Rework, re-delivery, correcting invoices, re-doing paperwork, handling claims. Everything spent finding and fixing errors. Inventory: more material or work than is needed right now. Excess spare parts, full yards of trailers waiting, stacks of unprocessed claims, emails waiting in an inbox. Inventory ties up money and space, and hides problems. Motion: unnecessary movement of people. Walking to the other end of the dock for a pallet jack, searching for tools, reaching, bending, clicking through ten screens. The person moves, not the product. Overprocessing: doing more than the customer needs. Double data entry, extra approvals, reports nobody reads, polishing a part beyond its specification, three signatures where one would do. Conveyance (transportation): unnecessary movement of materials or information. Moving freight between docks twice, routing documents through extra departments, sending a trailer to a yard and back. The product moves, but nothing about it improves. (For a carrier, moving freight to the customer is the value-added service; moving it around the terminal unnecessarily is the waste.) Waiting: people or things idle, waiting for the next step. Drivers waiting at the dock, trucks waiting for paperwork, an order waiting for credit approval, a technician waiting for parts. The eighth waste Many organizations add an eighth: unused talent (or skills, or human potential) . Not using people's knowledge, ideas and abilities, for example never asking drivers how to improve routing. The memory aid becomes DOWNTIME : Defects, Overproduction, Waiting, Non-utilized talent, Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Extra processing. Telling similar wastes apart Motion vs conveyance : motion = people moving; conveyance = materials or information moving. Overprocessing vs correction : overprocessing = doing more than needed (on a good product); correction = fixing what was done wrong. Overproduction vs inventory : overproduction is the act of making too much too soon; inventory is the resulting stock (it can also come from other causes, such as big purchase lots). Waiting : the thing or person is idle; nothing is happening to it. Worked example Classify each at a distribution center: Observation Waste 300 pallets of last season's product in racks Inventory Picker walks 200 m to the printer for each pick list Motion Orders keyed into the warehouse system and again into a spreadsheet Overprocessing Pallets moved from receiving to a holding area, then to the racks Conveyance Shipping waits 40 minutes for the trailer to be released Waiting Wrong item shipped, return and re-ship Correction Picking tomorrow's orders today "to get ahead" Overproduction Common mistakes and exam traps Double data entry is overprocessing , not correction (nothing was wrong). Walking to get tools is motion , not conveyance. Excess WIP is inventory. Overproduction drives the other wastes ; it is called the worst. IASSC wording : remember Correction = Defects and Conveyance = Transportation. Check yourself List the seven wastes using IASSC's words. A form needs five approval signatures when one person decides. Which waste? Why is overproduction called the worst waste? A mechanic walks to a distant crib for a socket set several times a day. Which waste? What is the eighth waste? Show answers Overproduction, correction, inventory, motion, overprocessing, conveyance, waiting. Overprocessing (also creates waiting). Because it causes other wastes: inventory, conveyance, motion, waiting and often correction. Motion. Unused talent (non-utilized skills or human potential). Key takeaways IASSC seven: Overproduction, Correction, Inventory, Motion, Overprocessing, Conveyance, Waiting. TIMWOOD wording: Correction = Defects, Conveyance = Transportation. Overproduction is the worst; the eighth waste is unused talent. Motion = people; conveyance = things. Overprocessing = more than needed; correction = fixing errors.
5S

Why this matters 5S is usually the first Lean tool an organization uses, because it is simple, visible and fast. A clean, organized workplace makes problems visible, cuts searching, improves safety and builds the discipline that every other improvement needs. The big idea 5S is a five-step method for organizing a workplace so that everything needed is at hand, everything unneeded is gone, and anyone can tell at a glance if something is wrong . It applies to a dock, a shop, a truck cab, an office or a shared computer drive. The five steps 1. Sort (seiri): remove what is not needed. Go through everything in the area. Keep only what is needed for the work. Questionable items get a red tag and go to a red-tag holding area for a set time; if no one claims them, they are disposed of or moved elsewhere. 2. Straighten, or set in order (seiton): a place for everything, and everything in its place. Arrange what remains so it is easy to find, use and return. Frequently used items closest. Use shadow boards (tool outlines painted on a board, so a missing tool is obvious), labels, floor markings, color codes. The goal: anyone can find anything in seconds. 3. Shine (seiso): clean and inspect. Clean the area and equipment, and use cleaning as inspection : while cleaning a forklift you notice a leaking hose. Find and remove sources of dirt. 4. Standardize (seiketsu): make the first three routine. Write down the standards: who cleans what, how often, what "good" looks like. Visual standards, such as photos of the correct layout, checklists and color codes, make deviations obvious. 5. Sustain, or self-discipline (shitsuke): make it a habit. Training, regular 5S audits , management attention and recognition. Without sustain, the area drifts back within weeks. This is the hardest S. The sixth S: Safety Many organizations add Safety as a sixth S (making it "6S"), explicitly checking for hazards during each step. IASSC lists five; know Safety as the common extension. Visual management 5S is the foundation of visual management : designing the workplace so that its status can be understood at a glance. Examples: floor lines showing where pallets go, labels on every shelf, shadow boards, color-coded bins, boards showing today's targets and actual performance, andon lights. If you need to ask or search to know whether things are normal, the workplace is not visual. Worked example A maintenance shop applies 5S. Match each action to its S: Action S Red-tagging three broken jacks and an unused parts washer Sort Painting tool outlines on a shadow board above each bench Straighten Daily 10-minute wipe-down of lifts, checking for leaks Shine Posting a photo of the correct bench layout with a cleaning schedule Standardize Monthly 5S audit scored by the supervisor, results posted Sustain Marking forklift aisles in yellow and pedestrian walkways in green Straighten (also Safety) Common mistakes and exam traps Shadow board = Straighten. Not Standardize. Red tag = Sort. Cleaning is also inspection (Shine). Standardize = rules and visual standards; Sustain = habit, audits, discipline. Questions often confuse these two. 5S is not a one-time cleanup. Without Standardize and Sustain it decays. Check yourself List the five S's in order. Which S uses red tags? A team photographs the organized workstation and posts it as the reference. Which S? Why is cleaning called a form of inspection? Which S is usually hardest, and why? Show answers Sort, Straighten, Shine, Standardize, Sustain (Self-discipline). Sort. Standardize. Because while cleaning you look closely at equipment and find leaks, wear and damage early. Sustain, because it depends on long-term habits and management attention rather than a one-time effort. Key takeaways Sort (red tag), Straighten (shadow boards, labels), Shine (clean and inspect), Standardize (rules and visual standards), Sustain (habit and audits). Safety is a common sixth S. 5S is the foundation of visual management: status visible at a glance.
Cause and Effect / Fishbone Diagrams

Why this matters When a problem appears, people jump to the first cause that comes to mind, usually something that confirms what they already believed. A fishbone diagram forces the team to list all the possible causes, in an organized way, before anyone decides which is the real one. It is the main brainstorming tool of Six Sigma. The big idea The cause-and-effect diagram , invented by Kaoru Ishikawa (so also called the Ishikawa diagram ), looks like the skeleton of a fish: The head is the effect : the problem, stated as a measurable outcome. The spine runs back from the head. The bones are categories of causes . Smaller bones on each bone are specific possible causes , and sub-causes branch off those. Effect: late deliveries Man (people) new drivers fatigue Machine breakdowns no GPS Method route plan dock order Material late freight bad pallets Measurement wrong ETA bad clocks Mother Nature weather traffic Each bone is a category; each small line is a possible cause the team suspects. The standard categories For manufacturing and operations, the 6M categories are the usual starting point: Man (people): skills, training, fatigue, staffing. Machine : equipment, tools, trucks, software. Method : procedures, work instructions, routes, scheduling. Material : raw materials, parts, freight, information inputs. Measurement : gauges, data accuracy, how results are recorded. Mother Nature (environment): weather, temperature, humidity, traffic, lighting. For service and transactional processes, 4P or 8P lists often fit better: People, Process, Policies, Procedures , and for marketing-type problems Place, Product, Price, Promotion . The categories are only prompts. Use whatever set helps the team think broadly; you can invent your own ("Customers", "Systems"). How to build one Write the effect at the head as a specific, measurable problem: "Late deliveries in the Southeast region", not "bad service". Draw the main bones with the chosen categories. Brainstorm causes with people who know the process. For each idea, ask "which category?" and add it to that bone. Drill down by asking "why does that happen?" and adding sub-causes. The 5 Whys technique asks "why?" repeatedly (roughly five times) until you reach a cause you can act on: Late delivery. Why? Truck left late. Why? Loading finished late. Why? Freight arrived late at the dock. Why? Picking started late. Why? Pick lists print only after the 6 a.m. batch run. Mark the suspects : the team votes or uses experience to circle the most likely causes for data checking. What the fishbone does not do A fishbone diagram is a list of hypotheses . It does not prove any cause. "The fishbone identified the root cause" is false: it identified possible causes. Proving which ones matter is the job of data in the Measure and Analyze phases (C&E matrix, data collection, hypothesis tests, regression). Where its output goes The candidate causes from the fishbone feed the C&E (X-Y) matrix (2.1.3), which ranks them, and the top-ranked ones go into the data collection plan and are tested statistically in Analyze. Worked example Effect: "Invoices sent with wrong amounts: 6% of invoices" . A billing team lists: People: new clerks, unclear who checks. Method: rates keyed by hand, no second check, accessorial charges added after. Machine (systems): rate table not updated automatically, two systems not linked. Material (inputs): delivery paperwork missing charges, illegible bills of lading. Measurement: error counted only when the customer complains. Environment: month-end rush. The team circles three suspects (manual rate entry, late accessorials, rate table updates) and plans to collect data on each invoice error's cause for four weeks. Common mistakes and exam traps A fishbone generates hypotheses, it does not prove causes. A vague effect gives vague causes. Make the head specific and measurable. Listing solutions instead of causes ("buy new software") on the bones. 6M names : Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Mother Nature. Check yourself What goes at the head of the fishbone? Name the 6M categories. True or false: a completed fishbone diagram identifies the root cause. What technique drills down from a cause to a deeper cause by repeatedly asking a question? Where do the fishbone's causes go next in DMAIC? Show answers The effect, the specific measurable problem. Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Mother Nature (environment). False. It lists possible causes; data must confirm them. The 5 Whys. Into the C&E matrix for ranking, then into data collection and statistical testing in Analyze. Key takeaways Effect at the head; categories as bones; causes and sub-causes as smaller bones. 6M for operations; 4P/8P for services; categories are prompts. Use 5 Whys to drill down. It produces hypotheses, not proof; feed them into the C&E matrix and test with data.
Process Mapping, SIPOC, Value Stream Map

Why this matters People who work in a process usually disagree about how it actually works. Drawing it out, together, reveals handoffs, loops, waiting and duplicated work that nobody could see. Process maps are the most-used Measure tools after data collection itself. The big idea There are maps at different levels of detail, for different purposes: SIPOC : one-page, high-level view, used in Define to agree on scope. Flowchart / process map : step-by-step detail, including decisions and loops. Swimlane map : a flowchart divided by who does each step, to show handoffs. Value stream map (VSM) : the Lean map, adding time, inventory and information flow, to show where lead time goes. SIPOC SIPOC stands for Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers . It is a table that describes the process at the highest level: Suppliers Inputs Process Outputs Customers Shipper Order, freight 1. Receive order Delivered freight Consignee Dispatch Load plan 2. Plan load Signed receipt Shipper Fleet Truck, driver 3. Pick up Invoice Billing Fuel vendor Fuel 4. Transport 5. Deliver Rules: The process column has only 4 to 7 high-level steps . Any more and it is not high-level. Building it usually starts in the middle (the process), then outputs and customers, then inputs and suppliers. It sets the start and stop points (scope) and shows everyone involved. Flowcharts and their symbols Start / End Terminator Do a task Process step Yes / No? Decision Paperwork Document Arrow: direction of flow The basic symbols. Most maps need only these. Terminator (rounded rectangle, or oval): start or end. Process (rectangle): a step where something is done. Decision (diamond): a question with branches (yes/no, pass/fail). Document (wavy bottom): a form, report or paperwork. Arrows : the order and direction of flow. Some maps also use a circle (connector to another page), a delay symbol (D-shape) and an inventory triangle. Swimlane maps A swimlane (cross-functional) map puts each person, department or system in its own horizontal or vertical lane. Every time the flow crosses a lane boundary, that is a handoff . Handoffs are where delays and errors gather: information gets lost, work waits in an inbox, responsibility is unclear. Counting lane crossings is often a quick way to find improvement opportunities. Levels and states Start with a high-level map (SIPOC level), then a detailed map of the area in scope. For each step, you can list its inputs and outputs , which later feed the C&E matrix. As-is (current state) maps show how the work really happens today, including rework loops and workarounds. Map what people actually do, not what the procedure says. Walk the process (a gemba walk ) instead of mapping from a conference room. To-be (future state) maps show the improved design, used in Improve. A spaghetti diagram traces the physical path of a person or item across a floor plan. The tangled lines show wasted motion and conveyance at a glance. Value stream maps A value stream map follows one product or service family from request to delivery and adds data: Process boxes with a data box below: cycle time (C/T), changeover time (C/O), uptime , number of operators, batch size. Inventory triangles between steps, with the quantity waiting or the waiting time. Push arrows (striped) where work is pushed, pull/kanban symbols where it is pulled. Information flow at the top: how orders and schedules move (electronic, paper, verbal). A timeline ladder at the bottom: the upper steps show waiting time, the lower steps show value-added (processing) time. I 2.0 days Receive C/T 20 min I 1.5 days Sort C/T 15 min I 0.5 days Load C/T 40 min Push arrows (dashed) between steps; triangles = inventory waiting 2.0 d 20 min 1.5 d 15 min 0.5 d 40 min Lead time = 4.0 days (upper steps: waiting) Value-added = 75 min (lower steps); PCE ≈ 75 ÷ 5,760 ≈ 1.3% Most of the 4-day lead time is waiting in front of steps; only 75 minutes is processing. Reading a VSM: lead time, VA time and PCE From the timeline: Total lead time = sum of the waiting times + sum of the processing times. Here: 2.0 + 1.5 + 0.5 days = 4.0 days, plus 75 minutes. Total value-added time = sum of the processing (cycle) times that add value: 20 + 15 + 40 = 75 minutes . Process cycle efficiency (PCE) = VA time ÷ lead time = 75 min ÷ (4 × 1,440 min) ≈ 1.3% . The largest non-value-added delay is the biggest waiting segment (2 days before Receive): the first target. Bottlenecks and capacity The bottleneck is the step with the longest cycle time (or lowest capacity). It limits the output of the whole process: nothing can come out faster than the bottleneck can work. In the map above, Load (40 min) is the bottleneck. In an 8-hour shift (480 min) it can load 480 ÷ 40 = 12 trailers, so the process makes at most 12 a shift, however fast Receive and Sort are. Compare with takt time (1.2.5): if customers need 16 trailers a shift, takt = 480 ÷ 16 = 30 min, and Load at 40 min cannot keep up. Improving any step other than the bottleneck does not increase output; it just grows the pile in front of the bottleneck. Worked example A VSM shows: Order entry (C/T 5 min), wait 3 days, Credit check (C/T 10 min), wait 1 day, Scheduling (C/T 15 min), wait 2 days, Dispatch (C/T 10 min). VA time = 5 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 40 min. Lead time ≈ 6 days (8,640 min) + 40 min ≈ 8,680 min. PCE = 40 ÷ 8,680 ≈ 0.46%. Largest delay: 3 days between order entry and credit check. Bottleneck by cycle time: scheduling (15 min). Common mistakes and exam traps SIPOC has 4 to 7 high-level steps. It is not a detailed map. Map the as-is truthfully , including rework and workarounds. PCE = VA time ÷ total lead time , not ÷ processing time. The bottleneck is the longest cycle time , not the longest wait. Handoffs show up in swimlanes as lane crossings. Check yourself What do the letters in SIPOC stand for? Which flowchart symbol is a diamond? On a VSM, what do the upper and lower steps of the timeline ladder show? Steps have cycle times of 12, 18 and 9 minutes. Which is the bottleneck, and how many units can the process make in 360 minutes? VA time 30 min, lead time 2 days. What is PCE? Show answers Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers. A decision. Upper: waiting (non-value-added) time. Lower: processing (value-added) time. The 18-minute step; 360 ÷ 18 = 20 units. 30 ÷ 2,880 ≈ 1.0%. Key takeaways SIPOC: one page, 4 to 7 steps, defines scope. Flowcharts: terminator, process, decision, document, arrows. Swimlanes show handoffs. Map the as-is honestly (walk the gemba); design the to-be in Improve. VSM adds cycle times, inventory, information flow and a timeline ladder. PCE = VA time ÷ lead time; bottleneck = longest cycle time, it sets the process's output.
X-Y Diagram (C&E Matrix)

Why this matters A fishbone can produce 40 possible causes, and there is not enough time to collect data on all of them. The C&E matrix is a quick, structured way to rank them by how much they are believed to affect what the customer cares about, so data collection focuses on the most likely few. The big idea The cause-and-effect matrix (also X-Y matrix or XY diagram ) is a table: Columns : the important outputs (Y's, usually the CTQs), each with an importance weight (often 1 to 10), from the customer's point of view. Rows : the process inputs (X's), from the fishbone and process map. Cells : the team rates how strongly each X affects each Y, usually with 0, 1, 3, 9 : 0 = no relationship, 1 = weak, 3 = moderate, 9 = strong. The big jump to 9 spreads the scores so strong relationships stand out. Row total for each X: multiply each rating by its column's importance and add across the row. Score for an X = Σ (importance of Y × rating of X on that Y) Sort the X's by score. The top few are the ones to measure and test first. Worked example Outputs: on-time delivery (importance 10), no damage (8), correct invoice (5). Input (X) On-time (10) No damage (8) Invoice (5) Score Loading method 3 9 0 3×10 + 9×8 + 0×5 = 102 Dispatch timing 9 1 0 90 + 8 + 0 = 98 Rate table accuracy 0 0 9 0 + 0 + 45 = 45 Driver experience 3 3 1 30 + 24 + 5 = 59 Ranked: loading method (102), dispatch timing (98), driver experience (59), rate table (45). The team collects data on loading method and dispatch timing first. What it is and is not It is a prioritization tool based on team judgment . The ratings are opinions from people who know the process. It is not proof . A high score means "worth testing", not "is the cause". The top X's must be validated with data in Analyze. It is only as good as the people in the room. Include operators, not just managers. Common mistakes and exam traps Forgetting the importance weights : multiply each rating by the Y's importance before adding. Using 1 to 5 ratings when the question says 0/1/3/9. Treating the ranking as validated : it still needs data. Check yourself What are the rows and columns of a C&E matrix? Why use 0, 1, 3, 9 instead of 0, 1, 2, 3? Y importances are 10 and 4. An X is rated 9 and 3. What is its score? Does the top-scoring X have to be a root cause? Which earlier tools feed the list of X's? Show answers Rows: inputs (X's). Columns: outputs (Y's) with importance weights. To spread scores apart so strong relationships stand out. 9 × 10 + 3 × 4 = 102. No. It is a judgment-based priority that must be confirmed with data. The fishbone diagram and the process map (inputs per step). Key takeaways Rank X's by their judged effect on weighted Y's. Ratings 0/1/3/9; score = Σ importance × rating. Top X's go into data collection; they are hypotheses until validated.
Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA)

Why this matters Most improvement tools react to problems that already happened. FMEA looks ahead: what could go wrong, how bad would it be, how likely is it, and would we catch it? It lets a team prevent failures, especially severe ones, before customers are hurt. The big idea For each step of a process (or each part of a design), the team asks: How could this step fail ? (failure mode) If it failed, what would happen? (effect) How bad? (severity) What would cause it? How often? (occurrence) What do we already do to prevent or catch it? (current controls) How likely would we catch it before the customer? (detection) Each answer gets a rating from 1 to 10, and the ratings combine into a priority. The FMEA columns Column Meaning Process step Where in the process Failure mode How the step could fail (load not secured) Effect What the customer or next step experiences (freight shifts, damage) Severity (S) How serious the effect is, 1 to 10 Cause Why the failure would happen (straps worn, no checklist) Occurrence (O) How often the cause happens, 1 to 10 Current controls Existing prevention or detection (supervisor spot check) Detection (D) How likely the failure escapes, 1 to 10 RPN S × O × D Recommended action, owner, date What to do about it New S, O, D, RPN Ratings after the action The rating scales Each organization writes its own descriptions, but the direction is standard: Severity : 10 = most severe (hazardous, safety or legal), 1 = no noticeable effect. Occurrence : 10 = very frequent (almost certain), 1 = extremely unlikely. Detection : reverse scale. 10 = cannot detect (the failure will almost certainly reach the customer), 1 = almost certain to be detected. Detection catches people out: a high detection number is bad . Risk priority number (RPN) RPN = S × O × D Since each rating is 1 to 10, RPN ranges from 1 to 1,000 . Higher RPN = higher priority for action. Severity first RPN treats the three ratings as equally important, which can hide danger. A failure mode with S = 10, O = 2, D = 3 has RPN = 60, lower than a nuisance with S = 4, O = 5, D = 5 (RPN = 100). But a severity 10 (for example, an injury) deserves attention regardless of RPN . Standard practice: any high-severity failure mode (9 or 10) gets reviewed and acted on first , whatever its RPN. The current AIAG-VDA FMEA Handbook (2019), used in the automotive industry, replaced RPN with Action Priority (AP) : a lookup table that rates each S-O-D combination High, Medium or Low priority, weighting severity first, then occurrence, then detection. The handbook says RPN thresholds are not a recommended way to decide on actions. For the IASSC exam, know RPN = S × O × D and the severity-first rule, and recognize AP as the newer method. Reducing risk Severity usually changes only if the design changes (the effect itself becomes less serious). Occurrence falls when you remove or reduce the cause: mistake-proofing, better materials, training. Detection improves when you add or strengthen controls that catch the failure before it reaches the customer. Prevention (lowering occurrence) is better than detection, for the same reason as in COPQ (1.2.3). After actions, the team re-rates S, O and D and recomputes RPN to show the risk reduction. Types and timing DFMEA (design FMEA) : failure modes of a product design. PFMEA (process FMEA) : failure modes of a process. Green Belt projects mostly use PFMEA. An FMEA is a living document : started in Measure (to help find risks and causes), updated in Improve (to assess the risks of the new process), and kept current in Control. Worked example Failure mode S O D RPN A: Load not secured, freight shifts 8 4 6 192 B: Wrong delivery address on paperwork 5 6 3 90 C: Reefer temperature alarm ignored, product spoils 10 2 5 100 D: Delivery receipt not scanned 3 7 4 84 By RPN alone, the order is A (192), C (100), B (90), D (84). But C has severity 10 (a spoiled food load can be a safety and legal problem), so it gets action alongside A, even though its RPN is lower than A's. After installing a reefer alarm that auto-alerts dispatch, C's detection drops from 5 to 2: new RPN = 10 × 2 × 2 = 40. Severity stays 10, because a spoiled load is still just as bad if it happens. Common mistakes and exam traps Detection is reverse-scaled : 10 = hardest to detect. Do not pick by RPN alone : check severity first. Severity does not drop because of better detection ; only design changes reduce severity. Re-score after actions : the FMEA should show before and after. RPN range is 1 to 1,000. Check yourself What does each letter in S, O, D stand for, and which scale is reversed? Calculate RPN for S = 7, O = 3, D = 8. Failure mode X: S 9, O 2, D 4. Failure mode Y: S 5, O 6, D 5. Which do you address first, and why? A new inspection camera is added. Which rating should improve? In which DMAIC phases is the FMEA used? Show answers Severity, occurrence, detection. Detection is reversed: 10 means least likely to be detected. 7 × 3 × 8 = 168. RPNs: X = 72, Y = 150. By RPN, Y is higher, but X has severity 9, so X should be reviewed and actioned first (or at least alongside Y). Detection. Measure (identify risks and causes), Improve (assess the new process), Control (keep it current). Key takeaways FMEA asks what could fail, how bad, how often, and would we catch it. RPN = S × O × D, from 1 to 1,000; detection is reverse-scaled. High severity gets action regardless of RPN; newer AIAG-VDA practice uses Action Priority. Reduce occurrence (prevent) before improving detection; re-score after actions. DFMEA = design, PFMEA = process; a living document.
Basic Statistics

Why this matters Six Sigma replaces opinions with data, and data has rules. The type of data you collect decides which charts and tests you can use later. Probability lets you reason about how likely things are. This topic is the vocabulary everything in Measure and Analyze is built on, so it is worth getting completely solid. The big idea Statistics answers two kinds of questions: Describing : what does our data look like? (descriptive statistics, 2.2.2) Inferring : what can a sample tell us about the whole process? (inferential statistics, Domain 3) Before either, you need to know what kind of data you have and where it came from . Continuous vs discrete data Continuous data (also called variable data) is measured on a scale that can be divided as finely as your instrument allows: time (4.73 hours), weight (38,412 lb), temperature, distance, cost. Between any two values there is always another possible value. Discrete data (also called attribute data) comes in separate, countable values or categories: Counts : number of defects on an invoice (0, 1, 2…), number of late loads. Pass/fail (binary) : on time or late, damaged or not. Categories : reason for delay (traffic, dock, paperwork), carrier name. Why it matters: continuous data carries much more information. "Load arrived 3.5 hours late" tells you more than "late". Continuous data needs smaller samples and supports more powerful tools. When you can measure continuously, do. Measurement scales Data also differ in what you can do with the numbers. There are four scales, from least to most informative: Scale What it is Example Meaningful operations Nominal Names or labels, no order Terminal (Dallas, Memphis), defect type Count, mode Ordinal Ordered categories, but gaps not equal Satisfaction 1 to 5, FMEA ratings, small/medium/large Rank, median Interval Equal gaps, but zero is arbitrary Temperature in °F or °C, calendar dates Add, subtract, mean Ratio Equal gaps and a true zero Weight, time, distance, cost, count All arithmetic, including "twice as much" Nominal and ordinal are discrete. Interval and ratio are usually continuous. A memory aid: NOIR (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio). Note that 80 °F is not "twice as hot" as 40 °F (interval scale, no true zero), but 80 lb is twice as heavy as 40 lb (ratio scale). Population vs sample A population is every item you care about: every load this carrier will ever haul under the current process. Its true values are parameters , written with Greek letters: μ (mu, population mean), σ (sigma, population standard deviation), N (population size). A sample is the part of the population you actually measure: 50 loads from last month. Its values are statistics , written with Latin letters: x̄ (x-bar, sample mean), s (sample standard deviation), n (sample size). We almost never know the true μ and σ. We estimate them from x̄ and s. Statistics (Domain 3) tells us how confident we can be in those estimates. For a sample to represent the population, it should be random (every item had a fair chance of being chosen) and collected under the same conditions you want to learn about. Probability basics Probability is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) describing how likely an event is. If 8% of loads are late, P(late) = 0.08. Complement rule. The probability something does not happen is 1 minus the probability it does: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) Addition rule (A or B). The probability that A or B (or both) happens: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) You subtract P(A and B) because otherwise the overlap is counted twice. If A and B cannot happen together ( mutually exclusive ), P(A and B) = 0 and it simplifies to P(A) + P(B). Multiplication rule (A and B). If A and B are independent (one happening does not change the chance of the other): P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) Conditional probability. The probability of A given that B has happened: P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) Independent vs mutually exclusive These are different ideas, and confusing them is a classic error: Mutually exclusive : the events cannot both happen . A single load cannot be both "on time" and "late". Knowing one happened tells you the other did not. Independent : one event does not affect the probability of the other. Whether today's load from Dallas is late has no effect on whether a load in Seattle is late. Two events with non-zero probabilities that are mutually exclusive are never independent: if one happens, the other's probability drops to zero. "At least one": use the complement Questions often ask for the probability of at least one event. Calculate the chance of none and subtract from 1. Each load has a 10% chance of being late, independently. In 3 loads, what is the chance at least one is late? P(a load is on time) = 0.9. P(all 3 on time) = 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.729. P(at least one late) = 1 − 0.729 = 0.271 . Two counting distributions Binomial : the number of "successes" (for example defectives) in n independent trials, each with the same probability p . Use it for pass/fail data. P(x) = [n! ÷ (x!(n − x)!)] × pˣ × (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ˣ 5 invoices, each with a 10% chance of an error: P(0 with errors) = 0.9⁵ = 0.590 . P(exactly 1) = 5 × 0.1 × 0.9⁴ = 5 × 0.1 × 0.6561 = 0.328 . P(at least 1) = 1 − 0.590 = 0.410 . Poisson : the number of events (for example defects) in a fixed amount of space or time, when they occur randomly at an average rate λ (lambda). Use it for defect counts. P(x) = (λˣ × e^(−λ)) ÷ x! Trucks average λ = 2 defects found at inspection: P(0 defects) = e^(−2) = 0.135 . P(exactly 1) = 2 × e^(−2) = 0.271 . P(at least 1) = 1 − 0.135 = 0.865 . Rule of thumb: defectives (pass/fail units) → binomial; defects (counts per unit) → Poisson. (See 1.2.5 for defects vs defectives.) Data collection plan Before collecting data, write a plan so the data is useful and consistent: What to measure (the Y and the suspect X's), with operational definitions. How to measure it (instrument, method, form). Who collects it (and are they trained?). When and where : how often, which shifts, which locations. How many : sample size. Stratification factors : extra information recorded with each point (shift, terminal, driver, product), so the data can later be split to find patterns. Common mistakes and exam traps Pass/fail is discrete; measured length or time is continuous. Even if you record time to the nearest minute, it is continuous. Independent is not mutually exclusive. Sample symbols are Latin (x̄, s, n); population symbols are Greek (μ, σ, N). "At least one" means 1 − P(none). Ordinal ratings (1 to 5) do not have equal gaps , so averaging them is questionable. Check yourself Classify as continuous or discrete: (a) seconds to answer a call, (b) whether a call was resolved, (c) number of errors on a form. Which scale is "customer satisfaction 1 to 5"? What symbol is the population standard deviation, and what is its sample counterpart? P(a pallet is damaged) = 0.02, independently. What is the probability that at least one of 10 pallets is damaged? Are "a load is late" and "a load is on time" independent, mutually exclusive, or both? Show answers (a) Continuous, (b) discrete (pass/fail), (c) discrete (count). Ordinal. σ (population); s (sample). 1 − 0.98¹⁰ = 1 − 0.817 ≈ 0.183. Mutually exclusive (they cannot both happen), and therefore not independent. Key takeaways Continuous (measured) vs discrete (counted or categorized); continuous carries more information. Scales: nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio (NOIR). Population parameters (μ, σ, N) vs sample statistics (x̄, s, n). Addition, multiplication (independent), conditional and complement rules; "at least one" = 1 − P(none). Binomial for defectives, Poisson for defects. Plan data collection: what, how, who, when, how many, stratification.
Descriptive Statistics

Why this matters A column of 200 numbers tells you nothing at a glance. Two or three well-chosen summary numbers, center and spread, tell you a lot. Almost every later calculation (capability, control limits, hypothesis tests) starts with a mean and a standard deviation. The big idea To describe data you need to know two things: Where is the middle? (central tendency) How spread out is it? (variation) And, often, a third: what shape is it? (symmetric or skewed). Measures of center Mean (average) : add all values and divide by how many. Symbol x̄ for a sample. x̄ = Σx ÷ n (Σ, capital sigma, means "add them all up".) Median : the middle value when the data are sorted. With an even number of values, average the two middle ones. Mode : the value that occurs most often. Example, load times in hours: 4, 7, 6, 9, 4. Mean = (4 + 7 + 6 + 9 + 4) ÷ 5 = 30 ÷ 5 = 6 . Sorted: 4, 4, 6, 7, 9. Median = 6 . Mode = 4 . The mean is pulled by extreme values; the median is not. If one load took 40 hours instead of 9, the mean jumps to 12.2, but the median stays 6. For skewed data, or data with outliers, the median is often a better description of a "typical" value. Measures of spread Range : largest minus smallest. Simple, but depends on only two points. For 4, 7, 6, 9, 4: range = 9 − 4 = 5 . Variance : the average squared distance from the mean. Standard deviation : the square root of the variance, in the same units as the data. The most used measure of spread. Interquartile range (IQR) : Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle 50%. Resistant to outliers, like the median. Calculating the sample standard deviation s = √[ Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1) ] Step by step for 4, 7, 6, 9, 4 (x̄ = 6): x x − x̄ (x − x̄)² 4 −2 4 7 1 1 6 0 0 9 3 9 4 −2 4 Sum 18 Sum of squared deviations = 18. Divide by n − 1 = 4: variance s² = 4.5 . Square root: s = √4.5 ≈ 2.12 hours . Why n − 1? A sample's values are on average a little closer to their own mean than to the true population mean, so dividing by n would underestimate the spread. Dividing by n − 1 corrects this. For the whole population , divide by N : σ = √[Σ(x − μ)² ÷ N]. With the same five numbers treated as a population, σ = √(18 ÷ 5) ≈ 1.90. Calculator trap: scientific calculators have two keys: σn (divides by n, population) and s or σn−1 (divides by n − 1, sample). For sample data, use the n − 1 key. You can convert: s = σn × √[n ÷ (n − 1)]. Shape and skew Data piled symmetrically around the center (like the normal curve) have mean ≈ median ≈ mode. Many real processes are skewed : Mode Median Mean Long tail to the right pulls the mean up Right (positive) skew: mean > median > mode A long right tail drags the mean toward it; the median sits between. Right (positive) skew : a long tail to the right. Common for times (delivery times, repair times: they cannot go below zero but can run very long). Mean > median > mode. Left (negative) skew : a long tail to the left. Mean < median < mode. So if a question says "the mean is larger than the median", the data are skewed right. Percentiles and quartiles The p-th percentile is the value below which p% of the data fall. The quartiles split sorted data into four equal parts: Q1 (25th percentile), Q2 (50th, the median), Q3 (75th). IQR = Q3 − Q1. "90% of deliveries arrive within 26 hours" means the 90th percentile of delivery time is 26 hours, which is often more meaningful to customers than the average. Within vs overall variation Data collected over time have two kinds of variation: Within (short-term) variation : the variation inside small groups of consecutive measurements (subgroups), when conditions are nearly the same. Overall (long-term) variation : the variation of all the data together, including shifts and drifts between subgroups. Overall is always at least as large as within. The difference shows how much the process moves over time. This distinction drives Cp versus Pp in capability (2.4) and the 1.5σ idea in 1.1.1. Variances add, standard deviations do not When two independent sources of variation combine (for example, time to load plus time to drive), their variances add : σ²(total) = σ²₁ + σ²₂ If loading time has σ = 3 minutes and transit time has σ = 4 minutes, the total has σ² = 9 + 16 = 25, so σ = 5 minutes , not 7. This is why measurement error and process variation combine the way they do in MSA (2.3). Other formulas worth recognizing Weighted mean : Σ(w × x) ÷ Σw. If 3 loads took 5 h and 1 load took 9 h, the weighted mean = (3 × 5 + 1 × 9) ÷ 4 = 6 h. Mean of grouped data : Σ(f × class midpoint) ÷ n, used when data come in a frequency table. Mean deviation : Σ|x − x̄| ÷ n, the average absolute distance from the mean (for 4, 7, 6, 9, 4: (2 + 1 + 0 + 3 + 2) ÷ 5 = 1.6). Coefficient of variation : s ÷ x̄, spread relative to the mean, useful to compare processes with different averages (low exam yield). Common mistakes and exam traps Outliers pull the mean, not the median. Mean > median means right skew. Sample s divides by n − 1. Use the right calculator key. Standard deviations do not add ; variances do, for independent sources. Check yourself Data: 2, 3, 3, 5, 12. Find the mean, median and mode. Which measure of center would you report for these data, and why? Compute s for 10, 12, 14. Two independent sources have σ = 6 and σ = 8. What is the combined σ? A delivery-time dataset has mean 31 hours and median 26 hours. Which way is it skewed? Show answers Mean = 25 ÷ 5 = 5; median = 3; mode = 3. The median (3), because the outlier 12 pulls the mean up. Mean 12; deviations −2, 0, 2; squares sum to 8; s² = 8 ÷ 2 = 4; s = 2. √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10. Right (positive) skew, because the mean is above the median. Key takeaways Center: mean (pulled by outliers), median (resistant), mode. Spread: range, variance, standard deviation, IQR. s = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)]; population σ divides by N. Right skew: mean > median > mode. Within (short-term) vs overall (long-term) variation. Independent variances add: σ_total = √(σ₁² + σ₂²).
Normal Distributions and Normality

Why this matters The normal distribution is the most important shape in statistics. Many processes produce roughly normal data, and many tools (capability indices, control limits, t-tests) assume it. You need to use it to calculate probabilities, and to check whether your data actually follow it. The big idea The normal distribution is the symmetric, bell-shaped curve. It is completely described by two numbers: μ (mean) : where the center is. σ (standard deviation) : how wide it is. Change μ and the bell slides left or right. Change σ and it gets wider and flatter, or narrower and taller. The total area under the curve is 1 (100% of the data), and the area over any interval is the probability of a value falling there. The empirical rule (68, 95, 99.7) For any normal distribution: -3σ -2σ -1σ μ +1σ +2σ +3σ 68% 95% 99.7% The shares are the same for every normal distribution, whatever its mean and σ. About 68% of values fall within ±1σ of the mean. About 95% within ±2σ . About 99.7% within ±3σ . If delivery times are normal with mean 40 hours and σ = 4 hours, about 68% take 36 to 44 hours, 95% take 32 to 48 hours, and nearly all take 28 to 52 hours. The z-score To find the probability for any value, convert it to a z-score : how many standard deviations it is from the mean. z = (x − μ) ÷ σ Every normal distribution becomes the standard normal distribution (mean 0, σ 1) after this conversion, so one table works for all of them. Using the z table A standard normal table gives the area to the left of a z value (the probability of being below it). 0 z = 1.5 0.9332 to the left 0.0668 to the right = 1 − 0.9332 The table gives the left area; the right tail is 1 minus it. Example 1: above a value. Delivery times: μ = 40, σ = 4. What fraction take more than 46 hours? z = (46 − 40) ÷ 4 = 1.5. Table: area left of 1.5 = 0.9332. Above: 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668 , about 6.7%. Example 2: below a value. Fraction under 34 hours? z = (34 − 40) ÷ 4 = −1.5. By symmetry, area below −1.5 = 0.0668 . Example 3: between two values. Fraction between 36 and 48 hours? z for 36 = −1; z for 48 = +2. Area left of 2 = 0.9772; area left of −1 = 0.1587. Between: 0.9772 − 0.1587 = 0.8185 , about 82%. Example 4: symmetric interval. P(−z < Z < z) = 2 × (left area at z) − 1. For z = 1.96: 2 × 0.975 − 1 = 0.95. A quirk of the IASSC reference document The reference document (version 1.4.2) has two z tables. One lists negative z values (−4.9 to 0) and gives the left-tail area, as expected (z = −1.96 gives 0.02500). The second is titled "Right Tail Area" for z from 0 to 4.9, but its values are actually the area to the left (it shows 0.97500 at 1.96). So for P(Z > z), use 1 − (that table's value), or look up −z in the negative table. The table stops at 4.9 and prints tiny tails as 0.00000, so for 6σ-level questions use the known 3.4 DPMO rather than the table. Check this against your own copy, since versions differ. Is my data normal? Normality tests Many tools assume normal data, so you check. A normality test is a hypothesis test (Domain 3) with: Null hypothesis (H₀) : the data come from a normal distribution. Alternative (H₁) : they do not. Common tests: Anderson-Darling (Minitab's default), Shapiro-Wilk , Ryan-Joiner , Kolmogorov-Smirnov . All produce a p-value : p ≤ 0.05 : strong evidence the data are not normal. Reject H₀. Memory aid: "if p is low, the null must go." p > 0.05 : not enough evidence to say the data are non-normal. You fail to reject H₀. This is not proof that the data are normal, just that the test found no strong evidence against it. Sample size matters: with very few points (say 10), a test can almost never detect non-normality; with thousands, it flags tiny, unimportant departures. Always look at the picture too. The normal probability plot A probability plot plots each data point against where it would fall if the data were perfectly normal. If the data are normal, the points lie close to a straight line (within the curved confidence bands software draws). Curves, S-shapes and points peeling away at the ends show skew, heavy tails or outliers. Why data are not normal Skewed processes : times, counts and anything bounded at zero. Mixed populations : two shifts, two machines or two suppliers combined (often bimodal, two humps). Outliers : a few wild points from special causes or data errors. Bounded data : values that cannot exceed a limit (100%, zero defects). Coarse measurement : values rounded so much that only a few distinct values appear. The fix depends on the cause: separate mixed populations (stratify), investigate outliers, use a transformation or a non-normal tool for naturally skewed data. Common mistakes and exam traps p = 0.02 on a normality test means the data are not normal (p is low, reject normality). p = 0.30 does not prove normality ; it means no strong evidence against it. Left-area tables : for "greater than", use 1 − table value. ±1σ, ±2σ, ±3σ = 68%, 95%, 99.7%. Check yourself What percentage of a normal distribution lies within ±2σ? μ = 100, σ = 10. What is the z-score of 85? For the same process, what fraction is above 120? (Area left of z = 2 is 0.9772.) An Anderson-Darling test gives p = 0.004. What do you conclude? A histogram shows two humps. What is the likely reason the data are not normal? Show answers About 95%. z = (85 − 100) ÷ 10 = −1.5. z = 2; above = 1 − 0.9772 = 0.0228, about 2.3%. Reject normality: the data are not normal. Two populations mixed together (for example two shifts or machines). Key takeaways Normal curve: symmetric, defined by μ and σ. 68% within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, 99.7% within ±3σ. z = (x − μ) ÷ σ; tables give the left area; right tail = 1 − left. Normality tests: H₀ = normal; p ≤ 0.05 means not normal; p > 0.05 is not proof of normality. Check the probability plot; non-normality comes from skew, mixtures, outliers, bounds or coarse rounding.
Graphical Analysis

Why this matters A good chart shows in seconds what a table hides for hours: patterns, shifts, outliers, clusters. Plot the data before calculating anything. The exam often describes a situation and asks which chart fits it. The big idea Every chart answers a different question. Match the chart to the question: Question Chart What is the shape of one set of data? Histogram, dotplot, stem-and-leaf How do several groups compare? Boxplot, individual value plot, interval plot How does it behave over time? Run chart (and control charts, 5.2) Are two continuous variables related? Scatterplot Is it normal? Normal probability plot Which categories matter most? Pareto chart Histogram A histogram groups data into ranges (bins) and draws a bar for how many values fall in each. It shows shape (symmetric, skewed, bimodal), center and spread . Bin choice matters: too few bins hide the shape, too many make it jagged. Software defaults are usually reasonable. Needs a fair amount of data (roughly 30 or more points, better 50 to 100) to show a reliable shape. Day shift Night shift Load time (minutes) for both shifts combined: two humps Two humps usually mean two different populations mixed together. A bimodal (two-humped) histogram is a strong clue that two populations are mixed: two shifts, two machines, two suppliers. Split (stratify) the data and plot each group separately. Boxplot A boxplot (box-and-whisker plot) summarizes a distribution with five numbers and flags outliers: Whisker end Q1 Median Q3 Whisker end Outlier IQR = Q3 − Q1 (middle 50%) Whiskers reach the furthest points within 1.5 × IQR of the box; anything beyond is plotted as a separate outlier point. The box holds the middle half of the data; the line inside is the median. The box runs from Q1 to Q3 (the middle 50%, the IQR). The line in the box is the median . Whiskers extend to the furthest data points within 1.5 × IQR of the box. Points beyond that are plotted individually as outliers . Boxplots are excellent for comparing groups side by side : delivery times by terminal, cycle time by shift. You can instantly see which group has a higher median or more spread. Other displays Dotplot : one dot per value along a scale. Great for small data sets; shows every point. Individual value plot : every data point plotted by group. Like a dotplot for comparing groups. Interval plot : the mean of each group with a confidence interval bar (usually 95%). Used to compare group means; if intervals barely overlap, the means likely differ. Stem-and-leaf plot : a text histogram that keeps the actual digits (stem = leading digits, leaves = last digit). Run chart A run chart plots data in time order with a center line at the median . It reveals behavior over time that a histogram hides: Shift : a run of many consecutive points (commonly 6 or more, some texts use 8) all on one side of the median, suggesting the process level changed. Trend : many consecutive points steadily rising or falling (commonly 5 to 7 or more). Cycles : a repeating up-and-down pattern (weekly, daily, seasonal). Oscillation, or too many runs : points zig-zagging up and down constantly, which can mean over-adjustment or mixed sources. Too few runs : points stay on one side for long stretches, which suggests shifts. Run charts need no statistical calculation beyond the median and work with little data, so they are useful early in a project. Control charts (5.2) add statistically calculated limits. Scatterplot A scatterplot plots pairs of continuous values: one variable on each axis. It shows whether they are related: Points rising left to right: positive relationship (more miles, more fuel). Falling: negative relationship (more experience, fewer errors). A cloud with no pattern: no relationship. A curve: a non-linear relationship. It shows association, not proof of cause. The relationship is quantified with correlation and regression (3.3). Normal probability plot and Pareto chart Covered in 2.2.3 (probability plot, to judge normality) and 1.2.4 (Pareto, to rank categories). Worked example Which chart? "Compare loading times at our four terminals." Boxplot (or individual value plot). "Has our on-time rate changed since the new dispatch system went live?" Run chart (time order). "Does trailer age relate to repair cost?" Scatterplot . "What does the distribution of fuel use per trip look like?" Histogram . "Which reasons for claims matter most?" Pareto chart . "Are the cycle-time data normal?" Normal probability plot . Common mistakes and exam traps Comparing groups = boxplot (or interval/individual value plot). Behavior over time = run chart. A histogram loses time order. Two continuous variables = scatterplot. Bimodal histogram = mixed populations , not a bad measurement. A boxplot outlier is beyond 1.5 × IQR from the box , not beyond 3σ. Check yourself What does the line inside a boxplot's box show? A team wants to see whether call volume varies by day of the week over three months. Which chart? Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 30. Beyond what values would points be plotted as outliers? What does a cloud of points with no pattern on a scatterplot suggest? On a run chart, 9 consecutive points are above the median. What does this suggest? Show answers The median. A run chart (time order); cycles by day of week will show as a repeating pattern. IQR = 10; 1.5 × IQR = 15; outliers are below 20 − 15 = 5 or above 30 + 15 = 45. No relationship between the two variables. A shift: the process level has probably changed. Key takeaways Histogram: shape; bimodal means mixed populations. Boxplot: median, Q1 to Q3 box, whiskers to 1.5 × IQR, outliers; best for comparing groups. Run chart: time order; look for shifts, trends, cycles, oscillation. Scatterplot: relationship between two continuous variables. Pick the chart that answers the question.
Precision and Accuracy

Why this matters Every decision in Six Sigma rests on data, and data comes from measurement. If the measurement itself is wrong or noisy, the team will chase variation that is not really there, or miss real problems. Measurement System Analysis (MSA) checks the measuring before you trust the measurements. It is a required Measure-phase deliverable. The big idea A measurement system is everything involved in getting a number: the instrument (gauge, scale, software), the people using it, the method, the environment and the part being measured. Like any process, it has variation. What you see in your data is a mix of two things: σ²(observed) = σ²(process) + σ²(measurement) The variation you observe is the real process variation plus the measurement system's own variation. (Variances add, as in 2.2.2.) If the measurement variation is large, it hides the real process. Example: observed σ = 5 minutes, measurement system σ = 3 minutes. Real process σ = √(5² − 3²) = √16 = 4 minutes . A quarter of what looked like process variation was really measurement noise. Accuracy vs precision Picture shooting at a target: Accurate and precise Precise, not accurate Accurate, not precise Neither Accuracy is about where the shots center; precision is about how tightly they group. Accuracy : how close the average of measurements is to the true value . An accurate scale, on average, reads the true weight. Precision : how close repeated measurements are to each other . A precise scale gives nearly the same reading every time you weigh the same thing, even if that reading is wrong. A measurement can be precise but not accurate (tight group, wrong place), which is usually easy to fix by calibration. It can be accurate but not precise (centered but scattered), which is harder: the instrument or method itself is noisy. The five measurement errors MSA breaks measurement error into two families: Location errors (accuracy problems) : is the average reading in the right place? Bias : the average reading differs from the true value. Linearity : bias changes across the range of sizes being measured. Stability : bias changes over time (drift). Spread errors (precision problems) : are the readings consistent? Repeatability : variation when the same person measures the same part with the same instrument several times. Also called equipment variation. Reproducibility : variation between different people measuring the same parts. Also called appraiser variation. 2.3.2 covers location errors; 2.3.3 covers repeatability and reproducibility. Resolution (discrimination) Resolution (or discrimination ) is the smallest change the instrument can show. A scale that reads only to the nearest 100 lb cannot tell a 40,020 lb load from a 40,080 lb load. Rule of thumb: the measurement increments should be no bigger than about one-tenth of the tolerance (specification width), or of the process spread. If the tolerance is ±1.0 mm (width 2.0 mm), the gauge should read to 0.2 mm or finer, ideally 0.1 mm. With too coarse a resolution, many different parts get the same reading and the data looks blocky. Calibration Calibration compares an instrument against a reference standard of known value (traceable to national standards) and adjusts it if needed. Calibration fixes bias at the points checked. It does not fix poor repeatability or reproducibility. A calibrated gauge can still be imprecise. Common mistakes and exam traps Precise but not accurate : a tight cluster far from the center.
