Observed variation = process + measurement , as variances. Calibration fixes bias, not precision. Resolution: about 1/10 of tolerance or process spread, or finer. Check yourself Define accuracy and precision in one sentence each. A gauge always reads 0.5 kg high, very consistently. Is it accurate? Precise? Observed σ is 10 and measurement σ is 6. What is the real process σ? Which errors are "location" errors? The tolerance is 0.50 mm wide. What resolution should the gauge have, at least? Show answers Accuracy: how close the average reading is to the true value. Precision: how close repeated readings are to each other. Precise but not accurate (it has bias). √(100 − 36) = √64 = 8. Bias, linearity, stability. About 0.05 mm or finer. Key takeaways Observed variance = process variance + measurement variance. Accuracy = centered on truth; precision = consistent. Location errors: bias, linearity, stability. Spread errors: repeatability, reproducibility. Resolution about one-tenth of the tolerance or process spread. Calibration fixes bias only.
Bias, Linearity and Stability

Why this matters A gauge that reads wrong in a consistent way can make a good process look bad, or a bad one look good. These three studies find and describe location errors so they can be corrected. Bias Bias is the difference between the average of repeated measurements and the true (reference) value : Bias = average measured value − reference value How to study it: take a reference part whose true value is known (measured by a more accurate lab method, or a certified standard). Measure it many times (often 10 or more) with the gauge under normal conditions. Average the readings. Example: a reference weight of 10.00 kg is weighed 10 times; the average is 10.03 kg. Bias = 10.03 − 10.00 = +0.03 kg : the scale reads high by 0.03 kg on average. Whether that bias matters depends on how it compares with the tolerance and with the variation of the readings (a statistical test can show whether the bias is significantly different from zero). Fix: calibrate or adjust the gauge. Linearity Linearity describes how bias changes across the operating range of the gauge. A gauge might be accurate for small parts but read high for large ones. 0 +1 −1 Reference value of the part (small to large) Bias = measured − reference Bias grows with size: a linearity problem If bias stayed flat at zero across all sizes, the gauge would have no linearity problem. How to study it: measure several reference parts that span the range the gauge is used for (small to large), several times each. Plot bias against reference value and fit a line. A flat line at zero means no linearity problem. A sloped line means bias depends on size. Fixes: a linearity problem is usually not solved by a single calibration offset. Options include calibrating at several points, repairing worn components, or using a different gauge or method for part of the range. Stability Stability (also called drift) describes how bias changes over time . A scale might read correctly on Monday and drift high by Friday as it warms up or wears. How to study it: measure the same master part periodically (for example daily) over weeks, and plot the results on a control chart (5.2). A stable gauge shows only random scatter around a steady center. Shifts, trends or out-of-control points show instability. Fixes depend on the cause: environment (temperature, vibration), wear, maintenance schedule, warm-up time, or a need for more frequent calibration. Telling them apart Description Error "Reads consistently 2 units high" Bias "Reads correctly on small parts, high on large parts" Linearity "Was fine last month, reads higher every week" Stability Common mistakes and exam traps Bias = average − reference , not a single reading. Linearity is across sizes; stability is across time. Stability is tracked with a control chart on a master part. One calibration offset fixes bias, not linearity. Check yourself A reference part is 50.0 mm. Readings average 49.8 mm. What is the bias? A thermometer is accurate at 20 °C but reads 3 degrees low at 80 °C. Which error? How would you monitor a gauge's stability? What does a flat line at zero on a linearity plot mean? Which of the three is usually fixed by a simple calibration? Show answers 49.8 − 50.0 = −0.2 mm (reads low). Linearity. Measure the same master part regularly over time and plot it on a control chart. No linearity problem: bias is zero across the whole range. Bias. Key takeaways Bias = average measured − reference; fix with calibration. Linearity = bias changing across the measurement range; check with several reference parts. Stability = bias changing over time; track a master part on a control chart.
Gage Repeatability and Reproducibility

Why this matters Gage R&R is the most important MSA study. It answers: how much of the variation in our data is caused by the measurement system itself? If the answer is "a lot", no analysis built on that data can be trusted, and the gauge or method must be fixed first. The big idea Total observed variation splits into pieces: Part-to-part variation : the real differences between parts. This is what we want to see. Measurement system variation (GRR) : noise added by measuring. It has two parts: Repeatability (equipment variation, EV): the same person measuring the same part repeatedly with the same gauge gets different readings. Reproducibility (appraiser variation, AV): different people measuring the same parts get different averages. Because independent variances add: GRR = √(repeatability² + reproducibility²) Total variation = √(GRR² + part-to-part²) (each term here is a standard deviation). Running a study A typical (not mandatory) design: About 10 parts that span the full range of the process, so the study can see real part differences. 2 or 3 operators (appraisers) who normally do the measuring. 2 or 3 repeat measurements per operator per part. Randomized order and blind measuring: operators should not know which part they are measuring or what they measured last time, otherwise they unconsciously repeat their earlier readings. This is a crossed study: every operator measures every part. When measuring destroys the part (a crash test, a tensile test), each operator must measure different but similar parts, which is a nested study. Analysis methods: the ANOVA method (preferred; it can also detect an operator-by-part interaction) and the older Xbar-R method (simpler, using ranges). The key metrics %Study Variation (%SV, also %GRR) : the measurement system's share of the total variation, on a standard deviation basis. %Study Var = GRR ÷ Total variation × 100 %Tolerance : the measurement system's spread compared with the specification width. %Tolerance = (6 × GRR) ÷ (USL − LSL) × 100 The "6" is the study spread: 6σ covers about 99.73% of measurements. Older material used 5.15σ (99%); check which a question uses. %Contribution : the same comparison using variances instead of standard deviations: %Contribution = GRR² ÷ Total variation² × 100 Because it is a squared ratio, %Contribution numbers are much smaller: a 10% Study Var is about a 1% Contribution, and 30% Study Var is about 9% Contribution. Number of distinct categories (ndc) : how many groups of parts the measurement system can reliably tell apart. ndc = 1.41 × (part-to-part σ ÷ GRR) ndc should be at least 5 . It is truncated to a whole number (5.9 counts as 5), not rounded up. Acceptance criteria The AIAG guidelines (as used by Minitab): %Study Var (or %Tolerance) Verdict Under 10% Acceptable 10% to 30% May be acceptable, depending on the importance of the measurement, the cost of the gauge and the cost of fixing it Over 30% Unacceptable: improve the measurement system Equivalent %Contribution cutoffs are about 1% and 9%. Which percentage to use? %Tolerance is the better guide when the gauge is used to sort parts as good or bad against specifications. %Study Var is the better guide when the data will be used to study and improve the process (seeing process variation). A gauge can look fine on one and poor on the other. Reading the results: what is causing the noise? Repeatability much larger than reproducibility : the problem is the equipment or method . The gauge needs maintenance, a better fixture, a more stable setup, or replacement. Reproducibility much larger than repeatability : the problem is how different people measure . Fix with training, clearer operational definitions, standard technique, or a fixture that removes judgment. Significant operator × part interaction (from ANOVA): some operators measure certain parts differently (for example, one operator struggles with very small parts). Investigate technique on those parts. Gage R&R software also shows graphs: R chart by operator : shows repeatability; points should be in control (operators are consistent). Xbar chart by operator : should show many points outside the limits , because the limits come from measurement noise and the parts should differ by much more. If most points are inside the limits, the gauge cannot tell the parts apart. Worked example A study on a tire tread gauge gives (as standard deviations, in mm): Repeatability = 0.03 Reproducibility = 0.04 Part-to-part = 0.24 Tolerance (USL − LSL) = 2.0 mm GRR = √(0.03² + 0.04²) = √(0.0009 + 0.0016) = √0.0025 = 0.05 . Total = √(0.05² + 0.24²) = √(0.0025 + 0.0576) = √0.0601 ≈ 0.245 . %Study Var = 0.05 ÷ 0.245 × 100 ≈ 20.4% : marginal (10% to 30%). %Tolerance = 6 × 0.05 ÷ 2.0 × 100 = 15% : marginal. %Contribution = 0.0025 ÷ 0.0601 ≈ 4.2% . ndc = 1.41 × 0.24 ÷ 0.05 = 6.77, truncated to 6 : acceptable (at least 5). Reproducibility (0.04) is larger than repeatability (0.03), so operator technique is the bigger issue. Training and a standard method would be the first fix. Common mistakes and exam traps Add variances, not standard deviations , to combine repeatability and reproducibility. %Contribution is on a variance basis ; do not compare its numbers with the 10%/30% cutoffs. ndc truncates ; 4.9 is 4, which fails. Repeatability = equipment; reproducibility = operators. Parts should span the process range ; if the parts are too similar, part-to-part variation looks small and the gauge looks worse than it is. 6σ vs 5.15σ study spread. Check yourself Define repeatability and reproducibility. Repeatability σ = 0.6, reproducibility σ = 0.8. What is GRR? GRR = 1.0 and total variation = 4.0. What is %Study Var, and is it acceptable? GRR = 0.5, tolerance = 12. What is %Tolerance (6σ basis)? Part σ = 3.2 and GRR = 1.0. What is ndc, and is it acceptable? Reproducibility is the dominant source. What do you fix? Show answers Repeatability: variation when one operator measures the same part repeatedly with the same gauge. Reproducibility: variation between different operators measuring the same parts. √(0.36 + 0.64) = √1 = 1.0. 1.0 ÷ 4.0 = 25%: may be acceptable depending on the application. 6 × 0.5 ÷ 12 = 25%. 1.41 × 3.2 ÷ 1.0 = 4.51, truncated to 4: not acceptable (needs at least 5). Operator technique: training, clear operational definitions, standard method or fixtures. Key takeaways GRR = √(repeatability² + reproducibility²); total = √(GRR² + part²). %Study Var = GRR ÷ total; %Tolerance = 6 × GRR ÷ (USL − LSL); %Contribution uses variances. Under 10% good, 10% to 30% maybe, over 30% unacceptable. ndc = 1.41 × part σ ÷ GRR, truncated, at least 5. Repeatability points to equipment; reproducibility points to operators.
Variable and Attribute MSA

Why this matters Not every measurement produces a number. Many inspections end in a judgment: pass or fail, damaged or not, good, minor defect or major defect. Those judgments need checking too, and they are often less reliable than people assume. Variable vs attribute MSA Variable MSA : the measurement is continuous (length, weight, time). Use Gage R&R (2.3.3) plus bias, linearity and stability. Attribute MSA : the measurement is a category (pass/fail, good/bad, defect type). Use attribute agreement analysis . Attribute agreement analysis A typical design: 30 to 50 items , chosen to include a good mix of good and bad, and some borderline cases, with the correct answer (the standard or reference) known for each, decided by an expert. 2 or 3 appraisers (inspectors). Each appraiser judges each item 2 or 3 times , in random order, without knowing which item it is. The analysis checks four kinds of agreement: Within appraiser : does each inspector agree with themselves across repeated trials? (like repeatability) Between appraisers : do the inspectors agree with each other ? (like reproducibility) Each appraiser vs standard : is each inspector right ? (accuracy) All appraisers vs standard : do all inspectors, on all trials, match the correct answer? Agreement is not accuracy. Three inspectors can agree perfectly with each other and all be wrong, for example if they were all trained on the same incorrect standard. Always check agreement against the known standard. Percent agreement and kappa The simplest measure is percent agreement : the share of items rated the same way. But some agreement happens by chance : if two inspectors pass 90% of items at random, they would agree most of the time without really looking. Kappa (κ) corrects for chance: κ = (Pₒ − Pₑ) ÷ (1 − Pₑ) Pₒ : the observed proportion of agreement. Pₑ : the proportion of agreement expected by chance alone. κ = 1: perfect agreement. κ = 0: no better than chance. κ below 0: worse than chance. Worked example. Two inspectors judge 50 trailers as "damaged" or "OK". They agree on 45 (Pₒ = 0.90). Inspector A called 30 "OK" (60%) and B called 32 "OK" (64%). Chance agreement on "OK": 0.60 × 0.64 = 0.384. Chance agreement on "damaged": 0.40 × 0.36 = 0.144. Pₑ = 0.384 + 0.144 = 0.528. κ = (0.90 − 0.528) ÷ (1 − 0.528) = 0.372 ÷ 0.472 ≈ 0.79 . The 90% raw agreement shrinks to 0.79 once chance is removed. How good is good enough? Sources differ, so read the question for clues: AIAG MSA manual : κ above 0.75 indicates good to excellent agreement; below 0.40 indicates poor agreement. Some software rules of thumb (for example SigmaXL): 0.9 or above good, 0.7 to 0.9 marginal or acceptable, below 0.7 unacceptable. By the AIAG rule the example's 0.79 is good. By the stricter rule it is marginal. It is not known which convention IASSC uses; when a question gives thresholds, use them. Misclassification rates When comparing with the standard, three rates describe the kinds of mistakes: Effectiveness : the share of items classified correctly . Miss rate : the share of bad items called good (defects escape to the customer). Usually the most serious error. False alarm rate : the share of good items called bad (unnecessary rework, scrap or rejections). The AIAG MSA manual gives example guidelines for each appraiser: Acceptable Marginal (may need improvement) Unacceptable Effectiveness 90% or more 80% or more Below 80% Miss rate 2% or less 5% or less Above 5% False alarm rate 5% or less 10% or less Above 10% Other agreement statistics (recognition only) Cohen's kappa : agreement between two raters (or one rater and the standard). Fleiss' kappa : agreement among three or more raters. Kendall's coefficient : for ordinal ratings (like severity 1 to 5), where some disagreements are bigger than others; it gives credit for being "close". Common mistakes and exam traps Kappa removes chance agreement ; raw percent agreement overstates reliability. Agreement with each other is not correctness : check against the standard. AIAG: κ ≥ 0.75 good, < 0.40 poor. Some texts use 0.9 / 0.7. Miss rate = bad passed as good; false alarm = good rejected as bad. Include borderline items : an easy sample makes every inspector look perfect. Check yourself When do you use attribute agreement analysis instead of Gage R&R? Pₒ = 0.85, Pₑ = 0.50. Calculate kappa. By the AIAG guideline, is κ = 0.62 good, poor, or in between? All three inspectors agree with each other on every item. Is the inspection system acceptable? An inspector passes 4 out of 50 damaged items. Which rate is affected? Show answers When the measurement is categorical (pass/fail, defect type) rather than continuous. (0.85 − 0.50) ÷ (1 − 0.50) = 0.35 ÷ 0.50 = 0.70. In between (above 0.40, below 0.75). Not necessarily. They must also agree with the known standard; they could all be wrong together. The miss rate. Key takeaways Variable data: Gage R&R. Attribute data: attribute agreement analysis. Check within appraiser, between appraisers, each vs standard, all vs standard. κ = (Pₒ − Pₑ) ÷ (1 − Pₑ) removes chance agreement. AIAG: κ above 0.75 good, below 0.40 poor; some software uses 0.9 and 0.7. Effectiveness, miss rate and false alarm rate describe the kinds of errors.
Capability Analysis

Why this matters "Is our process good enough?" is the central question of Measure. Capability analysis answers it with numbers: how well does the process's natural variation fit inside what the customer requires? Capability indices (Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk) are among the most frequently tested calculations on the exam. The big idea Two different things set the limits you will see on charts: Specification limits (LSL and USL) come from the customer : the voice of the customer. They say what is acceptable. "Fill weight 495 to 505 g." Control limits come from the process data : the voice of the process. They say what the process naturally does (5.2). The two are independent . A process can be perfectly stable (in control) and still make many out-of-spec parts, if its natural spread is wider than the specification. Capability compares the voice of the process (its spread and center) with the voice of the customer (the specs). Cp: does the spread fit? Cp compares the width of the specification with the natural width of the process, taken as 6σ (±3σ covers 99.73% of a normal process). Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6σ(within) Cp = 1: the process spread exactly fills the specification. Any drift creates defects. Cp = 1.33: the spec is a third wider than the process spread. Cp = 2: the process spread fills only half the specification (a six sigma process). Cp below 1: the process is wider than the spec; it will make defects even if perfectly centered. Cp ignores where the process is. It only asks whether the process could fit if it were centered. Cpk: does it actually fit, given where it is? Cpk measures the distance from the process mean to the nearest specification limit, in units of 3σ: Cpk = min[ (USL − μ) ÷ 3σ , (μ − LSL) ÷ 3σ ] The two parts are sometimes written separately: Cpu = (USL − μ) ÷ 3σ, the upper side. Cpl = (μ − LSL) ÷ 3σ, the lower side. Cpk is the smaller of the two. With a one-sided specification (only a USL, for example "no more than 2% moisture"), Cpk is simply Cpu. LSL USL target Centered: Cp = Cpk = 1.33 LSL USL target Off center: Cp = 1.33, Cpk = 0.89 Same spread, same specs: centering decides whether the process fits in practice. Cpk is never larger than Cp. They are equal only when the process is perfectly centered between the limits. Reading Cp and Cpk together Pattern Meaning Fix Cp high, Cpk equal to Cp Centered and capable Monitor Cp high, Cpk much lower Spread is fine; process is off-center Move the mean to the target Cp low (and Cpk low) Too much variation Reduce variation (or widen specs if justified) Example: "Cp = 1.8, Cpk = 0.9." The process has plenty of room (Cp 1.8) but sits close to one limit. Centering it would bring Cpk up toward 1.8. Recentering is often a quick adjustment; reducing variation usually takes real work. Benchmarks Since sigma level (short-term Z) = 3 × Cpk: Cpk Sigma level Long-term DPMO (with 1.5σ shift) 1.00 3σ 66,807 1.33 4σ 6,210 1.67 5σ 233 2.00 6σ 3.4 A common minimum requirement is Cpk ≥ 1.33 ; many automotive customers require 1.67 for new or critical processes. See 1.1.1 for the shift convention: if a question says "long-term" or mentions the shift, subtract 1.5 before reading a tail; if it just gives a mean, σ and limits, read the Z table directly. Pp and Ppk: overall (long-term) performance Pp and Ppk use the same formulas, but with the overall standard deviation (all the data together, including shifts and drifts between subgroups) instead of the within-subgroup standard deviation: Pp = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6σ(overall) Ppk = min[ (USL − μ) ÷ 3σ(overall) , (μ − LSL) ÷ 3σ(overall) ] Cp, Cpk (within σ): what the process could do if it held steady (often called "short-term" or potential capability). Pp, Ppk (overall σ): what the process actually delivered over the period (often called "long-term" or performance ). Because overall σ is at least as large as within σ, Pp ≤ Cp and Ppk ≤ Cpk. A big gap between them means the process moves around over time: shifts between shifts, days or batches. Stabilizing it would close the gap. From Z to defects You can turn the distance to each limit into an expected defect rate: Z(USL) = (USL − μ) ÷ σ Z(LSL) = (μ − LSL) ÷ σ Look up each tail in the Z table and add both tails for the total out-of-spec fraction. Worked example Bags of feed: LSL = 495 g, USL = 505 g. Mean = 501 g. Within σ = 1.25 g. Overall σ = 1.6 g. Cp = (505 − 495) ÷ (6 × 1.25) = 10 ÷ 7.5 = 1.33 . Cpu = (505 − 501) ÷ (3 × 1.25) = 4 ÷ 3.75 = 1.07. Cpl = (501 − 495) ÷ 3.75 = 1.60. Cpk = 1.07 (the smaller, upper side). Diagnosis: Cp 1.33 is acceptable, but Cpk 1.07 is lower because the mean (501) is 1 g above the center (500). Recentering to 500 g would give Cpk = Cp = 1.33. Expected defects (within): Z(USL) = 4 ÷ 1.25 = 3.2, tail ≈ 0.00069 ( about 690 ppm overweight). Z(LSL) = 6 ÷ 1.25 = 4.8, tail ≈ 0.8 ppm. Total ≈ 690 ppm . Pp = 10 ÷ (6 × 1.6) = 1.04 . Ppk = 4 ÷ (3 × 1.6) = 0.83 . Over the whole period, about 6,200 ppm were actually overweight. The gap between Cpk (1.07) and Ppk (0.83) shows the process also drifts over time. Conditions for valid capability The process must be stable (in statistical control, 2.4.2). Capability predicts future performance. If special causes are present, the process has no single predictable spread, and the indices are meaningless. Stabilize first, then assess capability. Data should be approximately normal for the standard indices and ppm estimates. For skewed data, use a transformation (such as Box-Cox) or a non-normal capability analysis. Enough data , collected in rational subgroups over a representative period. A good measurement system (2.3); measurement noise inflates σ and makes capability look worse. Decision matrix Capable Not capable Stable Monitor; maintain controls Reduce variation, recenter, or redesign Unstable Indices not trustworthy; remove special causes first Stabilize first, then work on capability Uncertainty in Cpk A Cpk from a small sample is uncertain. An approximate confidence interval: Cpk ± Z(α/2) × √[ 1 ÷ (9n) + Cpk² ÷ (2n − 2) ] With Cpk = 1.33 from n = 50 points, at 95% (Z = 1.96): √[1/450 + 1.769/98] = √0.0203 ≈ 0.142. Interval ≈ 1.33 ± 0.28, about 1.05 to 1.61 . So with 50 points you cannot be confident the process truly meets 1.33. Other forms you may see The IASSC reference sheet writes Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6s and Cpk = min(Z_upper ÷ 3, Z_lower ÷ 3), using the sample standard deviation s. Cpk from attribute data : Cpk = (1.5 + Z of the proportion good) ÷ 3 (see 2.4.3). Cpm (Taguchi index) also penalizes distance from the target, not just from the limits. Recognition only. Common mistakes and exam traps Spec limits are the customer's; control limits are the process's. Never compute capability from control limits. Cpk ≤ Cp , equal only when centered. Cp much higher than Cpk = centering problem , not a variation problem. Capability on an unstable process is invalid. The first step is removing special causes. Cp/Cpk use within σ; Pp/Ppk use overall σ. Add both tails for total ppm. Check yourself LSL = 10, USL = 22, mean = 17, σ = 1.5. Compute Cp and Cpk. What does Cp = 1.5 with Cpk = 0.6 tell you? Why must a process be stable before capability is assessed? Which uses overall standard deviation: Cpk or Ppk? A process has Cpk = 1.33. What sigma level and long-term DPMO does that correspond to? Show answers Cp = 12 ÷ 9 = 1.33. Cpu = (22 − 17) ÷ 4.5 = 1.11; Cpl = (17 − 10) ÷ 4.5 = 1.56; Cpk = 1.11. The spread would fit comfortably, but the process is far off-center. Recenter it. Because capability predicts future output, and an unstable process has no single predictable distribution; special causes make the indices meaningless. Ppk. 4σ, about 6,210 DPMO long-term. Key takeaways Specs = voice of the customer; control limits = voice of the process. Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6σ: potential. Cpk = min distance to a limit ÷ 3σ: actual, accounts for centering. Cpk ≤ Cp; a big gap means off-center. Low Cp means too much variation. Pp/Ppk use overall σ (actual long-term performance); Cp/Cpk use within σ. Cpk 1.33 = 4σ; stability (and roughly normal data) first.
Concept of Stability

Why this matters Stability is the foundation of statistical process control and of capability. A stable process is predictable: you can say with confidence what it will produce tomorrow. An unstable one can surprise you at any time. Knowing the difference also stops one of the most common management mistakes: reacting to random noise. The big idea All processes vary. The variation comes from two kinds of causes: Common causes : the many small, ever-present sources of variation built into the process: normal differences in traffic, driver pace, weather, materials. Together they produce the routine, random scatter. They are part of the system . Special causes (also called assignable causes ): unusual, identifiable events from outside the normal system: a truck breakdown, a new untrained operator, a bad batch of material, a software outage. They produce variation that stands out from the routine. A process with only common-cause variation is stable (in statistical control). Its output varies, but within predictable limits, with a steady average and spread. Stable: random scatter around a steady center Unstable: shifts and spikes (special causes) A stable process varies randomly around a steady center. An unstable one jumps and shifts. Why the distinction matters: two different fixes Special causes are found and removed locally : investigate what happened at that time, fix it, prevent recurrence. The people closest to the process can often do this. Common causes can only be reduced by changing the system itself: new methods, equipment, training, design. That is management's responsibility and the work of improvement projects. Deming estimated that most problems (around 85% or more) are common-cause, system problems, not worker problems. Treating a common-cause variation as if it were special (blaming the driver for a normal slow day) wastes effort and demoralizes people. Treating a special cause as common (ignoring a breakdown as "just normal variation") lets real problems continue. Tampering: making it worse by adjusting Tampering (over-adjustment) is reacting to every common-cause fluctuation as if it were a signal: "Yesterday's average was high, so let's lower the setting." Because the fluctuation was random, the adjustment just adds a new source of variation, and the process gets worse . Deming demonstrated this with the funnel experiment : dropping marbles through a funnel at a target. Leaving the funnel still (no adjustment) gives the smallest scatter. Moving the funnel after each drop to "compensate" for where the last marble landed increases the scatter (by about 40% in standard deviation, since the variance doubles), and some adjustment rules make the process drift away entirely. Control charts (5.2) exist to tell when an adjustment is justified and when to leave the process alone. Short-term vs long-term variation Short-term (within-subgroup) variation : variation among items made close together in time, under nearly the same conditions. It reflects the common causes. Long-term (overall) variation : variation of all the data, including movement between subgroups (shift to shift, day to day). If the process is stable, long-term is only a little larger than short-term. If it is unstable, long-term is much larger. This is why Cp/Cpk (within) and Pp/Ppk (overall) differ (2.4.1). Stability first Capability (2.4.1) predicts what a process will produce. That only makes sense if the process is predictable. So the sequence is always: Check stability with a control chart. Remove special causes until the process is stable. Then assess capability. If the stable process is not capable, reduce common-cause variation (a system change). Two classic scenarios Stable but incapable : predictable, but the natural spread does not fit the specs, or it is off-center. Fix: change the system: reduce variation or recenter. Adjusting it day to day will not help. Capable but unstable : the indices look good, but special causes are present, so the numbers cannot be trusted and the process may suddenly produce defects. Fix: find and remove the special causes first. Common mistakes and exam traps Stable means predictable, not good. A stable process can be stable at producing 10% defects. Special causes: find and remove locally. Common causes: change the system. Tampering increases variation. Stability must come before capability. Check yourself Define common-cause and special-cause variation. A supervisor changes the dispatch rule every time on-time delivery dips below average. What is this, and what is its effect? A stable process makes 4% defects. Is it in control? Is it acceptable? What fixes it? Who is usually responsible for reducing common-cause variation? What should come first: stability or capability? Show answers Common cause: the routine, built-in variation from many small sources. Special cause: unusual variation from an identifiable event outside the normal system. Tampering (over-adjustment); it increases variation. Yes, it is in control (stable). It is not necessarily acceptable. Fixing it requires changing the system to reduce common-cause variation (or recentering). Management (system owners), usually through improvement projects. Stability. Key takeaways Stable = only common-cause variation = predictable. Special causes: investigate and remove. Common causes: change the system. Tampering with a stable process increases variation (Deming's funnel). Short-term (within) vs long-term (overall) variation. Stability before capability.
Attribute and Discrete Capability

Why this matters Many processes produce counts, not measurements: late or on time, defects per invoice. Capability still matters for them, but the indices are calculated differently. You need to pick the right model (defects or defectives) and convert to a sigma level. The big idea For discrete data, capability is expressed as a defect rate , a yield , or a sigma level , not as Cp/Cpk directly. Which statistics to use depends on what you counted: Defectives (pass/fail units) : follow the binomial distribution. Capability = percent defective (or yield, the percent good). Example: 3.2% of loads delivered late. Defects (counts on each unit) : follow the Poisson distribution. Capability = DPU or DPMO . Example: 0.15 errors per invoice. The right choice also decides the control chart later: p or np charts for defectives, c or u charts for defects (5.2). Converting to a sigma level Find the defect rate as a proportion: percent defective ÷ 100, or DPMO ÷ 1,000,000. Treat it as a right-tail area and find the Z value that leaves that much in the tail (using the Z table backwards). Add 1.5 to get the short-term sigma level (the convention from 1.1.1). Example: 66,807 DPMO → tail area 0.066807 → Z ≈ 1.50 → sigma level = 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.0σ . Example: 2.4% of loads are late → tail area 0.024 → Z ≈ 1.98 → sigma level ≈ 3.5σ . Yield anchors to memorize Sigma level Yield (with shift) 3σ 93.32% 4σ 99.379% 5σ 99.977% 6σ 99.99966% Cpk from attribute data The IASSC reference document gives an equivalent Cpk for attribute data: Cpk = (1.5 + Z of the proportion good) ÷ 3 For 2.4% late (97.6% good): Z of 0.976 ≈ 1.98, so Cpk ≈ (1.5 + 1.98) ÷ 3 ≈ 1.16 . This is the same as sigma level ÷ 3. Stability first, again Just like variable data, discrete capability only predicts the future if the process is stable. Plot the defect rate on the right attribute control chart (p, np, c or u) and check for special causes before trusting the capability number. Common mistakes and exam traps Defectives → binomial → percent defective; defects → Poisson → DPU/DPMO. Add 1.5 to the Z to get the conventional sigma level. Do not mix defects and defectives in DPMO. Check stability first. Check yourself Which distribution models the number of defects per invoice? 6,210 DPMO corresponds to what Z and what sigma level? A process yields 99.379%. What sigma level is that? Why is percent defective not the same as DPU? 5% of shipments are damaged. Roughly what sigma level? (Z for a 0.05 tail is about 1.645.) Show answers Poisson. Z ≈ 2.5; sigma level ≈ 4.0. 4σ. Percent defective counts units with at least one defect; DPU counts every defect, so a unit with three defects adds 3 to DPU but only 1 defective. 1.645 + 1.5 ≈ 3.1σ. Key takeaways Defectives: binomial, percent defective, yield. Defects: Poisson, DPU, DPMO. Sigma level = Z of the defect tail + 1.5. Yields: 93.32% (3σ), 99.379% (4σ), 99.977% (5σ), 99.99966% (6σ). Attribute Cpk = (1.5 + Z of proportion good) ÷ 3.
Monitoring Techniques

Why this matters Capability is a snapshot. Processes change: equipment wears, people change, demand shifts. Monitoring keeps watching so that problems are caught early, and capability is re-checked at the right times. The IASSC body of knowledge names this topic without much detail, so exam questions tend to ask "which monitoring approach fits this situation?" The big idea Monitoring answers several different questions, and each needs its own tool: Question Tool Is the process still stable (no special causes)? Control chart , in time order Is the output still meeting specifications? Conformance checks: inspection data, percent defective Is the process still capable? Periodic capability reassessment after a stable period or a change What do we do when something goes wrong? Reaction (response) plan and escalation rules Control charts for ongoing monitoring Control charts (5.2) plot data in time order with limits calculated from the process's own variation. They signal special causes quickly. Match the chart to the data: Continuous data in subgroups: Xbar-R (or Xbar-S). Continuous individual values: I-MR (individuals and moving range). Defectives: p chart (proportion) or np chart (count). Defects: u chart (per unit) or c chart (count). Monitor stability with the control chart first . Recompute capability only after a period of stable operation or after a deliberate process change. Recomputing "rolling" capability numbers on an unstable process gives misleading results that jump around. Sampling frequency and rational subgroups What a chart can detect depends on how often and how you sample: Frequency : sample often enough to catch changes before many bad units are made, especially after known risk points (shift changes, new material lots, maintenance). Rational subgrouping : put items made under nearly the same conditions in the same subgroup (for example, 5 consecutive loads), so variation within a subgroup is only common-cause, and differences between subgroups reveal special causes. Mixing shifts or machines inside one subgroup hides the very differences you want to see. Run charts when data are scarce Early in a project, or with few data points, a run chart (2.2.4) is a simple way to watch for shifts and trends before enough data exist to calculate reliable control limits. Reading capability software output A typical capability report shows: A histogram with the specification limits and target drawn on it, and fitted curves for within and overall variation. Cp, Cpk (within) and Pp, Ppk (overall). Expected PPM (parts per million out of spec) for each side and in total, calculated within and overall , plus the observed PPM in the actual data. Compare within vs overall: a large gap means the process moves over time (stability problem). Compare observed vs expected: a large mismatch can mean the data are not normal. Pre-control (recognition only) Pre-control divides the specification into zones: the middle half of the tolerance is green , the outer quarters are yellow , and beyond the specs is red . Simple rules (for example, two consecutive yellows mean adjust) decide when to act. It is based on specifications rather than process variation, and it is easy for operators, but it is weaker than a control chart. Low exam yield. Common mistakes and exam traps Control charts monitor stability , not conformance to specs. Re-evaluate capability after a stable period or a change , not continuously on unstable data. Rational subgroups : same conditions within, differences between. Choose the chart by data type (continuous, defectives, defects). Check yourself Which chart would you use to monitor the proportion of late loads each week? When should capability be recalculated? Why should one subgroup not mix two shifts? A capability report shows Cpk = 1.4 but Ppk = 0.9. What does this suggest? What simple chart can you use for monitoring before you have enough data for control limits? Show answers A p chart (proportion defective). After a period of stable operation, or after a deliberate process change. Because differences between shifts would be hidden inside the subgroup instead of showing up as signals between subgroups. The process moves around over time (between-subgroup variation): a stability problem. A run chart. Key takeaways Monitor stability with time-ordered control charts; match the chart to the data type. Reassess capability after stable periods or changes, not on unstable data. Sampling frequency and rational subgroups decide what you can detect. Use run charts when data are scarce. Have a reaction plan for signals.
Multi-Vari Analysis

Why this matters Before running formal statistical tests, it helps to know where the variation is coming from. Is it inside each item, between items made one after another, or over time? A multi-vari study answers that with a simple chart, and it often points straight at the area hiding the main cause. It saves teams from testing dozens of possible causes in the wrong place. The big idea Variation can be sorted into families . The three classic ones: Within-piece (positional) variation : differences inside a single unit . A trailer floor thicker at the front than the back; a pallet heavier on one side; one tire worn more than the others on the same truck. Piece-to-piece (cyclical) variation : differences between consecutive units made under the same conditions. Load 1, load 2 and load 3 on the same dock in the same hour take different times. Time-to-time (temporal) variation : differences between time periods : hour to hour, shift to shift, day to day, batch to batch. Monday morning versus Friday afternoon. A multi-vari study measures enough of each so you can see which family is largest . The largest family is where to look for the dominant cause (sometimes called the Red X ). How to run one Pick time periods (for example, three different hours or shifts). In each period, take several consecutive pieces (for example, 3 to 5 in a row). On each piece, measure at several positions if within-piece variation is possible. Plot everything on a multi-vari chart : positions within a piece joined by a vertical line, piece averages joined within each period, and period averages joined across time. Compare the sizes of the three kinds of spread. Hour 1 Hour 2 Hour 3 Vertical line = one piece (3 positions) Squares joined = hour-to-hour averages The short vertical lines (within piece) and the small wiggles between pieces are tiny compared with the jumps between hours. Reading the chart Long vertical lines (big spread inside each piece) → within-piece variation dominates. Look at things that differ across one unit: fixture alignment, uneven heating, loading pattern. Big differences between consecutive pieces in the same period → piece-to-piece variation dominates. Look at things that change unit to unit: material lots, operator technique per unit, cycle-to-cycle machine behavior. Big jumps between period averages → time-to-time variation dominates. Look at things that change over time: shift change, temperature through the day, tool wear, supplier deliveries, staffing levels. In the example chart, the hour-to-hour averages jump by 20 units while pieces and positions vary by only 2 to 5. The team should investigate what changes between hours. Beyond the chart The same idea can be quantified with nested ANOVA or variance components analysis, which estimate how much of the total variance each family contributes (for example, 70% time-to-time, 20% piece-to-piece, 10% within-piece). That is more precise but the chart alone usually makes the answer obvious. Common mistakes and exam traps Multi-vari is for finding the family of variation, before formal tests. It does not prove a specific cause. Sample across enough time to capture the time-to-time family; a study done in one hour cannot see it. Identify the dominant family from the chart by comparing the size of each kind of spread. Check yourself Name the three families of variation in a multi-vari study. A chart shows long vertical lines for each piece, but piece averages and hourly averages barely change. Which family dominates? Why should a multi-vari study span several time periods? Which statistical technique quantifies the same breakdown? Does a multi-vari chart identify the root cause? Show answers Within-piece (positional), piece-to-piece (cyclical), time-to-time (temporal). Within-piece. Otherwise time-to-time variation cannot appear in the data. Nested ANOVA (variance components). No. It narrows down where the cause lives; further investigation and tests identify it. Key takeaways Families: within-piece, piece-to-piece, time-to-time. Sample several pieces per period, several periods, several positions per piece. The largest family on the chart shows where to look for the main cause. Variance components (nested ANOVA) quantify the same thing.
Classes of Distributions

Why this matters A distribution describes how values of a variable are spread out: which values are common and which are rare. Different kinds of data follow different distributions, and the right distribution determines the right calculations, charts and tests. Exam questions often describe a situation and ask which distribution fits. The big idea Distributions come in two families, matching the two data types from 2.2.1: Continuous distributions for measured data: normal, lognormal, Weibull, exponential, uniform. Discrete distributions for counts: binomial, Poisson, hypergeometric. A third group, sampling distributions (t, chi-square, F), describe statistics calculated from samples. They are the engines behind hypothesis tests. Continuous distributions Normal Exponential Lognormal (right skew) Uniform Shape is the quickest clue to which distribution fits. Normal : symmetric bell. Many measurements that result from lots of small independent influences (fill weights, dimensions). Lognormal : right-skewed; the logarithm of the data is normal. Positive values with a long right tail: repair times, delivery delays, income. Weibull : very flexible; used for time to failure (life data). Its shape parameter β tells the failure pattern: β below 1 = early-life failures ("infant mortality", failure rate falling); β = 1 = random failures (constant rate, same as exponential); β above 1 = wear-out (failure rate rising). Exponential : time between random events that happen at a constant rate: time between breakdowns, between customer arrivals. It is memoryless : the chance of failing in the next hour does not depend on how long the item has already lasted. Uniform : every value in a range equally likely (a random number from 0 to 1). Example (exponential): a reefer unit fails on average once every 200 operating hours, at random. The chance it fails within the next 100 hours = 1 − e^(−100/200) = 1 − e^(−0.5) ≈ 0.39 . Discrete distributions Binomial : the number of "successes" (often defectives) in a fixed number n of independent trials, each with the same probability p . P(x) = nCx × pˣ × (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ˣ mean = np where nCx = n! ÷ [x!(n − x)!] is the number of ways to choose x items from n. Example: 5% of invoices have errors. In a sample of 20: P(0 errors) = 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.358 ; P(exactly 1) = 20 × 0.05 × 0.95¹⁹ ≈ 0.377 ; P(2 or more) = 1 − 0.358 − 0.377 ≈ 0.264 . The average number expected is np = 20 × 0.05 = 1 . Poisson : the number of events (often defects) in a fixed amount of time, space or units, when events occur independently at a constant average rate λ . P(x) = e^(−λ) × λˣ ÷ x! mean = variance = λ Example: a dock averages λ = 3 forklift incidents a month. P(0 in a month) = e^(−3) ≈ 0.050 ; P(exactly 2) = e^(−3) × 3² ÷ 2 ≈ 0.224 . A Poisson distribution's mean and variance are equal, which is a handy check: if counts vary much more than their average, the data are "over-dispersed" and something else is going on. Hypergeometric : like the binomial, but sampling without replacement from a small population, so each draw changes the odds for the next. Example: picking 5 cartons from a lot of 40 that contains 4 damaged ones. When the sample is small compared with the population (less than about 5%), the binomial is a good approximation. Matching data to distributions Situation Distribution Number of defective loads in a sample of 50 Binomial Number of defects on one invoice, or per 100 miles Poisson Drawing samples from a small lot without putting them back Hypergeometric Time between equipment failures (random) Exponential Time to failure with infant mortality or wear-out Weibull Repair time with a long right tail Lognormal (often) Fill weight, part dimension Normal (often) Approximations Poisson approximates binomial when n is large and p is small (rare events). Normal approximates binomial when both np and n(1 − p) are at least 5 (some texts use 10). With n = 200 and p = 0.12, np = 24 and n(1 − p) = 176, so the normal approximation is fine. Sampling distributions These are not used to model raw data, but to describe statistics computed from samples: t distribution : like the normal but with heavier tails , used when σ is estimated from the sample (s). Its shape depends on degrees of freedom (df, usually n − 1); with large df it becomes the normal. Used for t-tests and confidence intervals for means. Chi-square (χ²) distribution : right-skewed, used for tests about a variance and for contingency tables. F distribution : the ratio of two variances, used to compare variances and in ANOVA. Common mistakes and exam traps Defects on a unit → Poisson; defectives in a sample → binomial. Time between events → exponential; time to failure with changing rate → Weibull. Poisson mean = variance = λ. Binomial needs fixed n, independent trials, constant p. Without replacement from a small population → hypergeometric. Check yourself Which distribution models the number of scratches on a painted trailer panel? What does a Weibull shape parameter β above 1 indicate? 10% of pallets are mis-labeled. In 10 pallets, what is the probability none are mis-labeled? A Poisson process averages 2 events per hour. What is the variance of the hourly count? Which sampling distribution is used to compare two variances? Show answers Poisson (defect counts on a unit). Wear-out: the failure rate increases with age. 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 0.349. 2 (variance equals the mean). The F distribution. Key takeaways Continuous: normal (symmetric), lognormal (right skew), Weibull (life data, β sets the pattern), exponential (time between random events, memoryless), uniform. Discrete: binomial (defectives, fixed n, constant p), Poisson (defects, mean = variance = λ), hypergeometric (without replacement, small population). Sampling distributions: t (means, σ unknown), χ² (variances, contingency tables), F (variance ratios, ANOVA).
Understanding Inference

Why this matters You almost never measure everything. You measure a sample, then draw conclusions about the whole process. Inference is how you do that honestly: it says not just "our best guess is 42 minutes", but "we are 95% confident the true average is between 39 and 45 minutes". Every hypothesis test in Analyze rests on this idea. The big idea Inference means using a sample to draw conclusions about a population (2.2.1). Because a sample is only part of the population, its results include sampling error : a different sample would give slightly different numbers. Inference measures that uncertainty. There are two kinds of estimate: Point estimate : a single best guess. The sample mean x̄ = 42 minutes is a point estimate of the population mean μ. Interval estimate (confidence interval) : a range likely to contain the true value. "39 to 45 minutes, with 95% confidence." A point estimate alone hides how uncertain it is. An interval shows it. Standard error The standard error (SE) of the mean is the typical amount a sample mean varies from sample to sample: SE = s ÷ √n It is smaller than the standard deviation of individual values, and it shrinks as the sample grows: averages are more stable than individual readings. Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error. Confidence interval for a mean x̄ ± t(α/2, n − 1) × s ÷ √n x̄: sample mean. s ÷ √n: the standard error. t: a multiplier from the t table , based on the confidence level and the degrees of freedom (df = n − 1). The ± part is called the margin of error . Worked example. 16 loads have an average unload time of 42 minutes, s = 6 minutes. Build a 95% confidence interval. SE = 6 ÷ √16 = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5. df = 15. For 95% two-sided, t(0.025, 15) = 2.131 (from the t table). Margin = 2.131 × 1.5 = 3.20. CI = 42 ± 3.20 = 38.8 to 45.2 minutes . z or t? If the population σ is known (rare), use the z multiplier: 1.96 for 95%, 2.576 for 99%, 1.645 for 90%. If σ is estimated from the sample (s), use t . The t multiplier is larger than z for small samples, which widens the interval to account for the extra uncertainty of estimating σ. For large n, t approaches z. Degrees of freedom Degrees of freedom (df) count how many independent pieces of information remain to estimate variation. For a single sample's standard deviation, df = n − 1: once you know the mean, only n − 1 values are free to vary (the last one is fixed by the mean). Small df means heavier-tailed t distributions and larger multipliers. What changes the width Change Effect on the interval Larger sample size n Narrower (SE falls) Higher confidence level (99% instead of 95%) Wider More variation (larger s) Wider The only way to get a narrower interval and keep the same confidence is a larger sample (or less variation). What "95% confident" really means A 95% confidence interval comes from a method that, if repeated on many samples, would capture the true mean in about 95% of them. true mean μ 20 samples, 20 intervals: about 19 capture μ, about 1 misses (red) Each sample gives a different interval. About 95 out of 100 such intervals contain the true mean. It does not mean "there is a 95% probability the true mean is inside this particular interval". The true mean is fixed; this particular interval either contains it or not. The 95% describes the long-run success rate of the method. Confidence interval for a proportion p̂ ± z × √[ p̂(1 − p̂) ÷ n ] Example: 24 of 200 shipments were late, p̂ = 0.12. SE = √(0.12 × 0.88 ÷ 200) ≈ 0.023. 95% CI = 0.12 ± 1.96 × 0.023 = 0.12 ± 0.045, about 7.5% to 16.5% . Reading the IASSC t tables The reference document has two t tables: Table 1 columns are cumulative probabilities from 0.600 to 0.995 (headed "Alpha Risk", but the numbers are actually 1 − α). For a two-sided 95% interval or test at α = 0.05, use the 0.975 column. Table 2 columns are one-tail α from 0.25 to 0.005, with more decimals. For two-sided α = 0.05, use 0.025 ; for one-sided α = 0.05, use 0.05 . Rows are df = n − 1 from 1 to 30, then 40, 60, 120 and ∞. For a df not listed, use the next lower listed df (more conservative). Check your own copy, since table layouts vary between versions. Common mistakes and exam traps To narrow an interval, increase n. SE = s ÷ √n , not s. The 95% describes the method , not one interval. t when σ is estimated; z when σ is known. Two-sided 95% uses α/2 = 0.025 in each tail (the 0.975 column). Check yourself n = 25, x̄ = 80, s = 10. What is the standard error? Using t = 2.064 (df 24, 95%), what is the 95% confidence interval? What happens to the interval if you use 99% confidence instead? Your boss says "so there is a 95% chance the true mean is in this interval." What is the more accurate statement? 30 of 150 calls were abandoned. What is the 95% confidence interval for the abandonment rate? Show answers 10 ÷ √25 = 2. 80 ± 2.064 × 2 = 80 ± 4.13, about 75.9 to 84.1. It gets wider. The method used to build it captures the true mean in 95% of samples; this interval either contains it or does not. p̂ = 0.20; SE = √(0.2 × 0.8 ÷ 150) ≈ 0.0327; 0.20 ± 0.064, about 13.6% to 26.4%. Key takeaways Inference: from sample to population, with measured uncertainty. Point estimate vs interval estimate. SE = s ÷ √n; CI for a mean = x̄ ± t × SE; for a proportion = p̂ ± z√[p̂(1 − p̂) ÷ n]. Wider with more confidence or more variation; narrower with larger n. Use t when σ is estimated; df = n − 1.
Sampling Techniques and Uses

Why this matters A sample is only useful if it represents the population. A biased sample gives confident-looking but wrong answers. And a sample that is too small cannot detect the differences you care about. This topic covers how to choose a sample and how big it needs to be. Sampling methods Probability methods (every item has a known chance of selection): Simple random sampling : every item has an equal chance; for example, random numbers pick which loads to audit. The gold standard when the population is uniform. Stratified sampling : divide the population into distinct subgroups ( strata ) such as terminals, shifts or customer types, then sample randomly within each . Ensures every subgroup is represented; ideal when subgroups differ. Systematic sampling : take every kth item (every 10th invoice) after a random start. Simple and spreads the sample over time. Danger: if the process has a cycle that matches k, the sample can be badly biased. Cluster sampling : divide the population into clusters (for example, days or trailers), randomly pick a few clusters, and measure everything in them. Cheaper when travel or access is costly, but less precise if clusters differ. Non-probability methods (higher risk of bias): Convenience sampling : whatever is easiest to get (the loads at the nearest dock). Quick, but often biased. Judgment sampling : an expert picks "typical" items. Useful for exploration, but depends on the expert's assumptions. Sampling bias Selection bias : the method favors some items (only sampling day shift). Non-response bias : in surveys, those who answer differ from those who do not (unhappy customers are more likely to respond, or less). Undercoverage : some parts of the population are left out entirely (no data from the smallest terminals). Random selection guards against these; a larger sample does not fix a biased method. Sample size for estimating a mean To estimate a mean within a margin of error E at a given confidence: n = (Z(α/2) × σ ÷ E)² Example: σ ≈ 8 minutes, and you want the average within ±2 minutes at 95% (Z = 1.96). n = (1.96 × 8 ÷ 2)² = (7.84)² ≈ 61.5, round up to 62 . Always round up , never down. Sample size for estimating a proportion n = Z² × p(1 − p) ÷ E² Example: you expect about 10% late, and want the estimate within ±2 percentage points at 95%. n = 1.96² × 0.1 × 0.9 ÷ 0.02² = 3.8416 × 0.09 ÷ 0.0004 ≈ 864.4, round up to 865 . If you have no idea of p, use p = 0.5 , which gives the largest (safest) n. Notice proportions need much larger samples than means: discrete data carries less information (2.2.1). Sample size for a hypothesis test (power) Estimating a value needs precision (a margin of error). Testing for a difference needs power : the chance of detecting a real difference of a given size (3.3.3). The inputs are: α : the false-alarm risk you accept (usually 0.05). Power (1 − β): the chance of detecting a real difference (usually 0.80 to 0.90). σ : the variation. δ (delta) : the smallest difference worth detecting . Approximate formulas: 1-sample t: n ≈ (Z(α/2) + Z(β))² × σ² ÷ δ² 2-sample t (each group): n ≈ 2 × (Z(α/2) + Z(β))² × σ² ÷ δ² Example: σ = 10, detect a 5-unit difference from a target, α = 0.05 (Z = 1.96), power 0.80 (Z(β) = 0.84). n ≈ (2.80)² × 100 ÷ 25 ≈ 31.4, about 32 . For comparing two groups, about 63 per group . n rises with more variation and more power; it falls with a bigger difference to detect or a larger α. Software (such as Minitab's power and sample size tool) does this calculation exactly. Worked example: which method? "Audit every 25th bill of lading." Systematic. "Pick 10 random loads from each of the 6 terminals." Stratified. "Randomly choose 4 days and inspect every trailer those days." Cluster. "The supervisor picks the loads he thinks are typical." Judgment. Common mistakes and exam traps Every kth item = systematic. Random within subgroups = stratified. All items in chosen groups = cluster. Round sample sizes up. A bigger sample does not fix a biased method. Estimation needs precision (E); testing needs power (α, power, σ, δ). Check yourself Which method ensures each shift is represented? σ = 12, desired margin E = 3, 95% confidence. What sample size? No idea of the defect rate; want ±5 percentage points at 95%. What sample size? What four inputs determine sample size for a hypothesis test? Why can systematic sampling be risky? Show answers Stratified sampling. (1.96 × 12 ÷ 3)² = (7.84)² ≈ 61.5, so 62. 1.96² × 0.25 ÷ 0.0025 ≈ 384.2, so 385. α, power (or β), σ, and the smallest difference worth detecting (δ). If the process has a repeating pattern that lines up with the sampling interval, the sample will be biased. Key takeaways Probability methods: random, stratified, systematic (every kth), cluster. Non-probability: convenience, judgment. Avoid selection bias, non-response and undercoverage. n for a mean = (Zσ ÷ E)²; for a proportion = Z²p(1 − p) ÷ E²; use p = 0.5 if unknown; round up. Test sample size depends on α, power, σ and δ.
Central Limit Theorem

Why this matters The central limit theorem (CLT) is the reason so much of statistics works even when data are not normal. It explains why averages behave so predictably, why Xbar control charts work, and why t-tests hold up with moderately non-normal data. The big idea Take many samples of size n from any population, compute each sample's average, and look at how those averages are distributed. The CLT says: The averages center on the population mean μ . Their spread is the standard error σ ÷ √n , smaller than the spread of individual values. As n grows, their distribution becomes approximately normal , whatever the shape of the original population . Individual values (skewed population) Averages of n = 10 (close to a bell, much narrower) Same center. Spread of the averages = σ ÷ √n. Even from a heavily skewed population, averages of just 10 values pile up in a narrow, nearly normal hump. Larger samples make it narrower and more normal still. Why? Averaging cancels out extremes: a very high value in a sample tends to be balanced by others. The more values averaged, the more the extremes cancel. How large must n be? The often-quoted "n ≥ 30" is a classroom rule of thumb, not a law: From a roughly symmetric population, averages look normal with n as small as 5 to 10. From a strongly skewed or heavy-tailed population (or one with outliers), you may need much more than 30. What the CLT does and does not do It does make the distribution of sample means approximately normal. It does not make the individual values normal. A skewed process stays skewed; only the averages are normal. Capability for individual parts (2.4) still needs to account for the real shape. Why it matters in practice Xbar charts (5.2) plot subgroup averages, so their limits work well even when individual values are somewhat non-normal. t-tests and confidence intervals for means rely on the sampling distribution of x̄ being roughly normal, which the CLT supports for reasonable sample sizes. Calculating with sample means Because x̄ is approximately normal with mean μ and standard error σ ÷ √n, you can use z: z = (x̄ − μ) ÷ (σ ÷ √n) Example: load times have μ = 50 minutes, σ = 10 minutes. For samples of n = 25 loads: SE = 10 ÷ √25 = 2 . Probability a sample average exceeds 54: z = (54 − 50) ÷ 2 = 2; P = 1 − 0.9772 = 0.0228 . Compare: the probability that a single load exceeds 54 is z = (54 − 50) ÷ 10 = 0.4, P ≈ 0.34. Averages rarely stray far; individual values often do. Common mistakes and exam traps Using σ instead of the standard error for questions about a sample mean. σ = 10 and n = 25 give SE = 2. Believing the CLT makes individual data normal. Only averages. Treating n ≥ 30 as a guarantee. It depends on the population's shape. Check yourself What are the mean and standard error of sample averages of size n? σ = 12 and n = 36. What is the standard error? True or false: by the CLT, individual delivery times become normal with enough data. μ = 200, σ = 20, n = 16. What is the probability a sample mean is below 190? (Area left of z = −2 is 0.0228.) Why do Xbar charts tolerate non-normal individual data? Show answers Mean μ; standard error σ ÷ √n. 12 ÷ 6 = 2. False. Only the distribution of averages becomes approximately normal. SE = 20 ÷ 4 = 5; z = (190 − 200) ÷ 5 = −2; probability ≈ 0.0228. Because they plot subgroup averages, which the CLT makes approximately normal. Key takeaways Sample means center on μ with spread σ ÷ √n and become approximately normal as n grows, whatever the population shape. n ≥ 30 is only a rule of thumb; skewed data need more. The CLT does not make individual values normal. It is why Xbar charts and t-tests work well in practice.
General Concepts and Goals of Hypothesis Testing

Why this matters "The new dispatch method is faster." "Night shift makes more errors." "The new supplier's pallets are stronger." Hypothesis testing is how Six Sigma checks claims like these with data instead of opinion. It is the central tool of the Analyze phase: it is how suspected X's become validated root causes. The big idea Every sample varies by chance. If night shift's error rate this week was 4.1% and day shift's was 3.6%, is night shift really worse, or is that difference just random noise? A hypothesis test answers: "If there were truly no difference, how surprising would data like ours be?" If the answer is "very surprising", we conclude there is a real difference. It works like a court trial: The defendant is presumed innocent (no difference) until proven guilty. The evidence must be strong enough to convict "beyond reasonable doubt". A "not guilty" verdict does not prove innocence; it means the evidence was not strong enough. The two hypotheses Null hypothesis (H₀) : the "nothing is going on" statement: no difference, no effect, the status quo, equality. "Mean load time = 40 minutes." "Day and night error rates are equal." H₀ always contains an equals sign. Alternative hypothesis (Hₐ or H₁) : what you are looking for evidence of: a difference (≠), or a difference in a specific direction (< or >). "Mean load time ≠ 40." "Night error rate > day error rate." The steps Practical problem : what business question are we answering? State H₀ and Hₐ. Choose α (the significance level, usually 0.05): how much risk of a false alarm you accept. Choose the test (3.3.4) based on data type, number of groups and so on. Determine the sample size needed (3.2.2), considering power. Collect the data (randomly, following the data collection plan). Compute the test statistic and p-value (usually with software). Decide : compare the p-value with α. State the practical conclusion in business language. The p-value The p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as yours, if H₀ were true . A small p-value means your data would be very unusual if there were no real difference, so you have evidence against H₀. A large p-value means your data are quite consistent with H₀. Decision rule: p ≤ α → reject H₀. There is statistically significant evidence for Hₐ. p > α → fail to reject H₀. There is not enough evidence for Hₐ. Memory aid: "If p is low, the null must go. If p is high, the null will fly." Never "accept" H₀ Failing to reject H₀ does not prove it is true. It means the evidence was not strong enough, perhaps because the sample was too small to detect a real difference. Say " fail to reject H₀ " or " no significant evidence of a difference ", never "accept H₀" or "proved there is no difference". One-tailed vs two-tailed Two-tailed test : Hₐ is "≠" (different in either direction). The α risk is split between both tails (2.5% in each for α = 0.05). One-tailed test : Hₐ is "<" or ">" (different in one specific direction). All of α sits in one tail. Fail to reject H₀ (95% of results if H₀ is true) Reject Reject 2.5% 2.5% −1.96 +1.96 0 A two-tailed test at α = 0.05: results beyond ±1.96 (for a z test) lead to rejecting H₀. Use a one-tailed test only when a difference in the other direction is genuinely irrelevant and was decided before seeing the data. Independent vs paired samples Independent samples : two separate groups of units (loads from Terminal A versus loads from Terminal B). Paired samples : two measurements on the same units (each driver's fuel economy before and after training). Pairing removes unit-to-unit differences and makes the test more sensitive (3.4.1). Confidence intervals and tests agree A two-sided test at α = 0.05 and a 95% confidence interval give the same decision: if the 95% interval for a difference excludes the hypothesized value (often zero), reject H₀; if it includes it, fail to reject. Worked example A carrier wants to know whether average unload time differs from the 40-minute standard. A sample of 25 unloads gives a p-value of 0.08 (α = 0.05). H₀: μ = 40. Hₐ: μ ≠ 40. p = 0.08 > 0.05 → fail to reject H₀ . Conclusion: there is not enough evidence that the average unload time differs from 40 minutes. (Not: "the average is 40 minutes.") If p had been 0.02, the conclusion would be: reject H₀; the average unload time differs significantly from 40 minutes. Common mistakes and exam traps p = 0.08 with α = 0.05 → fail to reject. Never say "accept H₀". H₀ contains the equals sign ; Hₐ contains ≠, < or >. The p-value is not the probability that H₀ is true. It is the probability of data this extreme if H₀ were true. Check yourself Write H₀ and Hₐ for: "Is the new route faster than the old average of 6.2 hours?" p = 0.03, α = 0.05. Decision? p = 0.30. What can you conclude, and what can you not? A 95% CI for the difference in means is 1.2 to 3.8. Is the difference significant at α = 0.05? Each driver's fuel economy is measured before and after training. Independent or paired? Show answers H₀: μ = 6.2 (or μ ≥ 6.2). Hₐ: μ < 6.2 (one-tailed). Reject H₀ (p ≤ α). Fail to reject H₀: no significant evidence of a difference. You cannot conclude there is no difference. Yes: the interval excludes zero. Paired. Key takeaways H₀: no difference (equality). Hₐ: the claim (≠, <, >). p-value: chance of data this extreme if H₀ were true. p ≤ α → reject H₀. Fail to reject is not acceptance. One-tailed vs two-tailed; independent vs paired. A CI that excludes the hypothesized value means reject.
Significance; Practical vs. Statistical

Why this matters "Statistically significant" sounds important, but it only means "probably not random chance". It says nothing about whether the difference is big enough to matter. Teams waste money acting on trivial but "significant" differences, and miss important ones because a small sample was "not significant". The big idea Two different questions: Statistical significance : is the difference real (unlikely to be chance)? Answered by the p-value. Practical significance : is the difference big enough to matter to the customer or the business? Answered by judgment, cost and specifications. A result can be any combination of the two. Huge samples find trivial differences With a very large sample, even a tiny difference becomes statistically significant, because the standard error becomes tiny. Example: two trailer-loading methods are compared on 50,000 loads. Method B is faster by 0.2 seconds, p = 0.001. Statistically significant? Yes. Practically significant? No: 0.2 seconds per load is worthless, and switching methods costs money. Small samples miss real differences With a small sample, even a large, important difference may not reach significance, because the test has low power (3.3.3). Example: a pilot of a new route on 6 trips shows an average saving of 45 minutes, but p = 0.07. Concluding "the route does not help" would be wrong. The correct conclusion: insufficient evidence so far; check the power and collect more data . Effect size and the minimum difference that matters The effect size is how big the difference actually is (45 minutes, 0.2 seconds, 1.5 percentage points). Before testing, decide the smallest difference worth detecting (the minimum practical difference, δ). Then: Size the sample so the test has enough power to detect δ (3.2.2). After testing, look at the confidence interval for the difference: does it include values that matter? Putting it together Statistically significant? Practically significant? Action Yes Yes Act on it Yes No Real but too small to matter; usually do not act No (large observed effect) Insufficient evidence; check power, gather more data No No No evidence of a meaningful difference Worked example A change reduces average tire wear by 0.01 mm per 10,000 miles, p = 0.001, with a tolerance of several millimeters. Statistically significant, not practically significant. Not worth the cost of changing. Common mistakes and exam traps Significant does not mean important. Not significant does not mean no effect , especially with small samples. Decide the practically important difference before testing. Look at the size of the difference (and its CI), not just the p-value. Check yourself Define practical significance. A study of 100,000 shipments finds a 0.05% difference in on-time rate between two systems, p < 0.001. What should you conclude? A small pilot shows a large improvement with p = 0.09. What is the right conclusion? Why should the minimum difference worth detecting be set before collecting data? What makes trivial differences "significant" in large samples? Show answers Whether a difference is large enough to matter to the customer or the business. The difference is real (statistically significant) but too small to matter (not practically significant). Insufficient evidence; the test may lack power. Check the sample size and collect more data before deciding. So the sample can be sized to have enough power to detect it, and so the decision is not biased by the results. Very small standard errors: with huge n, almost any difference is detectable. Key takeaways Statistical significance = probably real; practical significance = big enough to matter. Huge samples make trivial differences significant; small samples miss real ones. Define the minimum important difference first; size the sample for it. Report the effect size and confidence interval, not only the p-value.
Risk: Alpha and Beta

Why this matters Every decision from a sample can be wrong in two ways: you can see a difference that is not really there, or miss one that is. Understanding these two risks lets you set them sensibly and design tests that are worth running. The big idea There are four possible outcomes of a test: H₀ is actually true (no difference) H₀ is actually false (real difference) Reject H₀ Type I error (α) : false alarm Correct: real difference found ( power ) Fail to reject H₀ Correct Type II error (β) : missed real difference Type I error (α) Rejecting H₀ when it is actually true : concluding there is a difference or effect when there is not. A false alarm , a false positive. Its probability is α , the significance level you choose (usually 0.05 ). In acceptance-sampling language it is the producer's risk : rejecting a good lot, which hurts the producer. Example: concluding the new dispatch method is faster when it really is not. You switch, spend money, and get nothing. Type II error (β) Failing to reject H₀ when it is actually false : missing a real difference. A missed detection , a false negative. Its probability is β . In acceptance-sampling language, the consumer's risk : accepting a bad lot, which hurts the consumer. Example: concluding the new method is no better when it really is. You miss a real improvement. Power Power = 1 − β Power is the probability of detecting a real difference when one exists. A common target is 0.80 to 0.90 (80% to 90% chance of detecting the difference you care about). Confidence level = 1 − α (95% when α = 0.05) is the probability of correctly not rejecting a true H₀. If H₀ is true If the real shift exists decision line α β α (red): false alarm. β (blue): missed real change. Power = 1 − β. Moving the decision line trades one risk for the other. Only a larger sample (narrower curves) or a bigger true difference reduces both. What raises power (lowers β) Larger sample size : narrower sampling distributions, less overlap. The most common lever. Larger true difference (effect size) : bigger differences are easier to see. Larger α : accepting more false-alarm risk makes it easier to reject, so fewer misses (a trade-off). Less variation (smaller σ) : through better measurement or more consistent conditions. With the sample size fixed, lowering α (being stricter about false alarms) raises β. You can only reduce both at once with more data or less noise. Choosing α and β When a false alarm is very costly (an expensive change, a safety claim), use a smaller α (0.01). When missing a real effect is very costly (a safety problem goes undetected), demand higher power (0.90 or more), which needs a larger sample. Common mistakes and exam traps Type I = reject a true H₀ = false alarm = α = producer's risk. Type II = fail to reject a false H₀ = missed detection = β = consumer's risk. "Concluding the new process is better when it is not" = Type I. Power = 1 − β, not 1 − α. Bigger samples increase power. Check yourself A test concludes that a new supplier's parts fail less often, but they really do not. Which error? A test fails to detect that a machine has drifted out of adjustment. Which error? β = 0.15. What is the power? Name three ways to increase power. If you lower α from 0.05 to 0.01 without changing the sample, what happens to β? Show answers Type I (false alarm). Type II (missed detection). 0.85. Any three of: larger sample, larger effect size, larger α, smaller variation. β increases (power decreases). Key takeaways Type I (α): rejecting a true H₀, false alarm, producer's risk. Usually α = 0.05. Type II (β): failing to reject a false H₀, missed detection, consumer's risk. Power = 1 − β; aim for 0.80 to 0.90. Power rises with larger n, larger effect, larger α, lower variation.
Types of Hypothesis Test

Why this matters "Which test should I use?" is one of the most common exam questions and one of the most important practical skills. The choice follows a small number of questions about your data and your goal. Learn the logic and the table, and the question becomes routine. The big idea Choose the test by asking, in this order: What type of data is the Y? Continuous or discrete (attribute)? How many groups (samples) are you comparing? One (against a target), two, or three or more? Are the groups independent, paired, or blocked? What are you comparing? Means (or medians), variances, or proportions? Is the continuous data normal? If not, use a non-parametric test (or a transformation, or rely on robustness with large samples). The test selection table Continuous Y, comparing centers (means or medians): Groups Normal data (parametric, compares means) Non-normal data (non-parametric, compares medians) 1 sample vs a target 1-sample t (or Z if σ known) 1-sample sign or 1-sample Wilcoxon 2 independent samples 2-sample t Mann-Whitney 2 paired samples Paired t Sign or Wilcoxon on the differences 3 or more independent One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis , or Mood's median (if outliers) 3 or more with blocks Two-way ANOVA (blocked) Friedman Continuous Y, comparing spread (variances): Groups Normal Non-normal 1 sample vs a target 1-sample variance (chi-square) (requires normality; use with care) 2 samples F-test Levene's test 3 or more Bartlett's test Levene's test Discrete Y (counts, proportions, categories): Situation Test 1 proportion vs a target 1-proportion test 2 proportions 2-proportion test Two categorical variables (a table of counts) Chi-square test of independence (contingency table) Continuous Y and continuous X: correlation and regression (4.1). Parametric vs non-parametric Parametric tests (t, ANOVA, F) assume the data follow a particular distribution, usually normal, and compare means or variances. Non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, Mood's median, sign, Wilcoxon, Friedman) make fewer assumptions. They usually work with ranks or with counts above and below the median, and compare medians (or overall distributions). When the data really are normal, non-parametric tests have less power (need more data to detect the same difference). When data are clearly non-normal, especially with small samples or outliers, they are safer. With large samples, t-tests and ANOVA are fairly robust to non-normality (thanks to the central limit theorem, 3.2.3). But for exam purposes, follow the simple fork: normal → parametric, non-normal → non-parametric . Worked examples "Has the average delivery time of 26 hours changed? Data are normal." 1-sample t. "Compare cycle times of two shifts; data are badly skewed and samples are small." Mann-Whitney. "Compare mean fuel economy of three truck models; data normal." One-way ANOVA. "Same 12 drivers tested before and after training; normal differences." Paired t. "Did the new method reduce variation in fill weight?" Variance test : F-test if normal, Levene's if not. "Is the late-delivery rate different between two carriers?" 2-proportion test. "Is defect type related to shift?" (counts by type and shift) Chi-square contingency. "Three suppliers' lead times, skewed, with some outliers." Mood's median (or Kruskal-Wallis). Common mistakes and exam traps Same units before and after = paired , not 2-sample. Three or more groups = ANOVA (or Kruskal-Wallis) , not several t-tests. "Did variation change?" = variance test , not a mean test. Proportions and counts = proportion tests or chi-square , not t-tests. Non-normal 2 groups = Mann-Whitney; non-normal 3+ = Kruskal-Wallis or Mood's. Check yourself Which test compares the medians of two independent, non-normal samples? Which test checks whether the proportion of damaged loads differs between two terminals? Five suppliers' normal data on part strength: which test for means? Is a contingency table chi-square used for continuous or categorical data? A team wants to know if a new procedure reduced variation. Data are not normal. Which test? Show answers Mann-Whitney. 2-proportion test. One-way ANOVA. Categorical (counts in categories). Levene's test. Key takeaways Decide by: data type, number of groups, independent/paired/blocked, parameter (mean, variance, proportion), normality.
