Normal means: 1-sample t, 2-sample t, paired t, ANOVA. Non-normal: sign/Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, Mood's, Friedman. Variances: chi-square (1), F (2), Bartlett (3+, normal), Levene (non-normal). Discrete: 1- and 2-proportion tests, chi-square contingency. Non-parametric tests need fewer assumptions but have less power when data are normal.
1 and 2 Sample t-Tests

Why this matters The t-tests are the workhorses of Analyze. Whenever you ask "is this average different from the target?", "is A's average different from B's?" or "did the average change for the same units after the change?", one of three t-tests answers it. The big idea All t-tests share one structure: t = (observed difference) ÷ (standard error of that difference) The numerator is the signal (how big the difference is). The denominator is the noise (how much that difference would vary by chance). A large t means the signal stands out from the noise. Compare t with a critical value from the t table, or let software turn it into a p-value. The 1-sample t-test Question: does the mean of one process differ from a target or standard μ₀? t = (x̄ − μ₀) ÷ (s ÷ √n) df = n − 1 Worked example. The standard unload time is 40 minutes. A sample of 16 unloads averages 43 minutes with s = 6. Is the average different from 40 (α = 0.05, two-sided)? H₀: μ = 40. Hₐ: μ ≠ 40. SE = 6 ÷ √16 = 1.5. t = (43 − 40) ÷ 1.5 = 2.0 . df = 15; critical value t(0.975, 15) = 2.131 . 2.0 < 2.131 → fail to reject H₀ . There is not enough evidence that the average differs from 40 minutes. (With a bigger sample, the same 3-minute difference might become significant.) The 2-sample t-test Question: do two independent groups have different means? Welch version (does not assume equal variances; software's usual default): t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂) Its degrees of freedom come from a formula (on the IASSC sheet): df = (A + B)² ÷ [ A²/(n₁ − 1) + B²/(n₂ − 1) ], with A = s₁²/n₁ and B = s₂²/n₂ Pooled version (assumes equal variances): first combine the two standard deviations, s_p = √{ [ (n₁ − 1)s₁² + (n₂ − 1)s₂² ] ÷ (n₁ + n₂ − 2) } t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ÷ [ s_p × √(1/n₁ + 1/n₂) ] df = n₁ + n₂ − 2 Worked example. Terminal A: n = 10, mean load time 52 min, s = 4. Terminal B: n = 12, mean 47 min, s = 5. Do the means differ (α = 0.05)? Welch: A = 16 ÷ 10 = 1.6; B = 25 ÷ 12 ≈ 2.083; SE = √3.683 ≈ 1.919. t = (52 − 47) ÷ 1.919 ≈ 2.61 . df ≈ (3.683)² ÷ (1.6²/9 + 2.083²/11) ≈ 13.57 ÷ 0.679 ≈ 20.0 → use 19 (round down). Critical t(0.975, 19) = 2.093. 2.61 > 2.093 → reject H₀ . Terminal A is significantly slower. Pooled gives a similar answer: s_p ≈ 4.58, t ≈ 2.55 with df = 20 (critical 2.086), also reject. The paired t-test Question: for the same units measured twice (before and after, or with two methods), is the average difference zero? Compute the difference d for each unit, then do a 1-sample t-test on the differences against zero: t = d̄ ÷ (s_d ÷ √n) df = n − 1 (n = number of pairs) Worked example. 8 drivers' fuel economy (mpg) is measured before and after eco-driving training. Differences (after − before) average d̄ = 0.5 mpg with s_d = 0.4. SE = 0.4 ÷ √8 ≈ 0.141. t = 0.5 ÷ 0.141 ≈ 3.54 ; df = 7; critical t(0.975, 7) = 2.365. 3.54 > 2.365 → reject H₀ . Training improved fuel economy. Why pair? Drivers differ a lot from each other (some get 6 mpg, some 8). A 2-sample test would bury the 0.5 mpg improvement under those big driver-to-driver differences. Pairing compares each driver with themselves, removing that noise and making the test far more sensitive. Assumptions Independence : observations do not influence each other (random sampling, no carry-over). Approximate normality of the data (or of the differences, for paired); less critical for larger samples (central limit theorem). Equal variances for the pooled 2-sample version only. If unsure, use Welch. Reading the output Software reports: The p-value : compare with α. The confidence interval for the difference : if it excludes zero, the difference is significant. It also shows how big the difference might be, which tells you about practical significance (3.3.2). The Z-test If the population σ is known (rare in practice), use z = (x̄ − μ₀) ÷ (σ ÷ √n) with the normal table instead of t. The 2-sample Z similarly uses the known σ's. Common mistakes and exam traps Before and after on the same units = paired. Two separate groups = 2-sample. Pooled df = n₁ + n₂ − 2; 1-sample and paired df = n − 1. Use the 0.975 column (two-sided α = 0.05). If the CI for the difference contains 0, fail to reject. Check yourself n = 25, x̄ = 104, s = 10, μ₀ = 100. Compute t. Is it significant at α = 0.05 (critical 2.064)? Why is a paired test more sensitive than a 2-sample test for before/after data? What are the degrees of freedom for a pooled 2-sample t-test with n₁ = 12 and n₂ = 15? A 95% CI for the difference in means is −1.5 to 4.2. Significant? Which assumption does the Welch test drop? Show answers SE = 2; t = 4 ÷ 2 = 2.0 < 2.064 → not significant (fail to reject). It removes the unit-to-unit variation by comparing each unit with itself. 12 + 15 − 2 = 25. No: the interval includes zero. Equal variances. Key takeaways t = difference ÷ standard error. 1-sample: (x̄ − μ₀) ÷ (s/√n). 2-sample: Welch or pooled. Paired: d̄ ÷ (s_d/√n). Same units twice = paired; separate groups = 2-sample. Assumptions: independence, rough normality, equal variances (pooled only). Use the p-value and the CI for the difference.
1 Sample Variance

Why this matters Six Sigma is about reducing variation, so sometimes the question is not "did the average change?" but "did the variation change?" or "is the variation within our target?" Those questions need variance tests, not mean tests. The big idea Variance tests compare spread , measured by the variance s² (or standard deviation s), with a target or with another group. The 1-sample variance (chi-square) test Question: does the process variance differ from a target variance σ₀²? χ² = (n − 1) × s² ÷ σ₀² df = n − 1 Compare χ² with critical values from the chi-square table . The chi-square distribution is not symmetric, so the two tails have different critical values: Upper critical value: the column for α (one-sided) or α/2 (two-sided). Lower critical value: the column for 1 − α or 1 − α/2. Worked example. The target standard deviation of trailer weights is σ₀ = 2.0 tons. A sample of 20 trailers has s = 2.6. Has the variation increased (one-sided, α = 0.05)? H₀: σ = 2.0. Hₐ: σ > 2.0. χ² = 19 × 2.6² ÷ 2.0² = 19 × 6.76 ÷ 4 ≈ 32.1 . df = 19; upper critical value (α = 0.05) = 30.14 . 32.1 > 30.14 → reject H₀ . Variation has increased beyond the target. Important: the chi-square variance test is very sensitive to non-normality . If the data are skewed, it can give misleading results. Check normality first. Comparing two variances: the F-test F = s₁² ÷ s₂² df = (n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1) Put the larger variance on top , so F ≥ 1, and compare with the upper critical value from the F table. Worked example. Old method: s = 3.2 (n = 13). New method: s = 2.0 (n = 16). F = 3.2² ÷ 2.0² = 10.24 ÷ 4 = 2.56 , df = (12, 15). At α = 0.05 one-sided (did the new method reduce variation?), critical F(0.05; 12, 15) ≈ 2.48. 2.56 > 2.48 → reject: the new method has less variation. For a two-sided test at α = 0.05 you need the 0.025 column (about 2.96), and 2.56 would not be significant. The IASSC sheet provides F tables for α = 0.05, 0.01 and 0.10 (no 0.025 table). Putting the larger variance on top and using the 0.05 table gives a two-sided test at α = 0.10. The F-test, like chi-square, assumes normal data. Levene's test Levene's test compares variances of two or more groups and is robust to non-normality . Software often reports it alongside the F-test or Bartlett's test. When data are not normal, prefer Levene's. Common mistakes and exam traps "Did variation decrease?" needs a variance test , not a t-test. χ² = (n − 1)s² ÷ σ₀², df = n − 1. Larger variance on top for F. Chi-square and F tests need normal data; Levene's does not. Chi-square tables are right-tail areas ; two-sided tests need both an upper and a lower critical value. Check yourself n = 11, s = 5, σ₀ = 4. Compute χ². What are its degrees of freedom? Which test compares the variances of two non-normal samples? s₁ = 6 and s₂ = 4. What is F? Why is the F statistic computed with the larger variance on top? Show answers 10 × 25 ÷ 16 = 15.6. 10. Levene's test. 36 ÷ 16 = 2.25. So F ≥ 1 and only the upper-tail table is needed. Key takeaways Variance questions need variance tests. 1 sample: χ² = (n − 1)s² ÷ σ₀², df = n − 1; sensitive to non-normality. 2 samples: F = larger s² ÷ smaller s², df (n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1). Levene's test is the robust option for non-normal data.
One Way ANOVA

Why this matters When there are three or more groups (three terminals, four suppliers, five truck models), ANOVA tests whether their means differ, in one test. It is also the foundation of Gage R&R (2.3.3), regression output (4.1) and designed experiments. The big idea ANOVA (analysis of variance) compares means by looking at variation. It splits the total variation in the data into two parts: Between-group variation : how far the group means are from the overall (grand) mean. If the groups really differ, this is large. Within-group variation : how much individual values scatter around their own group mean . This is ordinary noise. grand mean Supplier A Supplier B Supplier C Between: how far group means sit from the grand mean Within: scatter of points around their own group mean If the group means spread far apart compared with the scatter inside each group, the groups really differ. If between-group variation is large compared with within-group variation, the group means are probably not all equal. Why not just run several t-tests? With 4 groups there are 6 possible pairs. Each t-test at α = 0.05 has a 5% false-alarm risk, so running all 6 gives roughly a 26% chance of at least one false alarm. ANOVA tests all groups at once while keeping the overall α at 5%. Hypotheses H₀: all group means are equal (μ₁ = μ₂ = … = μₖ). Hₐ: at least one mean is different. The ANOVA table Source SS (sum of squares) df MS (mean square) = SS ÷ df F Between (treatment, factor) SS_between k − 1 MS_between MS_between ÷ MS_within Within (error) SS_within N − k MS_within Total SS_total N − 1 (k = number of groups, N = total number of observations.) Relationships to remember: SS_total = SS_between + SS_within. df_total = df_between + df_within : (N − 1) = (k − 1) + (N − k). MS = SS ÷ df. F = MS_between ÷ MS_within. A large F (and a small p-value) means reject H₀. Worked example by hand Three suppliers' delivery delays (hours), 4 deliveries each: Supplier A Supplier B Supplier C 10, 12, 11, 13 14, 15, 13, 16 11, 10, 12, 11 mean 11.5 mean 14.5 mean 11.0 Grand mean = 148 ÷ 12 = 12.33. N = 12, k = 3. SS_between = Σ nᵢ(x̄ᵢ − grand mean)² = 4 × [(11.5 − 12.33)² + (14.5 − 12.33)² + (11 − 12.33)²] = 4 × (0.694 + 4.694 + 1.778) ≈ 28.67 . SS_within : squared deviations from each group's own mean. A: 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 = 5. B: 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 + 2.25 = 5. C: 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 2. Total 12.0 . SS_total = 28.67 + 12.0 = 40.67 . df: between = 2, within = 9, total = 11. MS_between = 28.67 ÷ 2 = 14.33. MS_within = 12.0 ÷ 9 = 1.33. F = 14.33 ÷ 1.33 ≈ 10.75. Critical F(0.05; 2, 9) = 4.26. 10.75 > 4.26 → reject H₀ (p ≈ 0.004). At least one supplier's mean delay differs. Shortcut formulas (on the IASSC sheet): with T = grand total and C = T² ÷ N (the "correction factor"): SS_total = ΣX² − C. Here ΣX² = 1,866 and C = 148² ÷ 12 = 1,825.33, so SS_total = 40.67. SS_between = Σ(Tᵢ² ÷ nᵢ) − C, where Tᵢ is each group's total: (46² + 58² + 44²) ÷ 4 − 1,825.33 = 1,854 − 1,825.33 = 28.67. SS_within = SS_total − SS_between. The sheet gives the SS formulas, but not the df, MS and F steps; you must know those. Filling in a missing cell Exam questions often give a partial ANOVA table. Use the relationships: SS adds up, df adds up, MS = SS ÷ df, F = MS_between ÷ MS_within. Example: SS_between = 60, df_between = 3, MS_within = 5: MS_between = 20, F = 20 ÷ 5 = 4.0 . Assumptions Independent observations. Normally distributed residuals (the differences between each value and its group mean); check with a normality test or probability plot of residuals. Equal variances across groups; check with Bartlett's test (assumes normality) or Levene's test (robust to non-normality). If assumptions fail badly, use Kruskal-Wallis or Mood's median (3.5). After a significant ANOVA: which groups differ? ANOVA only says at least one mean differs. To find which , use post-hoc comparisons: Tukey's method : compares all pairs while controlling the overall error rate (most common). Fisher's LSD : individual pairwise comparisons (higher false-alarm risk). Dunnett's method : compares each group with a control group only. Each gives confidence intervals for the pairwise differences. An interval that contains 0 means no evidence of a difference for that pair. In the example, Tukey would likely show B differs from A and C, while A and C do not differ. Do not declare the group with the biggest sample mean the "winner" without post-hoc evidence. An interval plot (2.2.4) of the group means is a good visual check. Sample size and power ANOVA's sample size depends on the number of groups, the smallest difference between means worth detecting, σ, α and the desired power. Software calculates it. Common mistakes and exam traps ANOVA says at least one mean differs , not which. Use Tukey or similar next. df: k − 1, N − k, N − 1. F = MS_between ÷ MS_within , and MS = SS ÷ df. Bartlett assumes normality; Levene does not. Multiple t-tests inflate α. Check yourself 4 groups, 5 observations each. What are df_between, df_within and df_total? SS_between = 45, SS_within = 90, using your df from question 1. Compute F. ANOVA gives p = 0.002. What can you conclude, and what should you do next? Why not run all pairwise t-tests instead of ANOVA? Data are not normal and you want to check equal variances. Which test? Show answers 3, 16, 19. MS_between = 45 ÷ 3 = 15; MS_within = 90 ÷ 16 = 5.625; F ≈ 2.67. At least one group mean differs. Run a post-hoc test (such as Tukey) to find which. Each test adds false-alarm risk; with many pairs the chance of at least one false alarm grows far above α. Levene's test. Key takeaways ANOVA compares 3 or more means by splitting variation into between and within groups. SS_total = SS_between + SS_within; df: k − 1, N − k, N − 1; MS = SS ÷ df; F = MS_between ÷ MS_within. Assumptions: independence, normal residuals, equal variances (Bartlett or Levene). Significant ANOVA → post-hoc (Tukey) to find which groups differ.
Mann-Whitney

Why this matters Real process data are often not normal, especially times and costs, which are usually skewed right with a few very long values. With small samples, a t-test on such data can mislead. The Mann-Whitney test compares two groups without assuming normality. The big idea: ranks instead of values Non-parametric tests replace the actual values with their ranks (1 for the smallest, 2 for the next, and so on). Ranks ignore how extreme the extreme values are: a 70-hour outlier counts as "the largest", the same as if it were 41 hours. This makes rank tests resistant to skew and outliers. The Mann-Whitney test (also called the Wilcoxon rank-sum test) compares two independent groups : Pool both groups and rank all values together, smallest to largest. Add up the ranks for each group. If one group's values are generally larger, its ranks will be mostly high and its rank sum large. If the groups are similar, the ranks will be mixed evenly. The test statistic measures how lopsided the ranks are; software gives a p-value. Example Repair times (hours) at two shops, small samples and skewed: Shop A: 3, 4, 6, 7, 30 Shop B: 8, 9, 12, 15, 40 Pooled ranks: 3 (1), 4 (2), 6 (3), 7 (4), 8 (5), 9 (6), 12 (7), 15 (8), 30 (9), 40 (10). Shop A ranks: 1, 2, 3, 4, 9 → sum 19. Shop B ranks: 5, 6, 7, 8, 10 → sum 36. Shop B's ranks are clearly higher. The outliers (30 and 40) count only as ranks 9 and 10, so they do not dominate. With only 5 values per shop, though, the exact two-sided p-value is about 0.095, so at α = 0.05 this small sample is not quite enough evidence. More data would be needed. Hypotheses and interpretation H₀: the two populations have the same distribution (often stated as equal medians ). Hₐ: one tends to give larger values (medians differ). Strictly, Mann-Whitney compares medians only when the two distributions have similar shape and spread . Otherwise it tests whether one group tends to produce larger values. For the exam, treat it as the non-normal alternative to the 2-sample t-test , comparing medians. When to use it Two independent groups. Continuous (or ordinal) data that are not normal , especially with small samples or outliers . With large samples, a 2-sample t-test is often reasonable even for non-normal data (central limit theorem). When data are truly normal, the t-test is more powerful. Check yourself Mann-Whitney is the non-parametric alternative to which test? Why are rank tests resistant to outliers? Two shifts' skewed cycle times, 8 values each. Which test? Show answers The 2-sample t-test. An outlier only gets the highest rank, however extreme its value. Mann-Whitney. Key takeaways Two independent groups, non-normal data: Mann-Whitney. Works on ranks, so it resists skew and outliers. Compares medians (strictly when shapes are similar).
Kruskal-Wallis

The big idea The Kruskal-Wallis test extends Mann-Whitney to three or more independent groups . It is the non-parametric alternative to one-way ANOVA . How it works: rank all values from all groups together, then compare the average rank of each group. If the groups come from the same distribution, the average ranks should be similar. If one group's average rank is far higher or lower, that group tends to give different values. H₀: all groups have the same distribution (equal medians). Hₐ: at least one group differs. The same shape caveat as Mann-Whitney applies: it is a clean comparison of medians when the groups have similar shapes. When to use it Three or more independent groups. Data not normal (skewed lead times, repair costs), especially with small samples. Example: three freight suppliers' lead times, all skewed right with occasional long delays. Kruskal-Wallis tests whether their median lead times differ. Like ANOVA, a significant result says at least one differs, not which; follow up with pairwise comparisons. Check yourself Kruskal-Wallis is the non-parametric version of which test? What does it compare across groups? Four warehouses' skewed picking times: which test? Show answers One-way ANOVA. The average ranks (in effect, the medians). Kruskal-Wallis (or Mood's median if outliers are a big concern). Key takeaways 3 or more independent groups, non-normal: Kruskal-Wallis. Ranks all data together and compares average ranks. Significant means at least one group differs.
Mood's Median

The big idea Mood's median test also compares the medians of two or more independent groups , but in a different way: Find the overall median of all the data combined. For each group, count how many values are above and how many are at or below the overall median. Use a chi-square test on that table of counts. If the groups have the same median, each should have roughly half its values above. Mood's median vs Kruskal-Wallis Mood's median uses only "above or below", ignoring how far above or below. That makes it very robust to outliers : an extreme value counts exactly the same as any value just above the median. The price is lower power : by throwing away information, it needs more data to detect the same difference. When data are not extremely outlier-prone, Kruskal-Wallis is usually more powerful . Rule of thumb: outliers a big concern → Mood's median; otherwise → Kruskal-Wallis. Check yourself What does Mood's median count for each group? Which is more powerful, Mood's median or Kruskal-Wallis? When might you prefer Mood's median? Show answers The number of values above, and at or below, the overall median. Kruskal-Wallis (usually). When the data contain serious outliers. Key takeaways Compares medians using counts above and below the overall median. Very robust to outliers, but less powerful than Kruskal-Wallis.
Friedman

The big idea Sometimes groups are not independent because the same subjects are measured under every condition. Example: the same 6 drivers each try 3 route-planning apps, and you record trip time for each. Drivers differ a lot from each other, and you want to remove that driver-to-driver noise, like a paired test but with three or more treatments. The driver is a block : a source of variation you want to account for but are not studying. The Friedman test handles this for non-normal data: Within each block (each driver), rank the treatments (apps) from 1 to k. Sum the ranks for each treatment across all blocks. If one treatment consistently ranks better within blocks, its rank sum will stand out. It is the non-parametric analog of a two-way ANOVA with blocks (a randomized block design), or of a repeated-measures design. H₀: all treatments have the same effect (equal medians). Hₐ: at least one treatment differs. Exam cue "The same operators rate (or use) several methods" or "each subject receives every treatment" with non-normal data → Friedman , with the operator or subject as the block . Check yourself What is a block? The same 10 inspectors each grade 4 types of damage photos; data are ordinal. Which test compares the 4 types? Friedman is the non-parametric version of which design? Show answers A source of variation (like operator or subject) that you account for but are not studying. Friedman, with inspector as the block. A two-way ANOVA with blocks (randomized block / repeated measures). Key takeaways Blocked or repeated-measures data, non-normal: Friedman. Ranks treatments within each block. The operator or subject is the block.
1 Sample Sign

The big idea The 1-sample sign test checks whether the median of one population equals a target value. It is the simplest test there is: For each observation, note only whether it is above (+) or below (−) the target. Drop values exactly equal to the target. If the true median equals the target, + and − should be equally likely, like coin flips. Use the binomial distribution (p = 0.5) to see how unusual the observed split is. Example Target median delivery time: 30 hours. 12 deliveries: 9 above, 2 below, 1 exactly 30 (dropped). So n = 11, with only 2 below. Probability of 2 or fewer "below" out of 11 if p = 0.5: (1 + 11 + 55) ÷ 2,048 ≈ 0.033 (one-sided). Two-sided p ≈ 0.065. At α = 0.05 (two-sided), fail to reject : not enough evidence that the median differs from 30, though it is close. One-sided (testing "is it above 30?"), 0.033 < 0.05 would reject. Strengths and weaknesses Fewest assumptions : no normality, no symmetry, just independent observations. Lowest power : it ignores how far each value is from the target, so it needs more data to detect a difference. It also works on the differences from paired data (a non-parametric alternative to the paired t-test). Check yourself What information does the sign test use from each observation? Which distribution gives its p-value? Why is it less powerful than other tests? Show answers Only whether it is above or below the target. The binomial distribution with p = 0.5. It ignores the size of each difference from the target. Key takeaways One median vs a target, using only signs (+ or −). Fewest assumptions, lowest power. Also usable on paired differences.
1 Sample Wilcoxon

The big idea The 1-sample Wilcoxon (signed-rank) test also tests whether one median equals a target, but uses more information than the sign test: Compute each value's difference from the target. Drop zero differences. Rank the absolute differences (ignoring sign), smallest = 1. Give each rank the sign of its difference (+ or −). Add the positive ranks and the negative ranks. If the median equals the target, they should be roughly equal. Because it uses the size of the differences (through their ranks), it is more powerful than the sign test. The assumption: symmetry The Wilcoxon test assumes the distribution is roughly symmetric around its median. It does not need normality, but it does need symmetry. For strongly skewed data, the sign test is the safer choice. Sign vs Wilcoxon Sign test Wilcoxon signed-rank Uses Direction only (+/−) Direction and ranked size Assumes symmetry? No Yes Power Lower Higher (when symmetric) Exam cue: "no symmetry assumption" → sign test. Like the sign test, Wilcoxon also works on paired differences. Check yourself What does the Wilcoxon test rank? What assumption does it make that the sign test does not? Strongly skewed data, one median vs target: sign or Wilcoxon? Show answers The absolute differences from the target. A roughly symmetric distribution. The sign test. Key takeaways One median vs target, using signed ranks of the differences. Assumes symmetry; more powerful than the sign test when that holds.
One and Two Sample Proportion

Why this matters Many Six Sigma metrics are proportions: percent late, percent defective, percent of claims paid. Proportion tests check whether a rate meets a target, or whether two rates really differ (before and after an improvement, or between two terminals). 1-proportion test Question: does the population proportion p differ from a target p₀? z = (p̂ − p₀) ÷ √[ p₀(1 − p₀) ÷ n ] Example. A carrier claims at most 5% late deliveries. An audit of 400 deliveries finds 28 late: p̂ = 0.07. H₀: p = 0.05. Hₐ: p > 0.05 (one-sided). SE = √(0.05 × 0.95 ÷ 400) ≈ 0.0109. z = (0.07 − 0.05) ÷ 0.0109 ≈ 1.84 . One-sided critical z at α = 0.05 = 1.645. 1.84 > 1.645 → reject H₀ : the late rate is significantly above 5%. (A two-sided test, with critical value 1.96, would not reject.) 2-proportion test Question: do two populations have different proportions? Software usually tests H₀: p₁ = p₂ with a pooled proportion: p̂(pool) = (x₁ + x₂) ÷ (n₁ + n₂) z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂) ÷ √[ p̂(pool) × (1 − p̂(pool)) × (1/n₁ + 1/n₂) ] The IASSC reference sheet gives the unpooled form: z = (p₁ − p₂) ÷ √[ p₁(1 − p₁)/n₁ + p₂(1 − p₂)/n₂ ] The two give slightly different numbers; for hand calculations use the sheet's form unless the question says otherwise. Example. Before a new load-securing procedure, 30 of 400 loads (7.5%) had damage. After, 15 of 400 (3.75%). Pooled: p̂ = 45 ÷ 800 = 0.05625; SE ≈ 0.0163; z = 0.0375 ÷ 0.0163 ≈ 2.30 . Unpooled (sheet): SE ≈ 0.0162; z ≈ 2.31 . Two-sided critical z = 1.96. Reject H₀ : the damage rate fell significantly. Confidence interval for the difference (p₁ − p₂) ± z(1 − α/2) × √[ p₁(1 − p₁)/n₁ + p₂(1 − p₂)/n₂ ] For the example: 0.0375 ± 1.96 × 0.0162 ≈ 0.0375 ± 0.032, about 0.6 to 6.9 percentage points . The interval excludes zero (significant), but it is wide: the true reduction could be small or substantial. Conditions These z-tests rely on the normal approximation to the binomial (3.1.2). Check that np and n(1 − p) are both at least 5 (some texts use 10) for each sample. With small counts, use an exact binomial test (one sample) or Fisher's exact test (two samples). Sample size Detecting a small difference between proportions needs large samples, often hundreds per group, because attribute data carries little information per observation (3.2.2). Common mistakes and exam traps Defective rate before vs after = 2-proportion test. Use p₀ (the hypothesized value) in the 1-proportion standard error , not p̂. Check np ≥ 5 and n(1 − p) ≥ 5. Pooled vs unpooled give slightly different z values. Check yourself Target 10% defective; sample 200 with 30 defective. Compute z. Which test compares on-time rates at two terminals? Sample n = 40 with p̂ = 0.05. Is the normal approximation OK? 2-proportion test: p̂₁ = 0.12 (n = 300), p̂₂ = 0.08 (n = 300). What is the pooled proportion? Show answers p̂ = 0.15; SE = √(0.1 × 0.9 ÷ 200) ≈ 0.0212; z ≈ 2.36. 2-proportion test. No: np = 2, below 5. Use an exact test. (36 + 24) ÷ 600 = 0.10. Key takeaways 1 proportion: z = (p̂ − p₀) ÷ √[p₀(1 − p₀)/n]. 2 proportions: pooled (software) or unpooled (IASSC sheet) z. CI for the difference shows the size of the change. Needs np and n(1 − p) ≥ 5; otherwise exact tests.
Chi-Squared (Contingency Tables)

Why this matters Some questions involve two categorical variables: Does the type of defect depend on the shift? Does complaint type depend on the region? The chi-square test of independence answers these from a table of counts. The big idea Arrange the counts in a contingency table : one variable in rows, the other in columns. H₀: the two variables are independent (defect type does not depend on shift). Hₐ: they are related . If H₀ were true, each cell's count would be predictable from the row and column totals. The test compares the observed counts (O) with these expected counts (E). The calculation Expected count for each cell: E = (row total × column total) ÷ grand total Test statistic : χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E df = (rows − 1) × (columns − 1) Compare with the critical value from the chi-square table (upper tail) for that df and α. Worked example Defect types by shift: Damage Shortage Paperwork Total Day 30 20 50 100 Night 40 10 50 100 Total 70 30 100 200 Expected (Day, Damage) = 100 × 70 ÷ 200 = 35. Similarly: Day shortage 15, paperwork 50; Night damage 35, shortage 15, paperwork 50. Contributions (O − E)² ÷ E: Day damage (30 − 35)² ÷ 35 = 0.714; Day shortage (20 − 15)² ÷ 15 = 1.667; Day paperwork 0; Night damage 0.714; Night shortage 1.667; Night paperwork 0. χ² = 0.714 + 1.667 + 0 + 0.714 + 1.667 + 0 ≈ 4.76 . df = (2 − 1) × (3 − 1) = 2. Critical χ²(0.05, 2) = 5.99 . 4.76 < 5.99 → fail to reject H₀ . No significant evidence that defect type depends on shift. (The cells with the biggest contributions, shortages, show where any pattern would be.) The expected-count formula is not on the IASSC sheet; know it. Conditions Expected counts should generally be at least 5 in each cell. It is a rule of thumb; expected counts below 1 are especially problematic. Combine categories, collect more data, or use Fisher's exact test (for sparse 2×2 tables) when counts are small. Observations must be independent , and each counted in exactly one cell. Related uses A 2×2 contingency table gives the same answer as a two-sided 2-proportion test (pooled). The goodness-of-fit chi-square compares observed counts in one variable with expected proportions (for example, are defects equally spread across five days?). Low exam yield. Common mistakes and exam traps Counts of category by category = chi-square contingency. E = row total × column total ÷ grand total. df = (r − 1)(c − 1) , not (r × c) − 1. Use counts, not percentages , in the table. Expected counts at least 5. Check yourself A table has 3 rows and 4 columns. What are the degrees of freedom? Row total 60, column total 50, grand total 200. What is the expected count? O = 18 and E = 12. What is that cell's contribution to χ²? What does rejecting H₀ mean in a contingency test? Several expected counts are below 5. What can you do? Show answers (3 − 1)(4 − 1) = 6. 60 × 50 ÷ 200 = 15. (18 − 12)² ÷ 12 = 36 ÷ 12 = 3. The two categorical variables are related (not independent). Combine categories, collect more data, or use an exact test. Key takeaways Two categorical variables in a table of counts: chi-square test of independence. E = row total × column total ÷ grand total; χ² = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E; df = (r − 1)(c − 1). Expected counts at least 5; otherwise combine or use Fisher's exact test.
Correlation

Why this matters Once Analyze has narrowed the suspects, Improve needs to know how much an X affects the Y, so the team can set it to the right level. Correlation is the first step: does a relationship exist, and how strong is it? This domain carries a heavy share of exam questions for its few topics, so it is high-yield. The big idea Correlation measures how strongly two continuous variables move together in a straight-line pattern. Always plot a scatterplot first (2.2.4), then put a number on what you see. r ≈ +0.9 strong positive r ≈ −0.9 strong negative r ≈ 0 no linear relation r ≈ 0 but clearly curved The correlation coefficient describes straight-line patterns only. The bottom-right pattern is a strong relationship with r near zero. Pearson's correlation coefficient, r r = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) ÷ √[ Σ(X − X̄)² × Σ(Y − Ȳ)² ] (This formula is on the IASSC reference sheet.) What it means: r ranges from −1 to +1 . Sign = direction: positive means Y rises as X rises; negative means Y falls as X rises. Size (ignoring the sign) = strength: values near 1 or −1 mean the points lie close to a straight line; near 0 means no straight-line pattern. Rough guide to strength (|r|): above 0.8 strong, 0.5 to 0.8 moderate, below 0.5 weak. These cutoffs vary by field. r = −0.9 is a stronger relationship than r = +0.6. The sign only shows direction. r² (the coefficient of determination) Squaring r gives r² : the share of the variation in Y that is explained by the straight-line relationship with X. If r = 0.9, r² = 0.81: 81% of the variation in Y is explained by X. (In regression, this is R², 4.1.2.) What correlation does not tell you r near 0 does not mean "no relationship". It means no straight-line relationship. A strong curved (U-shaped) relationship can have r ≈ 0. Always look at the plot. Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and drownings are correlated because both rise in summer: a lurking variable (temperature) drives both. Two things moving together can be a coincidence, a common cause, or causation in either direction. Proving cause needs a controlled experiment or strong process knowledge. One point can change everything. A single extreme point (an outlier or an influential point ) can create a strong correlation from nothing, or destroy a real one. Check the plot for points far from the rest. Spearman rank correlation Spearman's rank correlation applies Pearson's formula to the ranks of the data. It measures any monotonic relationship (consistently increasing or decreasing, not necessarily straight) and resists outliers. Use it for non-normal or ordinal data. Worked example Load weight (tons) and fuel use (gallons per 100 miles) for 5 trips: (10, 14), (15, 15), (20, 17), (25, 18), (30, 21). Means: X̄ = 20, Ȳ = 17. Deviations of X: −10, −5, 0, 5, 10. Deviations of Y: −3, −2, 0, 1, 4. Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) = 30 + 10 + 0 + 5 + 40 = 85 . Σ(X − X̄)² = 100 + 25 + 0 + 25 + 100 = 250 . Σ(Y − Ȳ)² = 9 + 4 + 0 + 1 + 16 = 30 . r = 85 ÷ √(250 × 30) = 85 ÷ 86.6 ≈ 0.98 : a very strong positive relationship. r² ≈ 0.96. Heavier loads go with higher fuel use, as expected. Physics supplies the causal explanation here; in less obvious cases, be careful. Common mistakes and exam traps Strength is |r|; the sign is direction. r ≈ 0 can hide a curve. Plot first. Correlation does not prove causation. Check for influential points. Check yourself Which is stronger: r = −0.75 or r = 0.70? r = 0.6. What share of Y's variation is explained by X? A scatterplot shows a clear U shape, and r = 0.05. What do you conclude? Shipments and late deliveries are highly correlated across months. Does more volume cause lateness? When would you use Spearman instead of Pearson? Show answers r = −0.75 (|−0.75| > 0.70). r² = 0.36, so 36%. There is a strong curved relationship that Pearson's r cannot detect; it is not "no relationship". Not necessarily. It is plausible, but a lurking variable (season, staffing) could drive both; it needs further investigation. For non-normal or ordinal data, monotonic but non-linear relationships, or data with outliers. Key takeaways Plot first. r measures straight-line association from −1 to +1. |r| is strength, sign is direction; r² is the share of variation explained. r ≈ 0 does not rule out a curved relationship. Correlation is not causation; watch for lurking variables and influential points. Spearman: rank-based, for monotonic or non-normal data.
Regression Equations

Why this matters Correlation says variables are related. Regression gives the actual equation, so you can predict Y for any X, and so you know how much to change X to move Y where you want it. That is exactly what Improve needs: "set the X here to get the Y there." The big idea Simple linear regression fits the straight line that best describes how Y changes with X: Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X Ŷ (Y-hat): the predicted value of Y. b₁ : the slope , how much Y changes, on average, for a one-unit increase in X . b₀ : the intercept , the predicted Y when X = 0. The IASSC sheet writes the same line as Ŷ = a + bX. "Best" means least squares : the line that makes the sum of the squared vertical distances from the points to the line as small as possible. 10 20 30 14 18 22 Load weight X (tons) Fuel Y (gal per 100 mi) Ŷ = 10.2 + 0.34X residual Each red segment is a residual. Least squares picks the line that makes the sum of their squares smallest. Calculating the slope and intercept b₁ = Sxy ÷ Sxx = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) ÷ Σ(X − X̄)² b₀ = Ȳ − b₁X̄ Using the fuel example from 4.1.1: Sxy = 85, Sxx = 250, X̄ = 20, Ȳ = 17. b₁ = 85 ÷ 250 = 0.34 : each extra ton adds 0.34 gallons per 100 miles. b₀ = 17 − 0.34 × 20 = 10.2 . Equation: Ŷ = 10.2 + 0.34X . Predict fuel use at 22 tons: Ŷ = 10.2 + 0.34 × 22 = 17.68 gallons per 100 miles. Interpreting the intercept: at X = 0 tons, predicted fuel is 10.2: roughly an empty truck. Here it makes sense. Often the intercept has no real meaning (X = 0 may be impossible or far outside the data). Do not extrapolate The line is only trustworthy within the range of X values in the data (here 10 to 30 tons). Predicting at 60 tons assumes the straight-line relationship continues, which may not be true (different gearing, engine limits). This is called extrapolation , and it is risky. How good is the fit? R², S and the p-value R² (R-squared) : the share of variation in Y explained by the model. R² = SS(regression) ÷ SS(total) For the example, R² = 28.9 ÷ 30 = 0.963 : 96.3% of the trip-to-trip variation in fuel use is explained by load weight. "R² = 0.72" means 72% of the variation in Y is explained by the model; the other 28% is unexplained (other X's and noise). Adjusted R² : R² corrected for the number of predictors. It matters most in multiple regression (4.2.2), where adding useless terms always raises R² but can lower adjusted R². S (standard error of the regression) : the typical size of the residuals, in Y's units. Here S ≈ 0.61 gallons: predictions are typically off by about 0.6 gallons. p-value for the slope : tests H₀: slope = 0 (X has no linear effect on Y). If p ≤ α, X is a significant predictor. A confidence interval for the slope that contains 0 matches failing to reject H₀ at that α. The regression ANOVA table Regression output includes an ANOVA table that splits the total variation: Source SS df MS F Regression SSR 1 (k in multiple regression) SSR ÷ df MS_reg ÷ MS_error Error (residual) SSE n − 2 (n − k − 1) SSE ÷ df Total SST n − 1 For the example: SST = 30, SSR = 28.9, SSE = 1.1; df = 1, 3, 4; MS_reg = 28.9, MS_error = 0.367; F ≈ 78.8 , a highly significant model. S = √MS_error ≈ 0.61. Exam questions often give a partly blank table to fill in. Reading a coefficient table Term Coef SE Coef T P Constant 10.20 0.81 12.6 0.001 Weight 0.340 0.038 8.88 0.003 Coef : the estimated b₀ and b₁. SE Coef : the uncertainty of each estimate. T = Coef ÷ SE Coef; P : the p-value for "this coefficient = 0". Below the table: S , R-sq , R-sq(adj) , and sometimes R-sq(pred) (how well the model predicts new data). The sign of r matches the sign of the slope. Common mistakes and exam traps Slope = change in Y per one-unit change in X. R² = share of Y's variation explained , not the share of points on the line. Do not extrapolate. Regression df: 1, n − 2, n − 1 (simple); k, n − k − 1, n − 1 (multiple). The slope and intercept formulas are not on the IASSC sheet : know them. Check yourself Ŷ = 50 − 2.5X. What is the predicted Y at X = 8? What does −2.5 mean? Sxy = 120, Sxx = 40, X̄ = 6, Ȳ = 30. Find b₁ and b₀. SSR = 80, SST = 100. What is R²? Simple regression with n = 22: what are the error and total df? The slope's 95% CI is −0.3 to 1.2. Is X significant at α = 0.05? Show answers Ŷ = 50 − 20 = 30. Each one-unit increase in X lowers Y by 2.5 on average. b₁ = 3; b₀ = 30 − 3 × 6 = 12. 0.80 (80% explained). Error df = 20; total df = 21. No: the interval contains 0. Key takeaways Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X, fitted by least squares; b₁ = Sxy ÷ Sxx; b₀ = Ȳ − b₁X̄. Slope: change in Y per unit of X. Intercept: Y at X = 0 (may be meaningless). R² = SSR ÷ SST; S = typical residual size; slope p-value tests slope = 0. ANOVA df: 1, n − 2, n − 1; F = MS_reg ÷ MS_error. Do not extrapolate beyond the data.
Residuals Analysis

Why this matters A regression equation can look excellent (high R², tiny p-values) and still be wrong, because the model's assumptions are violated. Residual plots are how you check. They are also a favorite exam topic: you are shown a plot and asked what is wrong and how to fix it. The big idea A residual is what the model got wrong for each point: e = Y − Ŷ (observed minus predicted) In the fuel example, at 30 tons the observed value is 21 and the prediction is 10.2 + 0.34 × 30 = 20.4, so the residual is +0.6 . All five residuals are 0.4, −0.3, 0, −0.7, 0.6: they sum to zero, as least-squares residuals always do. If the model is right, the residuals should look like pure random noise . Any pattern in them is information the model missed. The assumptions behind regression Linearity : the true relationship is a straight line (or whatever form you fitted). Independence : residuals do not influence each other (no time-order effects). Constant variance : residuals spread the same amount everywhere ( homoscedasticity ). Normality : residuals are approximately normal (needed for valid p-values and intervals). Residuals should also center on zero. The residual plots Software usually shows a "four-pack": Normal probability plot of residuals : points should follow the straight line (normality, 2.2.3). Histogram of residuals : should look roughly bell-shaped and centered at zero. Residuals vs fitted values : should be a random, even band around zero. Residuals vs observation order : should show no pattern over time. Random scatter: good fitted value → Funnel: unequal variance fitted value → Curve: wrong model form fitted value → Left: what you want. Middle and right: the two most common problems. Diagnosing patterns What you see Problem Fix Random band around zero None Model OK Funnel (spread grows or shrinks across the fits) Non-constant variance Transform Y (log, square root, Box-Cox, 4.2.5) Curve (U-shape or arch) Wrong functional form : relationship is not linear Add a squared term (4.2.1) or transform X or Y Pattern vs order (trend, cycles, runs) Dependence or a time effect Investigate time-related causes; add a time variable; collect data differently S-shape or curve on the normal plot Non-normal residuals Transform; check for outliers or a missing variable One extreme point Outlier or influential point Check the data is correct; assess its influence (4.2.4) Outliers, leverage and influence An outlier has a large residual: its Y is far from the line. A high-leverage point has an unusual X : far from the other X values. It has the potential to pull the line toward itself. An influential point actually changes the fitted line a lot: removing it would change the slope noticeably. High leverage combined with a large residual is the dangerous combination. Never delete a point just because it is inconvenient. First check if it is a data error; if it is real, it may be telling you something important. Common mistakes and exam traps Residual = observed − predicted. Funnel → non-constant variance → transform Y. Curve → missing curvature → add a squared term or transform. Pattern vs order → dependence or a time effect. A high R² does not prove the model is valid. Check yourself Observed Y = 48, predicted Ŷ = 45. What is the residual? Residuals vs fits fan out wider as fitted values increase. What is wrong, and what is the usual fix? Residuals vs fits form an arch. What does this mean? Residuals vs order show steadily increasing values. What should you investigate? What makes a point influential? Show answers 48 − 45 = +3. Non-constant variance; transform Y (for example log or Box-Cox). The relationship is curved; add a squared term (or transform). A time-related effect or dependence (drift, wear, learning, seasonal change). It substantially changes the fitted line, typically a point with high leverage (unusual X) and a large residual. Key takeaways Residual e = Y − Ŷ; good models leave random residuals centered at zero. Assumptions: linearity, independence, constant variance, normal residuals. Funnel: transform Y. Curve: add a squared term or transform. Order pattern: time effect. Extreme point: check influence and data. Outlier = big residual; leverage = unusual X; influential = changes the line.
Non-Linear Regression

Why this matters Not every relationship is a straight line. Fuel use rises faster at high speeds; error rates fall quickly with early training, then level off. Forcing a straight line onto a curve gives poor predictions and wrong conclusions about where to set an X. The big idea When the scatterplot or the residuals show a curve , change the model so it can bend: Add polynomial terms : a quadratic model adds X², a cubic adds X³. Quadratic: Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X + b₂X² A quadratic can make one bend (a U-shape or an arch); a cubic can make two. Transform X or Y : for example, use log(X) or √Y, which can straighten some curves (see 4.2.5). How you know you need it The scatterplot shows a clear bend. The residuals vs fits plot from a straight-line model shows a curved pattern (4.1.3). That arch is the clearest signal. After adding the X² term, its p-value is significant , the residual pattern disappears and S (typical error) drops. Example Fuel economy (mpg) vs speed (mph): economy improves from 45 to about 55 mph, then drops at higher speeds. A straight line through these points has a poor fit and arched residuals. A quadratic model, Ŷ = b₀ + b₁(speed) + b₂(speed)², captures the peak, and its fitted curve shows the best speed (where the curve tops out). Higher R² is not always better Adding terms always increases R² a little, even useless ones. A cubic or higher model may wiggle through the sample points perfectly yet predict new data badly. This is overfitting : the model fits the noise in this particular sample. Guard against it: Choose the simplest model that fits (the principle of parsimony ). Check that new terms are significant and that adjusted R² (and predicted R², if available) improve, not just R². Make sure the curve makes physical sense for the process. Choosing from a fitted-line plot When an exam shows linear and quadratic fits of the same data: If the points clearly curve and the quadratic term is significant (and S is lower, adjusted R² higher), choose the quadratic . If the points look straight and the quadratic term is not significant, choose the linear model (simpler). Check yourself What term turns a linear model into a quadratic one? Which residual pattern signals that a non-linear model is needed? A cubic model has R² = 0.97 and a linear model has R² = 0.95, but the cubic terms are not significant. Which do you choose? What is overfitting? Show answers An X² (squared) term. A curve (arch or U-shape) in the residuals vs fits plot. The linear model: simpler, and the extra terms add nothing significant. A model so complex it fits the random noise in the sample and predicts new data poorly. Key takeaways Curved data: add X² (or X³), or transform. Curved residuals are the main signal. Higher R² is not automatically better; prefer the simplest adequate model.
Multiple Linear Regression

Why this matters Real outputs depend on several inputs at once: delivery time depends on distance, stops, traffic and load time. Multiple regression models them together, estimates each X's effect while holding the others constant , and reveals which X's matter most. It is often the main tool for building the "Y = f(X)" model (1.1.4) in Analyze and Improve. The big idea Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + … + bₖXₖ Each coefficient bᵢ is the change in Y for a one-unit increase in Xᵢ, holding all the other X's constant . That "holding constant" is what simple regression cannot do. Example: Ŷ (delivery hours) = 1.2 + 0.018 (miles) + 0.45 (stops). Each extra stop adds 0.45 hours, for the same distance. Each extra mile adds 0.018 hours, for the same number of stops. Testing the model Overall F-test (in the ANOVA table): H₀: all slopes are zero. A small p-value means at least one X is useful. df: regression k, error n − k − 1, total n − 1. Individual t-tests for each coefficient: is this X useful given the others are already in the model ? R² : share of variation explained by all the X's together. Adjusted R² : R² penalized for the number of terms. Adding a useless X raises R² slightly but can lower adjusted R², which tells you to leave it out. S : typical size of the residuals. On the IASSC sheet: S = √[Σ(Y − Ŷ)² ÷ (n − (k + 1))]. Multicollinearity Multicollinearity occurs when the X's are correlated with each other , for example miles and fuel used, or truck age and mileage. The model cannot tell which one deserves the credit, so: Coefficients become unstable: they can change a lot, or even flip sign, when data or terms change. Standard errors inflate, so individual p-values look insignificant. Classic symptom : the overall F-test is highly significant and R² is high, but none of the individual t-tests is significant. Measure it with the variance inflation factor (VIF) for each X: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − R²ⱼ) where R²ⱼ is the R² from regressing Xⱼ on all the other X's. VIF = 1 means no correlation with the others. If R²ⱼ = 0.8, VIF = 5. A common rule of thumb flags VIF above 5 (some use 10) as a problem; this is a convention, not an IASSC-defined cutoff. Fixes: remove one of the correlated X's, combine them, or collect data where they vary independently (a designed experiment). Building the model Backward elimination : start with all candidate X's, remove the term with the highest p-value (above α), refit, and repeat until all remaining terms are significant. This is the standard approach. Stepwise : software adds and removes terms one at a time based on p-values. Best subsets : software compares all combinations and reports the best models of each size by adjusted R², S and other criteria (such as Mallows' Cp, low exam yield). Aim for parsimony : the fewest terms that explain Y well. Do not drop a term on its p-value alone if it is important for the purpose (for example, a factor you control and must set). Interactions An interaction means the effect of one X depends on the level of another . Example: extra stops add much more time in a city than on rural routes, so "stops × urban" is an interaction term. Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + b₃(X₁ × X₂) Hierarchy rule : if an interaction term stays in the model, keep both of its main effects (X₁ and X₂), even if one of them has a weak p-value on its own. Categorical predictors X's like shift, supplier or machine are categories, not numbers. Software includes them as indicator (dummy) variables (for example, 1 if night shift, 0 if day). Each coefficient then compares that category with a baseline. You only need to recognize this, not code it by hand. Worked example: reading output Term Coef P VIF Constant 1.20 0.010 Miles 0.018 0.000 1.3 Stops 0.45 0.002 1.3 Driver age −0.004 0.640 1.1 R² = 84.0%, adjusted R² = 82.1%. Miles and stops are significant (p < 0.05); driver age is not (p = 0.64). Backward elimination: remove driver age and refit. Adjusted R² will likely rise slightly. VIFs are all low, so multicollinearity is not a concern. Common mistakes and exam traps Each coefficient holds the other X's constant. High F and R² but no significant t-tests = multicollinearity. Check VIF. Adjusted R² can fall when a useless term is added. Backward elimination removes the highest-p term first, one at a time. Keep the main effects of any retained interaction. Check yourself In Ŷ = 5 + 2X₁ − 3X₂, what happens to Y if X₂ increases by 1 and X₁ stays the same? An X has R²ⱼ = 0.9 when regressed on the other X's. What is its VIF, and is that a concern? Why can adjusted R² fall when a term is added? A model's interaction A×B is significant, but A alone has p = 0.3. Do you remove A? Multiple regression with n = 30 and k = 3: what are the regression, error and total df? Show answers Y decreases by 3. VIF = 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10: a concern (above the 5 rule of thumb). Because it penalizes extra terms; a useless term adds complexity without enough explained variation. No. Keep main effects of a retained interaction (hierarchy). 3, 26, 29. Key takeaways Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X₁ + … + bₖXₖ; each b is the effect holding other X's constant. Overall F, individual t-tests, R² and adjusted R². Multicollinearity: correlated X's; VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − R²ⱼ); above 5 (or 10) is a warning. Build by backward elimination, stepwise or best subsets; keep the model parsimonious. Interactions: effect of one X depends on another; keep their main effects.
Confidence and Prediction Intervals

Why this matters A regression prediction is a single number, but decisions need a range. There are two different ranges, answering two different questions, and mixing them up is a classic exam trap. The big idea At a given value of X, the model predicts Ŷ. Two intervals can surround it: Confidence interval (CI) for the mean response : the range for the average Y of all units at that X. "What is the average fuel use for all 22-ton loads?" Prediction interval (PI) : the range for one single new observation at that X. "How much fuel will the next 22-ton load use?" Why the prediction interval is wider The CI only has to account for uncertainty about where the line is (sampling error in b₀ and b₁). The PI must account for that plus the scatter of individual points around the line (the residual variation). Individual values vary much more than averages, so the prediction interval is always wider . x̄ (narrowest here) Shaded: confidence interval for the mean response Dashed: prediction interval for one new value (wider) Both bands are narrowest at the mean of X and widen toward the ends of the data. Narrowest at the center Both intervals are narrowest at X̄ (the mean of the X data) and widen as X moves away from it. The model is most certain in the middle of its data and least certain near the edges, and beyond the data (extrapolation) the uncertainty grows fast. Choosing the right interval Wording cues: "the average delivery time for 300-mile trips", "the mean output at X = 10" → confidence interval . "the next truck", "a single new unit", "this one shipment" → prediction interval . Example Software output at load weight = 22 tons: Fit: 17.68 gallons per 100 miles. 95% CI: 16.8 to 18.6 (the average for all 22-ton loads). 95% PI: 15.6 to 19.8 (the next individual 22-ton load). For setting a fuel budget across many loads, use the CI. For promising a customer a range for one load, use the PI. Check yourself Which interval is used for a single future unit? Why is the prediction interval wider? Where along X are the intervals narrowest? "What will the average cycle time be for all orders of 50 lines?" Which interval? Show answers The prediction interval. It includes the scatter of individual values around the line, not just uncertainty about the line itself. At the mean of X (X̄). The confidence interval for the mean response. Key takeaways CI: the mean response at X. PI: one new observation at X. PI is always wider than CI. Both narrowest at X̄, wider toward the edges; do not extrapolate.
Residuals Analysis (Multiple Regression)

The big idea Multiple regression rests on the same assumptions as simple regression (4.1.3): linearity, independence, constant variance and normal residuals. The same four residual plots check them: normal probability plot, histogram, residuals vs fits, residuals vs order. The same patterns mean the same problems: a funnel means non-constant variance, a curve means a missing term, a pattern over order means a time effect. With several X's, add these checks: Residuals vs each X Plot residuals against each predictor separately. A curve against one particular X shows exactly which variable needs a squared term or a transformation. Multicollinearity (VIF) Check the VIF of each predictor (4.2.2). High VIFs make coefficients unstable and p-values unreliable. Leverage and influence With several X's, a point can be unusual in a combination of X values even if each value looks normal on its own (a short trip with an unusually large number of stops). Software flags: High leverage : points with unusual X combinations (large "hat" values). Large standardized residuals : points the model fits badly (often beyond ±2 or ±3). Cook's distance : combines leverage and residual size to measure how much each point influences the fitted coefficients. Points with large Cook's distance deserve investigation. Interpreting a full four-pack Typical exam reasoning: Normal plot straight, histogram bell-shaped, residuals vs fits random, residuals vs order random → assumptions met; trust the p-values and intervals. Normal plot curved and residuals vs fits funneled → transform Y (Box-Cox, 4.2.5), then refit and recheck. Residuals vs fits arched → add a squared term for the X that shows the curve. Residuals vs order trending → look for a time-related variable (wear, learning, season) and consider adding it. One point far from the rest with large Cook's distance → check the data; if real, analyze with and without it and report both. Check yourself What extra plot helps find which X needs a squared term? What does Cook's distance measure? Residuals funnel and the normal plot bends. What is the first fix to try? Show answers Residuals vs each individual X. How much a single point influences the fitted model (combining leverage and residual size). Transform Y (for example with Box-Cox), refit and recheck. Key takeaways Same four residual checks as simple regression. Add residuals vs each X, VIF, leverage, standardized residuals and Cook's distance. Diagnose, fix (transform or add terms), refit, recheck.
Data Transformation, Box-Cox

Why this matters Many tools assume normal data or constant variance. Real data (times, costs, counts) are often skewed, with spread growing as values grow. A transformation re-expresses the data on a different scale where those assumptions hold, so the standard tools work. The big idea A transformation applies the same mathematical function to every data point: take the square root, the logarithm, or the reciprocal. Skewed data with a long right tail often become close to normal on a log scale, because the log compresses large values more than small ones. Box-Cox transformations The Box-Cox method searches a family of power transformations , Y raised to a power λ (lambda), and finds the λ that makes the data most nearly normal with constant variance: λ Transformation 2 Y² (square) 1 Y (no transformation) 0.5 √Y (square root) 0 ln(Y) (natural log) , by definition −0.5 1 ÷ √Y −1 1 ÷ Y (reciprocal) (For λ = 0, Y⁰ would be 1 for every value, which is useless, so the natural log is used instead; it is the mathematical limit of the family.) Reading Box-Cox output Software reports: The optimal λ (best estimate). A confidence interval for λ . A rounded λ to use in practice. Rules: If the CI for λ includes 1 , no transformation may be needed (λ = 1 means "leave the data alone"), even if the optimal λ is not exactly 1. Otherwise, pick a rounded, interpretable λ inside the CI : 0.5 (square root), 0 (log), −1 (reciprocal). A log is often chosen when 0 is inside the interval, because log scales are easy to explain. Example: optimal λ = 0.12, 95% CI −0.20 to 0.45. The CI excludes 1 (transform) and includes 0, so use the natural log . Requirements and cautions Box-Cox needs positive data. If there are zeros or negative values, add a constant first so all values are positive. When using transformed data for capability (2.4), transform the specification limits the same way , or the comparison is meaningless. Results on the transformed scale (means, intervals) should be converted back to the original units when reporting to people. Transforming is not always the answer: if non-normality comes from mixed populations or outliers, fix that cause instead (2.2.3). Other options The Johnson transformation is a more flexible alternative that can handle data Box-Cox cannot. Recognition only. Check yourself Which λ means "no transformation"? Which transformation corresponds to λ = 0? Box-Cox gives λ = 0.6 with CI 0.3 to 1.1. What do you do? The data include zeros. What must you do before Box-Cox? After log-transforming cycle times for a capability study, what else must be transformed? Show answers λ = 1. The natural log. The CI includes 1, so a transformation may not be needed; if one is used, λ = 0.5 (square root) is a reasonable rounded choice. Add a constant so all values are positive. The specification limits. Key takeaways Transformations re-express data to make it more normal or the variance more constant. Box-Cox λ: 1 = none, 0.5 = square root, 0 = log, −1 = reciprocal. If λ's CI includes 1, maybe no transform; otherwise pick a rounded λ in the CI. Needs positive data; transform spec limits too for capability.
Control Methods for 5S

Why this matters 5S (1.4.5) is easy to start and easy to lose. Most organizations have done a "big clean-up" that looked great for a month and then slid back. The Control phase is about making improvements stick, and for 5S that means building routines that keep the workplace organized without heroic effort. The big idea 5S decays unless something actively holds it in place. The last two S's, Standardize and Sustain (Self-discipline) , exist exactly for this, and the control methods below put them into practice. If a 5S area has slipped back, the failure is almost always in Sustain . Control methods 1. Audits and scored checklists. A short checklist covers each S ("Only needed items at the workstation? Every tool on its shadow? Floor clean, no leaks? Standards posted and current?"). Each item is scored (for example 0 to 4), giving a total 5S score that can be tracked over time. Scores are posted visibly, and low scores trigger action, not blame. 2. Visual controls. Make the standard and any deviation obvious at a glance: Floor markings : lanes, pallet locations, keep-clear zones. Shadow boards : an empty outline shows a missing tool immediately. Labels and color codes : every location named; a place for everything. Photos of the standard : "this is what right looks like". Min/max lines on shelves and bins. 3. Standard work and ownership. Each area has a named owner and a written routine: who does what cleaning and checking, how often. When everyone owns it, no one does. 4. A regular schedule. Daily : quick operator checks (5 minutes at shift end). Weekly : area leader audit. Monthly or quarterly : management audit or walk, which shows that leaders care. Management attention is the single strongest sustainer: what leaders check, people keep doing. Worked example A dock was 5S'd in March, scoring 92%. By July it scores 58%: tools left out, pallets in walkways, labels missing. Sort, Straighten and Shine were clearly done once. What failed was Sustain : no regular audits, no owner, no leadership walks. The fix: assign an area owner, add a daily 5-minute end-of-shift check, post weekly scores, and include the dock in the monthly management walk. Check yourself 5S gains faded within months. Which S failed? Name three visual controls. Why does every 5S area need a named owner? What does a scored audit add beyond "looks clean"? Show answers Sustain (Self-discipline). Any three of: floor markings, shadow boards, labels, color codes, photos of the standard, min/max lines. Shared responsibility tends to mean no one takes action; an owner is accountable for keeping it up. A consistent, comparable measure over time that shows decay early and focuses attention. Key takeaways 5S decays without active control; decay means Sustain failed. Controls: scored audits and checklists, visual controls, standard work with area owners, a daily/weekly/management schedule. Leadership attention sustains 5S.
Kanban

Why this matters Kanban is the practical mechanism behind pull (1.4.1). It keeps inventory and work in process low and visible, prevents overproduction, and makes the system self-regulating: nothing is made or moved until it is needed. The big idea A kanban (Japanese for "signboard" or "card") is a signal that authorizes a process to produce or move a specific quantity, only when the next step has used something . No signal, no production. The signal can be a card, an empty bin, a marked floor space, or an electronic message. Types of kanban Production kanban : authorizes a process to make a quantity to replace what was taken. Withdrawal (move, conveyance) kanban : authorizes moving a quantity from a storage point to the user. Supermarkets and two-bin systems A supermarket is a small, controlled store of items between processes. The downstream process "shops" (takes what it needs); the upstream process restocks only what was taken, signaled by kanban. A two-bin system is the simplest kanban: parts are used from bin 1; when it is empty, it becomes the signal to refill, while work continues from bin 2. Common for fasteners, packaging, office supplies, spare parts. The rules of kanban The downstream process pulls (withdraws) only what it needs, when it needs it. The upstream process produces only what was withdrawn , in the order the kanbans arrive. No defects are passed on. A defective item stops the flow and gets attention. Nothing moves or is made without a kanban. Level the load (heijunka) so demand on upstream processes is steady. Reduce the number of kanbans over time : fewer kanbans mean less inventory, and the problems the extra inventory was hiding become visible and can be fixed. How many kanbans? N = (demand × lead time × (1 + safety factor)) ÷ container size Always round up to the next whole kanban. Demand : usage per time period. Lead time : time to replenish one container (in the same time unit as demand). Safety factor : extra buffer for variation (for example 0.2 = 20%). Container size : quantity per kanban. Worked example. A dock uses 200 stretch-wrap rolls a day. Replenishment takes half a day. Safety factor 20%. Rolls come in cases of 25. N = (200 × 0.5 × 1.2) ÷ 25 = 120 ÷ 25 = 4.8 → 5 kanbans (5 cases circulating). CONWIP (recognition only) CONWIP (constant work in process) caps the total work allowed in a whole line rather than item by item: a new job starts only when one finishes. Low exam yield. Common mistakes and exam traps Kanban authorizes production or movement only after downstream consumption. Round the number of kanbans up. Production kanban = make; withdrawal kanban = move. Fewer kanbans over time, not more. Check yourself What does a kanban authorize? Demand 600 per day, lead time 0.25 day, safety factor 10%, container 40. How many kanbans? What is a two-bin system? Why reduce the number of kanbans over time? Which kanban type authorizes moving parts from a supermarket to the line? Show answers Producing or moving a specific quantity, only to replace what was used downstream. (600 × 0.25 × 1.1) ÷ 40 = 165 ÷ 40 = 4.125, round up to 5. Two containers: when the first empties, it signals replenishment while the second is used. To lower inventory and expose the problems excess inventory was hiding. A withdrawal (move) kanban. Key takeaways Kanban = a pull signal; nothing is made or moved without one. Production vs withdrawal kanbans; supermarkets and two-bin systems. Rules: downstream pulls, make only what was taken, no defects passed on, level the load. N = demand × lead time × (1 + safety) ÷ container size, rounded up.
Poka-Yoke (Mistake Proofing)

Why this matters People make mistakes, no matter how trained or careful. Training, warnings and inspections help, but they rely on attention, which fails. Poka-yoke designs the process so that mistakes cannot happen , or are caught immediately . It is one of the strongest controls in the Control phase because it does not depend on anyone remembering. The big idea Poka-yoke (Japanese for "mistake-proofing", developed by Shigeo Shingo at Toyota) separates errors from defects : An error is a mistake (picking the wrong part, skipping a step). A defect is the bad result that reaches the customer. Errors may be inevitable, but defects are not, if the process catches the error at the moment it happens and before it becomes a defect. Two levels of strength Control (prevention) type : makes the error impossible , or stops the process when it occurs. A fuel nozzle for diesel that does not fit a gasoline tank. A fixture that accepts a part in only one orientation. A truck that will not start until the seat belt is fastened, or a liftgate that will not lower unless the truck is in park. Software that will not let you submit an order without a delivery address. Warning (detection) type : makes the error immediately obvious , alerting a person to act. A beeper for an open door, a light when tire pressure is low. A scanner that beeps red when the wrong item is picked. A checklist with a missing-item alarm. Prevention is stronger than warning , because warnings can be ignored. Three methods of detection Contact method : detects shape, size, position or color by physical or sensor contact. "Does the part touch the limit switch?" Guide pins, keyed connectors, sensors. Fixed-value (counting) method : checks that a set number of actions or parts is complete. A kit tray with exactly 12 pockets: any empty pocket shows a missing part. Counters that require 8 bolts before release. Motion-step (sequence) method : checks that steps are done in the right order. Systems that will not proceed until the previous scan or step is confirmed. Source inspection Traditional inspection checks finished products (judgment inspection): it only finds defects after they are made. Shingo's approach favors source inspection : checking the conditions that cause errors at their source, before the operation, plus 100% automatic checking at the point where errors happen. Poka-yoke devices make 100% checking cheap. Worked example Problem: wrong paperwork sometimes goes with a trailer (shipping documents for another load). Warning : the yard scanner beeps if the bill of lading barcode does not match the trailer's barcode. Prevention : the gate system will not release the trailer until the bill of lading and trailer barcodes match. Common mistakes and exam traps A fixture that accepts parts in only one orientation = prevention (control) type. Alarms and lights = warning (detection) type. Prevention beats warning. Contact, fixed-value, motion-step : the three methods. Poka-yoke is associated with Shigeo Shingo. Check yourself What is the difference between an error and a defect? A connector that only plugs in one way: which type? A kit tray with a pocket for every part: which method? Why is prevention preferred to warning? What is source inspection? Show answers An error is the mistake; a defect is the bad result. Poka-yoke stops errors from becoming defects. Control (prevention) type, contact method. Fixed-value (counting). Warnings rely on people noticing and acting; prevention makes the error impossible. Checking the conditions that cause errors at their source, before they produce defects. Key takeaways Poka-yoke (Shingo): make errors impossible or immediately obvious. Control/prevention type (stronger) vs warning/detection type. Methods: contact, fixed-value (counting), motion-step (sequence). Source inspection and 100% automatic checks at the point of error.
Data Collection for SPC

Why this matters A control chart is only as good as the data behind it. Choosing what to measure, how to group it and which chart to use decides whether the chart catches real problems quickly or cries wolf. This topic is the foundation for all the charts that follow. The big idea: what a control chart is A control chart is a time-ordered plot of a process statistic (an individual value, a subgroup average, a range, a proportion…) with three lines calculated from the process's own data : Center line (CL) : the average of the statistic. Upper and lower control limits (UCL, LCL) : usually ±3 standard deviations of the plotted statistic from the center line. Zone A Zone A Zone B Zone B Zone C Zone C UCL CL LCL ±1σ, ±2σ, ±3σ of the plotted statistic Points scattering randomly inside the limits, with no patterns, mean the process is stable (2.4.2). Control limits are the voice of the process : they show the range of routine, common-cause variation. They are not specification limits (the voice of the customer, 2.4.1). A point outside the limits, or an unusual pattern, signals a likely special cause to investigate (5.2.10). Rational subgrouping Many charts plot subgroups : small groups of measurements taken together (for example, 5 consecutive loads). The rule of rational subgrouping : Form subgroups so that variation within a subgroup comes only from common causes (items made close together, same conditions, same shift, machine, operator). Then differences between subgroups reveal special causes (changes over time). Why it matters: the chart's limits are calculated from the within-subgroup variation. If a subgroup mixes conditions (two machines, two shifts), the within variation is inflated, the limits widen, and real shifts hide inside them. Subgroup size and frequency Size : larger subgroups detect smaller shifts but cost more. Variable-data charts commonly use 3 to 5 . Attribute charts (p, np) need much larger samples (often 50 to several hundred) to see changes in a proportion. Frequency : sample often enough to catch a change before many bad units are produced, and around known risks (shift changes, material lots, setups). Too far apart misses signals; too close together can make consecutive points too similar (autocorrelation). Choosing the chart The chart depends on the data type and the subgroup size : Data Subgroup Chart Continuous 1 (individual values) I-MR (5.2.2) Continuous 2 to about 10 Xbar-R (5.2.3) Continuous more than about 10 Xbar-S (5.2.7) Discrete: defectives (pass/fail units) varying sample size p chart (5.2.5) Discrete: defectives constant sample size np chart (5.2.6) Discrete: defects (counts) varying area of opportunity u chart (5.2.4) Discrete: defects constant area of opportunity c chart (5.2.4) Small sustained shifts matter any CuSum or EWMA (5.2.8, 5.2.9) Memory aid for the attribute charts: p and np = defectives (binomial); c and u = defects (Poisson) ; the "n" versions (np, c) need constant sample sizes. Phase I and Phase II Phase I (establishing limits) : collect historical or initial data, often about 20 to 25 subgroups (a guideline, not a rule), calculate trial limits, find and remove special causes, and recalculate until the chart shows a stable baseline. Phase II (monitoring) : keep the limits fixed and plot new data against them to detect changes. Operational definitions and check sheets Everyone collecting data must measure the same way (operational definitions, 1.2.2) and record it consistently. Check sheets (simple forms with tally marks or boxes) make collection quick and consistent, and should record time, shift, operator and other context so special causes can be traced later. Common mistakes and exam traps Control limits come from the process data, not from specifications. Rational subgroups: common cause within, special causes between. Pick the chart by data type and subgroup size. p/np = defectives; c/u = defects. Check yourself What do control limits represent? Why should a subgroup not contain parts from two different machines? One reading per day of a continuous measure: which chart? Number of damaged trailers out of a constant 100 inspected daily: which chart? What happens in Phase I? Show answers The range of routine, common-cause variation of the plotted statistic (the voice of the process). Machine-to-machine differences would inflate within-subgroup variation, widen the limits, and hide real changes. I-MR. np chart (defectives, constant sample size). Initial data are collected, trial limits calculated, special causes removed, and limits recalculated to establish a stable baseline. Key takeaways Control chart: statistic over time, center line, ±3σ limits from process data. Rational subgroups: common cause within, special causes between. Chart by data type and subgroup size: I-MR, Xbar-R, Xbar-S, p, np, u, c; CuSum/EWMA for small shifts. Phase I sets limits; Phase II monitors with fixed limits.
I-MR Chart

Why this matters Many processes give only one measurement at a time: one reading per day, per batch, per load, per week. When subgrouping is not possible or not sensible, the Individuals and Moving Range chart is the tool. The big idea The I-MR chart is really two charts: I chart (Individuals) : plots each individual value. MR chart (Moving Range) : plots the moving range , the absolute difference between each value and the one before it. It tracks short-term variation. With no subgroups, the moving range of consecutive points is used to estimate the common-cause variation. Formulas MR = |xᵢ − xᵢ₋₁| MR̄ = average of the moving ranges I chart: CL = X̄, UCL/LCL = X̄ ± 2.66 × MR̄ MR chart: CL = MR̄, UCL = 3.267 × MR̄, LCL = 0 σ estimate = MR̄ ÷ 1.128 Where the constants come from: a moving range is a subgroup of size 2, so the n = 2 row of the constants table applies. d₂ = 1.128, so 3σ = 3 × MR̄ ÷ 1.128 = 2.66 × MR̄ . D₄ = 3.267 and D₃ = 0 for n = 2. These I-MR formulas are not written out on the IASSC sheet, but the n = 2 row of its constants table gives them. Worked example Daily average dwell time at a customer site (minutes). After 25 days, X̄ = 50 and MR̄ = 3. I chart: UCL = 50 + 2.66 × 3 = 57.98 ; LCL = 50 − 7.98 = 42.02 . MR chart: UCL = 3.267 × 3 = 9.80 ; LCL = 0. σ ≈ 3 ÷ 1.128 ≈ 2.66 minutes . A day at 59 minutes is above the UCL: investigate what was different that day. When to use it, and cautions Use for slow processes , low volume , batch processes , data that arrives once per period, and expensive or destructive tests . The I chart is sensitive to non-normality : with skewed data it gives more false alarms on the long-tail side. Consider a transformation or a different chart if data are strongly non-normal. It is less sensitive to small shifts than subgroup charts. Check yourself Values 10, 13, 11, 15. What are the moving ranges and MR̄? X̄ = 100, MR̄ = 5. What are the I-chart limits? Why is the MR chart's LCL zero? One measurement per batch, batches once a day: which chart? Show answers 3, 2, 4; MR̄ = 3. 100 ± 13.3: UCL 113.3, LCL 86.7. D₃ = 0 for subgroups of size 2 (a range cannot be negative). I-MR. Key takeaways One value at a time: I-MR. I limits = X̄ ± 2.66 MR̄; MR UCL = 3.267 MR̄, LCL = 0; σ = MR̄ ÷ 1.128. Sensitive to non-normality.
Xbar-R Chart

Why this matters When you can take small subgroups regularly (for example 5 consecutive loads every hour), the Xbar-R chart is the classic choice. Averages are more sensitive to shifts than individual values (central limit theorem, 3.2.3), and the range shows whether variation is changing. The big idea Two charts, one for center and one for spread : Xbar chart : plots each subgroup's average (x̄). Shows shifts in the process center.
