R chart : plots each subgroup's range (largest minus smallest). Shows changes in short-term variation. Typical subgroup size: 2 to 10 , most often 4 or 5 . Formulas X̿ = average of the subgroup averages (grand mean) R̄ = average of the subgroup ranges Xbar chart: X̿ ± A₂ × R̄ R chart: UCL = D₄ × R̄, LCL = D₃ × R̄ σ estimate = R̄ ÷ d₂ The constants The constants depend on the subgroup size n (the IASSC sheet has a full table for n = 2 to 25): n A₂ d₂ D₃ D₄ 2 1.880 1.128 0 3.267 3 1.023 1.693 0 2.575 4 0.729 2.059 0 2.282 5 0.577 2.326 0 2.114 10 0.308 3.078 0.223 1.777 Find the row for your subgroup size and the A₂ column (A₃ is for Xbar-S). For n of 6 or less, D₃ = 0, so the R chart's LCL is 0. Worked example Subgroups of 5 trailer weights (tons). After 25 subgroups: X̿ = 100.0, R̄ = 4.0. Xbar chart: 100.0 ± 0.577 × 4.0 = 100.0 ± 2.31 → UCL 102.31, LCL 97.69 . R chart: UCL = 2.114 × 4.0 = 8.46 ; LCL = 0. σ ≈ 4.0 ÷ 2.326 ≈ 1.72 tons . Note: the Xbar limits (±2.31) are much narrower than the spread of individual weights (±3σ = ±5.16), because averages vary less (σ ÷ √n). Never compare individual values with Xbar limits. Read the R chart first The Xbar limits are calculated from R̄. If the R chart is out of control (variation unstable), R̄ is not a reliable estimate, and the Xbar limits are meaningless. So: check the R chart first (is variation stable?), then the Xbar chart (is the center stable?). Check yourself n = 4, X̿ = 50, R̄ = 2. What are the Xbar limits? Using the same data, what is the R chart UCL? Why check the R chart before the Xbar chart? Estimate σ for n = 5 and R̄ = 9.3. Which constant column do you use for the Xbar chart with an R chart? Show answers 50 ± 0.729 × 2 = 50 ± 1.458: UCL 51.46, LCL 48.54. 2.282 × 2 = 4.56. Because the Xbar limits depend on R̄; if variation is unstable, the Xbar limits are not valid. 9.3 ÷ 2.326 ≈ 4.0. A₂. Key takeaways Subgroups of 2 to 10 (usually 4 or 5): Xbar-R. Xbar: X̿ ± A₂R̄. R: UCL D₄R̄, LCL D₃R̄. σ = R̄ ÷ d₂. Use the constants row for your n. Check the R chart first.
U Chart

Why this matters Many processes count defects : errors per invoice, damage incidents per 100 loads, defects per inspection. When the amount inspected changes from period to period, raw counts are not comparable, and the u chart solves that by charting defects per unit . The big idea The u chart plots defects per unit (u = defects ÷ units inspected) for each subgroup. It is based on the Poisson distribution (defect counts, 3.1.2) and handles varying sample sizes (varying "area of opportunity"). Formulas uᵢ = cᵢ ÷ nᵢ (defects ÷ units in subgroup i) ū = Σc ÷ Σn (total defects ÷ total units) Limits (IASSC sheet form): ū ± 3√(ū ÷ n̄), n̄ = Σnᵢ ÷ k Software calculates limits for each subgroup's own nᵢ , so they step in and out (narrower for big samples, wider for small). The IASSC sheet uses the average subgroup size n̄ for hand calculation; use that unless told otherwise. If the LCL comes out negative, set it to 0 (you cannot have fewer than zero defects). Worked example Invoice errors: over 20 days, 4,000 invoices were checked and 160 errors found (daily volumes vary, averaging 200). ū = 160 ÷ 4,000 = 0.04 errors per invoice . n̄ = 4,000 ÷ 20 = 200. Limits: 0.04 ± 3√(0.04 ÷ 200) = 0.04 ± 3 × 0.01414 = 0.04 ± 0.0424 → UCL 0.0824 , LCL −0.0024 → 0 . The c chart When the area of opportunity is constant (same number of units, or the same size of item, each period), you can chart the count of defects directly with a c chart : c̄ = total defects ÷ number of subgroups Limits: c̄ ± 3√c̄ Example: each weekly audit inspects exactly 10 trailers, averaging c̄ = 4 defects. Limits = 4 ± 3 × 2 = UCL 10 , LCL −2 → 0 . Check yourself Defects per invoice with batch sizes that vary daily: which chart? ū = 0.09, n̄ = 100. Compute the limits. c̄ = 9. What are the c chart limits? Which distribution underlies u and c charts? Show answers u chart. 0.09 ± 3√(0.0009) = 0.09 ± 0.09: UCL 0.18, LCL 0. 9 ± 3 × 3: UCL 18, LCL 0. Poisson. Key takeaways u chart: defects per unit, varying sample size (Poisson). ū = Σc ÷ Σn; sheet limits ū ± 3√(ū ÷ n̄); negative LCL → 0. c chart: defect counts with a constant area of opportunity; c̄ ± 3√c̄.
P Chart

Why this matters Percent late, percent defective, percent of claims rejected: many key metrics are proportions of units that fail. The p chart tracks them over time, even when the number of units changes from day to day. The big idea The p chart plots the proportion defective (p = defective units ÷ units inspected) for each subgroup. It is based on the binomial distribution (defectives, 3.1.2) and handles varying sample sizes . Formulas pᵢ = defectives in subgroup i ÷ nᵢ p̄ = Σ(defectives) ÷ Σn Limits (IASSC sheet form): p̄ ± 3√[ p̄(1 − p̄) ÷ n̄ ], n̄ = Σnᵢ ÷ k As with the u chart, software uses each subgroup's own nᵢ (so limits vary), while the sheet uses n̄ for hand calculation. A negative LCL is set to 0 , and the UCL cannot meaningfully exceed 1 (100%). Worked example Late orders: over 25 days, 6,000 orders shipped, 300 late (daily volume varies, averaging 240). p̄ = 300 ÷ 6,000 = 0.05 (5% late). n̄ = 240. Limits: 0.05 ± 3√(0.05 × 0.95 ÷ 240) = 0.05 ± 3 × 0.01407 = 0.05 ± 0.0422 → UCL 0.0922 (9.2%) , LCL 0.0078 (0.8%) . A day at 11% late signals a special cause. So does an unusually good day below 0.8%: worth finding out what went right. Check yourself Percent of orders shipped late with varying daily volume: which chart? p̄ = 0.10, n̄ = 100. Compute the limits. Why might the LCL be set to 0? Defectives or defects: which does a p chart count? Show answers p chart. 0.10 ± 3√(0.1 × 0.9 ÷ 100) = 0.10 ± 0.09: UCL 0.19, LCL 0.01. When the formula gives a negative value; a proportion cannot be below zero. Defectives (units with at least one defect). Key takeaways p chart: proportion defective, varying sample size (binomial). p̄ = total defectives ÷ total inspected; limits p̄ ± 3√[p̄(1 − p̄) ÷ n̄]. Negative LCL → 0; UCL at most 1.
NP Chart

The big idea The np chart plots the number of defective units in each subgroup, when every subgroup has the same sample size n . It is the same idea as the p chart, but in counts instead of proportions, which is easier for operators to plot and read. Center line = np̄ Limits = np̄ ± 3√[ np̄(1 − p̄) ] A negative LCL is set to 0 , and the UCL cannot exceed n. Worked example Each day, exactly 200 delivery receipts are audited; on average 4% are defective (missing signature or wrong count). np̄ = 200 × 0.04 = 8 defective receipts per day. Limits: 8 ± 3√(8 × 0.96) = 8 ± 3 × 2.77 = 8 ± 8.31 → UCL 16.3 , LCL −0.31 → 0 . A day with 18 defective receipts is out of control. p or np? Constant sample size → np chart (or p chart; both work). Varying sample size → p chart (np counts are not comparable when n changes). Check yourself Constant sample of 200, counting defective units: which chart? n = 50, p̄ = 0.10. Compute np̄ and the limits. Why not use an np chart when sample sizes vary? Show answers np chart. np̄ = 5; 5 ± 3√(5 × 0.9) = 5 ± 6.36: UCL 11.4, LCL 0. Counts from different sample sizes are not comparable; a bigger sample naturally has more defectives. Key takeaways np chart: number of defectives, constant sample size. np̄ ± 3√[np̄(1 − p̄)]; negative LCL → 0. Varying n → p chart.
Xbar-S Chart

The big idea When subgroups are larger than about 10 , the range becomes a poor measure of spread (it uses only the two extreme values and ignores everything in between). The Xbar-S chart replaces the range with the subgroup standard deviation (s) , which uses every value. Xbar chart : subgroup averages. S chart : subgroup standard deviations. Formulas Xbar chart: X̿ ± A₃ × s̄ S chart: UCL = B₄ × s̄, LCL = B₃ × s̄ σ estimate = s̄ ÷ c₄ Constants for n = 10 (from the IASSC table): A₃ = 0.975, B₃ = 0.284, B₄ = 1.716 . The constant c₄ (0.9727 for n = 10) is not in the sheet's table. (An older 2010 version of the reference sheet misprinted B₄ for both S chart limits; version 1.4.2 is correct: LCL uses B₃.) Worked example Subgroups of 10 package weights: X̿ = 50.0 kg, s̄ = 1.2 kg. Xbar chart: 50.0 ± 0.975 × 1.2 = 50.0 ± 1.17 → UCL 51.17, LCL 48.83 . S chart: UCL = 1.716 × 1.2 = 2.06 ; LCL = 0.284 × 1.2 = 0.34 . σ ≈ 1.2 ÷ 0.9727 ≈ 1.23 kg . Unlike the R chart for small n, the S chart for n = 10 has a positive LCL. A point below it means variation dropped unusually, which is worth understanding (and keeping, if it is a real improvement). Check yourself Subgroups of 15 readings: which chart? Which constant replaces A₂ for the Xbar chart here? Why is s better than R for large subgroups? Show answers Xbar-S. A₃. The range uses only two values; s uses all of them, so it estimates spread more efficiently. Key takeaways Subgroups above about 10: Xbar-S. Xbar: X̿ ± A₃s̄. S: UCL B₄s̄, LCL B₃s̄. σ = s̄ ÷ c₄ (c₄ not on the sheet).
CuSum Chart

Why this matters Ordinary (Shewhart) control charts are great at catching large, sudden changes but slow to notice small, persistent shifts: a process that drifts 0.5σ or 1σ and stays there can sit inside the limits for a long time. The CuSum chart is designed for exactly that. The big idea CuSum stands for cumulative sum . Instead of plotting each value, it plots the running total of deviations from a target : Sₙ = Σ (xᵢ − T) (the IASSC sheet's standardized form divides by σ: Sₙ = (1 ÷ σ) × Σ(xᵢ − T)) If the process is on target, deviations are randomly positive and negative and cancel out: the CuSum wanders around zero. If the process shifts even slightly above target, every deviation tends to be positive, and the CuSum climbs steadily . The slope reveals the shift. Individuals chart: small 0.8σ shift at point 15 hides inside the limits CuSum of the same data: the running total climbs clearly shift starts The same data: a small shift that hides inside the individuals chart's limits shows as a steady climb in the CuSum. Design parameters Practical CuSum charts (the "tabular" CuSum used by software) use: A target T (the desired mean). A reference value k , often about 0.5σ : deviations smaller than k are ignored as noise. It is tuned to detect a shift of about 2k. A decision interval h , often about 4 to 5σ : when the cumulative sum exceeds h, the chart signals. These are design choices, not fixed thresholds. Strengths and weaknesses Faster than Shewhart charts at detecting small, sustained shifts (about 0.5 to 1.5σ). Slower than Shewhart charts for large, sudden shifts. Harder to explain to operators. Check yourself What does a CuSum chart plot? What does a steadily rising CuSum mean? When is CuSum better than an ordinary control chart? Show answers The running total of deviations from a target. The process mean has shifted above the target and stayed there. For detecting small, persistent shifts. Key takeaways CuSum plots cumulative deviations from target. Detects small sustained shifts quickly; slower for large shifts. Parameters: target, k ≈ 0.5σ, h ≈ 4 to 5σ.
EWMA Chart

The big idea The EWMA (exponentially weighted moving average) chart also targets small shifts . Each plotted point is a weighted average of the current value and the previous EWMA , so it carries a fading memory of all past data: EWMAₜ = λ × Yₜ + (1 − λ) × EWMAₜ₋₁ λ (lambda) is the weight on the newest value, between 0 and 1. Typical choices are 0.05 to 0.25 (0.2 is common). EWMA₀ starts at the target or the historical mean. Small λ gives a long memory (very smooth, sensitive to small shifts); λ = 1 is just the individuals chart. Control limits are about ±3σ of the EWMA statistic , which is much narrower than for individual values, because averaging smooths out noise. Worked example Target 50, λ = 0.2. New values: 52, 53, 49, 54. EWMA₁ = 0.2 × 52 + 0.8 × 50 = 50.40 . EWMA₂ = 0.2 × 53 + 0.8 × 50.40 = 50.92 . EWMA₃ = 0.2 × 49 + 0.8 × 50.92 = 50.54 . EWMA₄ = 0.2 × 54 + 0.8 × 50.54 ≈ 51.23 . The EWMA drifts upward steadily as the process runs slightly high, while individual values bounce around. Strengths Detects small shifts , like CuSum. Weights recent data more , which suits processes where recent behavior matters most. Fairly robust to non-normality , because it averages. CuSum vs EWMA vs Shewhart Situation Best chart Large, sudden shifts Shewhart (I-MR, Xbar-R, p…) Small, sustained shifts CuSum or EWMA Non-normal individual data, small shifts EWMA (robust) Minitab applies only the "point beyond the limits" test to these time-weighted charts, not the run rules (5.2.10). Check yourself EWMA₀ = 100, λ = 0.1, Y₁ = 110. What is EWMA₁? What does a smaller λ do? Which charts are best for detecting small sustained shifts? Show answers 0.1 × 110 + 0.9 × 100 = 101. Gives more weight to past data: a smoother chart that is more sensitive to small shifts but slower to react to large ones. CuSum and EWMA. Key takeaways EWMAₜ = λYₜ + (1 − λ)EWMAₜ₋₁; λ typically 0.05 to 0.25. Detects small shifts, weights recent data, robust to non-normality. Small shifts: CuSum/EWMA. Large shifts: Shewhart charts.
Control Methods

Why this matters A control chart is only useful if people know how to read it and what to do. This topic covers the anatomy of a chart, the rules for spotting special causes, the right reactions, and the other (non-chart) methods that keep a process under control. Chart anatomy and zones Every Shewhart chart has a center line and limits at ±3σ of the plotted statistic (see the diagram in 5.2.1). The space between is divided into zones on each side: Zone C : center line to 1σ. Zone B : 1σ to 2σ. Zone A : 2σ to 3σ. Remember that σ here is the standard deviation of the plotted statistic . For an Xbar chart, that is σ ÷ √n, not σ of individual values. Rules for special causes A point beyond the limits is the classic signal, but patterns inside the limits also signal special causes, because random variation rarely produces them. 1 point beyond a limit 9 in a row on one side 6 in a row steadily rising Red points mark the signal. Each means: look for a special cause. All three charts signal a special cause, even though two of them have every point inside the limits. Western Electric rules (the original set): 1 point beyond 3σ (outside a control limit). 2 of 3 consecutive points beyond 2σ on the same side (in zone A or beyond). 4 of 5 consecutive points beyond 1σ on the same side (zone B or beyond). 8 in a row on the same side of the center line. Nelson rules (used by Minitab as its "tests for special causes"): 1 point more than 3σ from the center line. 9 points in a row on the same side of the center line. 6 points in a row all increasing or all decreasing (trend). 14 points in a row alternating up and down. 2 out of 3 points more than 2σ from the center line (same side). 4 out of 5 points more than 1σ from the center line (same side). 15 points in a row within 1σ (zone C) on either side: suspiciously little variation, often stratification (subgroups mixing sources, so limits are too wide). 8 points in a row more than 1σ from the center line on either side, none in zone C: often a mixture of two processes. The current AIAG-VDA SPC manual (2026) lists a similar set (beyond 3σ, 2 of 3 beyond 2σ, 4 of 5 beyond 1σ, 9 in a row, 15 within 1σ). Western Electric (8 in a row) and Nelson (9 in a row) are different rule systems , not a contradiction. Use whichever set a question gives, and do not mix them. The false-alarm trade-off With 3σ limits, each independent point has about a 0.27% chance of falling outside by pure chance (about 1 false alarm in 370 points). Every extra rule adds sensitivity to real patterns, and adds false alarms. Use the rules that make sense for the process, not all of them by default. Reacting correctly No signal (only common-cause variation) : leave the process alone . Adjusting it is tampering and increases variation (2.4.2). If the stable process is not good enough, improve the system (a project). Signal (special cause) : investigate what happened at that time, contain any affected product if needed, fix the cause, prevent recurrence, and document it (the response plan, 5.3.3). When to recalculate limits Do not recalculate limits just because a point is out of control. That hides the signal. Investigate first. Recalculate only after a verified, deliberate process change (an improvement), once the new process has a stable baseline (Phase I again). And note: "all points within the limits" does not prove control. A point inside the 3σ limits can still violate a run or trend rule. Control limits are not specification limits A process can be in control (stable) but still produce out-of-spec product (not capable). A point can be out of control (a special cause) while still within specification . They answer different questions (2.4.1), and the responses differ (5.3.3). Other control methods Charts are one control among several. The Control phase also relies on: Standard work and documented procedures . Training (and retraining when procedures change). Mistake-proofing (5.1.3). Visual management (5.1.1). Audits of whether controls are being followed. Process-owner handoff with a control plan (5.3.2). Worked example An Xbar chart of daily average dock time (minutes) shows all points inside the limits, but the last 9 points are all above the center line. Rule: 9 in a row on one side (Nelson rule 2; it also exceeds Western Electric's 8). Meaning: the process mean has probably shifted upward. Action: investigate what changed when the run started (new staffing pattern? new customer mix?), not "everything is fine because no point is outside the limits". Common mistakes and exam traps Patterns inside the limits can be signals. Western Electric 8 in a row; Nelson 9 in a row. Do not mix. Common cause: leave alone, improve the system. Special cause: investigate and react. Do not recalculate limits to make a signal disappear. Control limits ≠ spec limits. More rules = more false alarms. Check yourself Which zone lies between 1σ and 2σ from the center line? Six consecutive points each higher than the last: which Nelson test? A chart shows 15 points in a row hugging the center line. What might be wrong? A point falls outside the UCL. What should happen to the control limits? A stable process produces 3% out-of-spec parts. Is it in control? Is it capable? Show answers Zone B. Test 3 (trend: 6 in a row increasing or decreasing). Stratification: subgroups probably mix different sources, so the limits are too wide. Nothing yet: investigate the special cause. Recalculate only after a verified process change and a new stable baseline. In control (stable), but not capable. Key takeaways Limits at ±3σ of the plotted statistic; zones C (0 to 1σ), B (1 to 2σ), A (2 to 3σ). Western Electric: beyond 3σ, 2 of 3 beyond 2σ, 4 of 5 beyond 1σ, 8 in a row. Nelson adds 9 in a row, 6 trending, 14 alternating, 15 in zone C, 8 outside zone C. About a 0.27% false-alarm rate per point; more rules, more false alarms. Common cause: leave alone. Special cause: investigate. Do not recompute limits to hide signals. Control methods also include standard work, training, mistake-proofing, audits and handoff.
Cost Benefit Analysis

Why this matters Every control costs something: inspection time, audits, training, monitoring software, calibration. A project that adds expensive controls everywhere can eat its own savings. Cost-benefit analysis decides which controls are worth keeping, and proves that the project's gains are protected at a sensible cost. The big idea Controls exist to prevent regression : the process sliding back to its old performance. So the question is: Is the cost of sustaining this control less than the expected cost of losing the improvement without it? Cost of the control : setup (one-time) plus ongoing costs: people's time for checks and audits, data collection, equipment, training, maintenance. Benefit of the control : the savings it protects (hard and soft, 1.3.3), multiplied by how likely regression would be without it. Worked example A project cut damage claims from $480,000 to $200,000 a year, saving $280,000. Proposed controls: Control Annual cost Weekly load-securing audits $15,000 Annual driver refresher training $10,000 Monthly claims p chart and review $3,000 Total $28,000 Without controls, the team estimates half the gain would erode within a year: $140,000 at risk. Spending $28,000 a year to protect $140,000 (or more) is clearly justified: the expected net benefit is $112,000 a year. If a further control (say, cameras on every dock at $150,000 a year) would only protect an extra $20,000, it is not justified. Using ROI and payback The same tools as project selection (1.3.3) apply: ROI = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost. Payback = investment ÷ annual net benefit. Include ongoing costs , which are easy to forget, and both hard and soft benefits (the soft ones, such as customer retention, can be decisive even when hard numbers are close). Choosing the cheapest effective control Controls range from cheap to expensive, and strong to weak. Prefer, roughly in this order: Mistake-proofing (5.1.3): built in, little ongoing cost, very strong. Standard work, visual controls and training : low cost, moderately strong. SPC monitoring : moderate cost, catches drift early. Inspection and audits : ongoing labor cost, catches problems after the fact. Check yourself What does a control protect against? A control costs $50,000 a year and protects an expected $30,000 of savings. Justified? Name two ongoing costs of a control. Why is mistake-proofing often the best-value control? Show answers Regression: the process sliding back to its old performance. Not on these numbers (cost exceeds the protected benefit), unless important soft benefits or risks justify it. Any two of: audit time, data collection, training, monitoring software, calibration, maintenance. It is strong (prevents the error) and usually has low ongoing cost once installed. Key takeaways Compare the cost of sustaining a control with the benefit it protects. Use ROI and payback, including ongoing costs and soft benefits. Prefer strong, low-cost controls: mistake-proofing first, inspection last.
Elements of the Control Plan

Why this matters When the project team hands over, the gains depend on the people who run the process every day. The control plan is the document that tells them exactly what to watch, how, how often, and what to do if something goes wrong. Without it, improvements fade. The big idea A control plan is a table (one row per controlled characteristic) that documents how the process will be kept in its improved state. It is the main Control-phase deliverable and is handed to the process owner . The columns Element What it says Example Process step Where in the process Load securing Characteristic (CTQ or critical X) What is controlled: an output (Y) or a key input (X) Strap tension; claims per 1,000 loads Specification / target The requirement At least 4 straps per 10 ft of freight Measurement method How it is measured (with a capable measurement system, 2.3) Visual check with photo; claims system report Sample size How many 5 trailers per shift Frequency How often Every shift; monthly for claims Control method The tool used Checklist and photo; p chart of claims Owner (who) Who does it Dock lead; terminal manager Reaction plan What to do if out of control or out of spec See response plan R-07 Document reference Where the procedure lives SOP-LS-03 Remember monitor the Y, control the X's (1.1.4): control plans usually include the critical X's that drive the result, not only the output. Supporting items Standard operating procedures (SOPs) and work instructions updated to the new method. Training records : everyone doing the work trained on the new method. Process owner named and accepting responsibility. Transition plan : how and when the project team hands over (often with a period of joint monitoring). A living document The control plan belongs to the process owner , not the project team, and it is updated whenever the process, specifications or measurement methods change. It should match the current FMEA (2.1.4): the high-risk failure modes in the FMEA should have controls in the plan. Worked example: what is wrong? A control plan row reads: "Claims per 1,000 loads; target under 1.5; p chart; monthly." What is missing? No owner : who reviews the chart? No reaction plan : what happens if the chart signals? No measurement method or sample size details , and no document reference. A plan without an owner and a reaction plan is the most common weakness: the data gets collected and nobody acts on it. Check yourself Who owns the control plan after the project closes? Name five columns of a control plan. A control plan lists what to measure and how often, but not what to do when a problem appears. What is missing? Why should a control plan include critical X's, not just the Y? Show answers The process owner. Any five of: process step, characteristic, specification/target, measurement method, sample size, frequency, control method, owner, reaction plan, document reference. The reaction plan. Controlling the inputs prevents problems; watching only the output finds them after they happen. Key takeaways The control plan documents how gains are held: step, characteristic, spec, measurement, sample size, frequency, control method, owner, reaction plan, document reference. Supported by SOPs, training, a named process owner and a transition plan. A living document owned by the process owner, aligned with the FMEA.
Elements of the Response Plan

Why this matters Detecting a problem is only half of control. The response plan (reaction plan) makes sure that when a chart signals or a product fails specification, people act quickly, correctly and consistently, instead of improvising, ignoring it, or tampering. The big idea A response plan is a pre-agreed set of steps, written before problems happen, that says: when this trigger occurs, who does what, in what order, and when to escalate. The elements Trigger : the exact condition that starts the plan. An out-of-control signal (which rules, 5.2.10), an out-of-spec result, an audit failure. Immediate containment : stop the damage. Hold suspect product, stop the process if needed, segregate affected loads, notify the next step or the customer. Who acts : the named person responsible for each step, and their authority (for example, the operator may stop the line). Investigation : find the special cause. What changed? Use quick tools: 5 Whys, checking recent changes, stratifying the data. Corrective action : fix the cause, and prevent recurrence (update the FMEA, mistake-proof if possible). Escalation : when to involve the supervisor, the process owner, quality or management (for example, if not resolved within 2 hours, or if the customer is affected). Documentation : record what happened, the cause found and the action taken (on the chart and in a log), so patterns become visible over time. Resume : the criteria for restarting normal operation and releasing held product. Product disposition For out-of-spec product, the plan states the decision rules: use as is (with approval), rework , sort and inspect , return to supplier , or scrap , and who may decide. Out of control vs out of spec These are different situations and need different responses: Situation Meaning Response Out of control, within spec A special cause has appeared, though product still meets requirements Investigate and remove the special cause before it causes defects In control, out of spec The stable process is not capable No special cause to find; contain product and improve the system (reduce variation or recenter, a project) Out of control and out of spec A special cause is producing defects Contain product immediately, investigate, correct In control and within spec Normal Leave it alone (no tampering) Worked example A p chart of late deliveries shows a point above the UCL on Tuesday. Trigger : point beyond UCL (rule 1). Contain : dispatch reviews Wednesday's at-risk loads and calls affected customers. Investigate (dispatch supervisor): Tuesday's data show most late loads came from one terminal, where a dock door was out of service. Correct : reroute loads while the door is repaired; add dock-door status to the morning huddle. Escalate : not needed (resolved within the day). Document : annotate the chart ("Dock door 4 down") and log the incident. Resume : normal operation once the door is repaired and the next day's rate is back within limits. Common mistakes and exam traps After an out-of-control signal: contain, investigate, correct, document. Not "adjust and move on", and not "recalculate the limits". Out of control is not the same as out of spec. A response plan names who acts and when to escalate. Stable but out of spec needs a system change , not a hunt for a special cause. Check yourself List the main steps after an out-of-control signal. A stable process makes some out-of-spec parts. Is there a special cause to investigate? Why should a response plan be written before problems occur? What is containment? A point is out of control but the product is within spec. Should anything be done? Show answers Contain, investigate, correct (and prevent recurrence), escalate if needed, document, resume. No. The process is stable; the problem is the system (capability). Contain product and improve the process. So the response is fast, consistent and correct under pressure, with clear ownership. Immediate action to stop the problem spreading: holding suspect product, stopping the process, notifying those affected. Yes. Investigate the special cause before it produces defects. Key takeaways Response plan: trigger, containment, who acts, investigation, corrective action, escalation, documentation, resume. Includes disposition rules for out-of-spec product. Out of control ≠ out of spec: investigate special causes; improve the system for capability problems.
